articles.title_orig: China draft rules offer millions of gig workers employment contracts
articles.title_zh: China draft rules offer millions of gig workers employment contracts
articles.content_orig:
They have few protections and face long working hours for relatively low pay.
(AFP) â Millions of gig workers in China could benefit from stronger labor protections under proposed rules announced Thursday that would require online platforms to sign employment contracts with them.
The draft measures from China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security require internet platforms that “recruit, organize, and manage workers … to complete platform work tasks” to enter into standardized employment agreements with their workers.
The draft, open for public comment until Nov. 8, could affect millions of takeout delivery drivers, parcel couriers and ride-hailing drivers who often lack formal labor contracts.
Online platforms, including tech giants such as Alibaba, Meituan and DiDi, would also be prohibited from encouraging gig workers to register as individual business owners to avoid signing employment contracts with them.
Currently, many gig workers in China work as freelancers or through subcontractors.
The world’s second-largest economy had 280 million flexible workers in 2025, according to a report by the China New Employment Forms Research Centre, a think tank.
They have few protections and face long working hours for relatively low pay in sectors such as food delivery, which are characterized by fierce competition and price wars between rival online platforms.
Under the proposed rules, gig workers would be entitled to the minimum wage, extra pay for work on public holidays and “appropriate rest.”
Platforms would also have to explain their management algorithms to workers, according to the proposal. Decisions to stop orders or ban worker accounts could not be made by algorithms alone and would require manual review.
In April, Chinese authorities said they would strengthen management of the gig economy through better legal protections for workers, targeting “substantial progress” in working conditions within three years.

articles.title_orig: Genre-defying Canadian poet Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
articles.title_zh: Genre-defying Canadian poet Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
articles.content_orig:
Most prestigious literature prize goes to Canadian known for genre-crossing works such as Autobiography of Red
‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne Carson
Where to start with: Anne Carson
The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded to the Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson, the Swedish Academy has announced.
The academy cited the author’s “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”.
The Nobel prize, regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, is awarded for a lifetime body of work. The winner receives 12m Swedish kronor (£900,000).
Ingrid Carlberg, the permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had told Carson of the award on the phone shortly before the news broke. “She had time to tell me that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind,” Carlberg said. “She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”
Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson is known for work that moves freely between poetry, prose and translation , drawing heavily on the literature and mythology of the ancient Greek world. She has been a professor of classics at various institutions including Princeton, New York University and McGill University in Montreal. She is the 19th woman to win, out of 123 literature laureates.
Carson’s first book, Eros the Bittersweet, was published in 1986 and combined literary criticism with an exploration of desire and the ancient Greek tradition.
Her best-known work is Autobiography of Red, a 1998 novel in verse inspired by the fragments of the ancient Greek poet Stesichorus. It reimagines the myth of Geryon, the red-winged monster killed by Herakles, as the story of a modern teenage boy navigating heartbreak and desire.
In 2001, she became the first woman to win the TS Eliot prize, for her collection The Beauty of the Husband. She has also been awarded Guggenheim and MacArthur fellowships.
The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, congratulated the poet on X after the announcement. “With wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own, Canadian poet Anne Carson has reimagined the classics. She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature,” he said, adding that it was a “proud moment for Canada”.
David Leonard, the executive director of the Writers’ Trust of Canada , said: “Anne is such a brilliant writer. Her work is broad, but also extremely smart.” Calling Carson’s work “intoxicating”, he said her four-decade career had resulted in a peerless collection of poems and essays. “They’re beautiful, they’re smart, they’re true and they are humane. It’s exactly what we need in our writing.”
Carson’s work has attracted praise from fellow writers including Susan Sontag, who once said: “She is one of the few writers writing in English that I would read anything she wrote. If there’s a magazine that has something of hers in it, I buy it automatically.”
Anders Olsson, the chair of the Swedish Academy’s Nobel Committee for Literature, praised Carson for work that had “broken away from lyrical poetry bound to the narrative self and inspired new forms of contemporary literature”. He said: “This method of writing leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms.”
Carson’s books have ranged widely in form. Men in the Off Hours combined verse essays, poems, epitaphs and prose about artists and historical figures, and won the inaugural Griffin poetry prize in 2001. Decreation, another eclectic work, brought together poetry, essays and an opera.
Nox, published in 2010, is particularly characteristic of Carson’s avant-garde approach to literature – the book takes the form of an accordion-fold box containing a reproduction of a notebook Carson made after the death of her brother. Her later works include Red Doc> and Float.
In a Guardian review of Red Doc>, Sarah Crown wrote: “To engage so fluidly, so originally and compellingly, with a story first told more than 3,000 years ago, is astonishing: her ambition is one thing; the fact that it is so completely achieved is, frankly, something else.”
Much of Carson’s work has emerged from her fascination with language itself. The Swedish Academy noted: “Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” adding that Carson had identified the etymology of words as “the starting point for all her work”.
Asked why she continually moved between forms, Carson said in an interview: “Boredom, I guess. There is a restlessness. There are a lot of forms to try.”
She has acknowledged the difficulties that come with her experimental style. “[My work] does fall apart a lot,” she said in a 2018 interview. “It gets just too weird for anyone to care about reading, or else it gets diluted into a sort of parody of itself.”
Ira Wells, the president of PEN Canada, said Carson’s win felt “particularly significant at a moment in which Canada and Europe are strengthening cultural ties amidst broader global disruption”. He added: “On an aesthetic level, Carson’s verse vibrates on profound human frequencies, at a moment in which more and more language is formulated by machines.”
Carson has generally kept her personal life out of interviews. However, in an August 2024 article for the London Review of Books, she disclosed that she had been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.
The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded on 118 previous occasions since 1901. Recent laureates include Annie Ernaux, Bob Dylan, Abdulrazak Gurnah, Louise Glück, Peter Handke and Olga Tokarczuk. Last year’s recipient was the Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai, known for his dystopic and avant-garde writing.
Carson, 76, will formally receive the medal and diploma in a ceremony in Stockholm in December.

articles.title_orig: The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft from a green card program, alleging fraud
articles.title_zh: The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft from a green card program, alleging fraud
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Department of Labor announced it would suspend Microsoft and Adobe from its Permanent Labor Certification program on Thursday, Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said, as the Trump administration continues to take aim at immigration and foreign hiring programs ahead of November's midterm elections.
Sonderling said the Labor Department won't accept or process any new applications under the program for a host of companies, including Cognizant, Infosys, Capgemini, Tata, Wipro and HCL.
The secretary said Adobe and Microsoft were also suspended "due to multiple active federal investigations."
"Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost 3 million foreign workers. They've received over 230,000 H-1B visas approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers," Sonderling said.
Vice President JD Vance criticized Microsoft specifically, pointing to the firm's 6,000 layoffs in 2025. Vance claimed that the company "replaced" those workers with people on H-1B visas.
"So we're going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we're also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first," Vance said.
Microsoft responded to Vance's claims and defended its hiring practices in a statement Thursday, saying "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans."
"Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees," the company said.
President Donald Trump is set to award the National Medal of Science to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and other leading technology CEOs on Thursday at the same summit where the suspension announcement was made.
Nadella is from India and moved to the U.S. in 1988. He joined Microsoft in 1992.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su are also being honored at Thursday's medal ceremony. Each of the leaders immigrated to the U.S. Musk was born in South Africa and Su and Huang were born in Taiwan.
"It's one thing if you want to bring in a person like Elon Musk," Vance said. "I think 99% of American citizens look at somebody like Elon Musk or Lisa Su, the CEO of AMD, and they say, obviously, if that person wants to come in and build something great in the United States of America, we support that."
Tech giants like Microsoft, Google , Amazon and Apple have been among the top sponsors of H-1B visas for decades. This year, Amazon had the highest number of petitions at 35,426 workers, followed by Cognizant and EY, according to 2026 data from Levels.fyi .
Microsoft was a close fourth at 21,706 petitions for 2026, with a median base salary of $180,710.
Microsoft said that petitions were only filed for workers "who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," and said Microsoft's wages for H-1B workers were among the highest of all H-1B filings.
CNBC has reached out to Adobe for comment.

articles.title_orig: Margaret Hamilton dies at 90. Her programming helped astronauts reach the moon.
articles.title_zh: Margaret Hamilton dies at 90. Her programming helped astronauts reach the moon.
articles.content_orig:
Moment Margaret Hamilton receives Presidential Medal of Freedom
The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90.
Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering".
Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September.
"To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream.
Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division.
It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon.
"I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019.
In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring.
The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved.
But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT.
The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her.
Hamilton with the printed computer code in 1969
In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel.
At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space".
Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958.
She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree.
From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts.
"We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media.
"Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT.

articles.title_orig: At least 30 dead in Russian bus strike as Moscow closes in on Ukraine’s ‘fortress belt’
articles.title_zh: At least 30 dead in Russian bus strike as Moscow closes in on Ukraine’s ‘fortress belt’
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv's allies needed to take "concrete action"
At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern front line city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.
Authorities said three people were also killed in the village of Bilenke, part of the Kramatorsk community.
Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Moscow is trying to seize as part of Russian President Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said: "This strike will not go without our response."
In a post on Telegram, he said: "Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this. React harshly - exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have caused."
Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack. It follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across Ukraine and a heavy increase in civilian casualties.
According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.
In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who together with Zelensky visited the site of the Russian strike in Pryluky, said the attack showed Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy".
He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war" and told Zelensky the UK would stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes for you to prevail in this conflict".
After the deadly attack on Kramatorsk, Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the eastern front line region to move to safer parts of Ukraine.
Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.
Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine launched by Putin in 2022 - a claim rejected by Ukraine and its allies as baseless.
Donbas is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.
For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.
Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall.  In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.
Kramatorsk city council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".
"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it said.
Children killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 22 in block of flats
Civilians told to flee Ukraine's fortress cities as Russia bids to control Donbas
Russia has in recent weeks been launching constant air raids on the capital Kyiv, with sirens ringing virtually non-stop.
On Thursday, Kyiv police said four people were killed and two injured in the latest Russian attack on the city.
The attacks are forcing schoolchildren out of classes into underground shelters, shuttering businesses, and disrupting public transport.
Moscow's strikes on Ukraine's key infrastructure, particularly on its energy grid, are causing power outages already and are even affecting the water supply. Local water authorities in the capital warned on Thursday that pressure was dropping across the city's right bank due to power cuts.
Kyiv's metro network - which millions of residents rely on - on Thursday briefly halted all its train traffic due to a voltage drop from "external power centres". Trains later started moving again - but at greater intervals, local officials said.
Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine".
Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.
Such warnings are for now one of the only defences Ukrainians have.
Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little  chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics.
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.
On Thursday, Russian state-run media reported that a number of websites in the country were inaccessible following a Ukrainian drone attack on a data centre of Yandex - Russia's largest search engine.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias live updates: Gulf Coast braces for dangerous storm
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias live updates: Gulf Coast braces for dangerous storm
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Mandatory evacuations have been announced and schools closed across parts of coastal Florida after Isaias intensified into the Atlantic season's first hurricane , advancing towards the US Gulf Coast Thursday, the National Hurricane Center said.
Forecasters warned that Isaias could deliver destructive hurricane-force winds to the Florida Panhandle, alongside southern Alabama and southern Mississippi.
“A life-threatening storm surge is expected from the Mouth of the Mississippi River to Suwannee, Florida. Residents in the warning area should follow advice given by local officials and evacuate immediately if told to do so,” the National Weather Service said Thursday.
“Damaging wind gusts are possible over much of central and northern Alabama and portions of western and northern Georgia, especially in areas of higher terrain,’ the NWS continued.
It could also cause a life-threatening storm surge along areas of the northern Gulf Coast, while potentially bringing heavy rains of 3 to 7 inches (7 to 18 centimeters) across the central Gulf Coast, according to the hurricane center.
An advisory from the Miami-based hurricane center said the cyclone’s center was positioned approximately 740 kilometres (460 miles) south-southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River , carrying maximum sustained winds of around 121 kph (75 mph).
After the storm initially formed earlier Wednesday in the warm waters of eastern Mexico, communities in its potential path moved quickly to prepare with landfall forecast as soon as Friday evening.
Some Gulf oil wells paused production, and at least four Florida school districts canceled classes for later in the week while Okaloosa County announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. Governors in Florida and Alabama declared a state of emergency for dozens of counties.
The National Weather Service told communities from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to Gulf County, Florida, to prepare for the possibility of “long-duration power outages.”
Isaias is developing more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season, nearly tying a 121-year-old record for the area’s latest-forming hurricane. According to the National Weather Service, the record dates to 1905, when the year’s first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.
The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Tropical Storm Simon formed Wednesday off Mexico.
Isaias is expected to strike along a wide swath of coastline that’s very familiar with major hurricanes.
One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15 per cent of crude pumped annually in the U.S.
As of Wednesday about 25 per cent of the oil production in the region was temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf's 371 manned oil platforms were evacuated.
With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday’s college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama, a game President Donald Trump has planned to attend.
In Alabama, the cities of Gulf Shores and Orange Beach issued a statement encouraging people in low-lying areas to voluntarily evacuate.
Gulf Shores resident Maranie Adams gathered water and other supplies as her family moved belongings, including a hot tub motor, to higher ground. Her family planned to ride out the storm at home, roughly a half-mile from shore, sheltering indoors alongside their flock of chickens.
“We’re having to get crates to bring them into the house so they don’t blow away,” Adams said. “It’s going to be noisy.”
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties, while Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared one for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The state also planned to deploy a Miami-based urban search and rescue task force.
In Pensacola, electric utilities were pre-positioning crews to quickly repair any power outages. City officials provided sand for residents to fill sandbags to protect their homes against flooding. And Mayor D.C. Reeves urged people to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.
“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Oil Rises, Nasdaq Slips on Fresh Tanker Attack
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Oil Rises, Nasdaq Slips on Fresh Tanker Attack
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices rose sharply Thursday, as Iran ramped up its attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz and Hurricane Isaias threatened U.S. offshore production in the Gulf of Mexico.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, gained 4% to close at $104.28 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures advanced 3.6% to settle at $91.49 per barrel.
Nine tankers have come under attack in and around Hormuz over the past week, jeopardizing the recent recovery in crude oil flows through the strait
Oil prices backed off session highs after President Donald Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the November midterm elections. NBC News, citing unnamed sources, reported earlier that Trump and his national security team were considering renewing strikes in the coming weeks.
Some 9.5 million barrels per day exited Hormuz during the week ended Tuesday, about 30% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to Kpler data. Crude flows from the Middle East, including pipeline workarounds, stood at 16.4 million bpd which is nearly equivalent to prewar levels.
In the Gulf of Mexico, oil companies have shut in about 500,000 bpd, or 25% of offshore production in the region, as Hurricane Isaias churns toward the coasts of Alabama, Mississippi and the Florida panhandle.
Tensions are sharply escalating in the Middle East. Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen fired missiles at airports in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and the city of Abha on Tuesday and Wednesday. Three people died and 36 were injured, according to the state-owned media outlet Al Arabiya.
The Saudis intercepted another volley of ballistic missiles fired Thursday at Riyadh and Khamis Mushait, a spokesperson for the kingdom's military said.
"While flows from the region have largely normalized, the need for US navy escorts, increased costs and logistical frictions and constant risk of being attacked call into question the longer-term feasibility of the flows," said Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"This ultimately warrants a sticky risk premium to remain in pricing," McKay told clients in a Thursday note.

articles.title_orig: Trump: Anyone saying "AI" is "THE ENEMY!" The White House uses it
articles.title_zh: Trump: Anyone saying "AI" is "THE ENEMY!" The White House uses it
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Thursday opened up a new front in his ongoing war against commonly used terms and geographic names by warning that anyone referring to Large Language Models such as OpenAI's ChatGPT or Anthropic's Claude as "Artificial Intelligence" would earn themselves a place on his enemies list.
Writing on Truth Social, he declared that the White House "considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!"
The president's outburst-cum-veiled threat landed just over a week after he signed an executive order directing executive branch agencies to begin referring to artificial intelligence, which is now embedded across the federal government, as "super intelligence" following a lunch with leaders in the AI industry, including Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, Dario Amodei and others.
That widely mocked directive followed bizarre remarks to the U.N. General Assembly in which he declared that the U.S. "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme" for regulating AI and declaring that the technology would be "hereinafter officially called super intelligence" because "use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake."
"It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing," said Trump, who the week before had launched a poll in his Truth Social feed over the weekend asking respondents to vote for either "Super Intelligence," "Superior Intelligence," or "Extreme Intelligence."
The president's latest linguistic ultimatum is the most recent example of his ongoing effort to change the minds of voters — including many of his own supporters — who've increasingly soured on the industry that has tied itself tightly to his unpopular administration.
In recent months, that souring has shown up in nearly every poll that asks about AI. A Quinnipiac University survey of 1,032 registered voters taken late last month found 73 percent oppose "the building of an AI data center in your community," including 55 percent of Republicans, and 79 percent said safety matters more than keeping the United States at the forefront of AI development.
Just 25 percent approve of Trump's handling of the technology against 58 percent who disapprove, and 71 percent said they'd be more likely to back a candidate who supports "stricter guardrails" on it — a figure that includes a majority of Republicans, at 52 percent, and nearly three-quarters of independents.
A separate Fox News poll of 1,211 registered voters conducted earlier in September put overall opinion of AI at 37 percent favorable to 60 percent unfavorable, a net rating of minus 23 that has worsened from minus 11 in April and minus 9 in July. The same survey found voters trust Democrats over Republicans to handle data centers by 14 points, and that among those who oppose the facilities anywhere, Democrats lead the generic ballot by at least 19 points.
Trump's demand for widespread adoption of "super intelligence" in lieu of AI comes just over a month after his last attempt at linguistic coercion, an executive order directing the executive branch to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America."
The order to rename one of the five Great Lakes along the U.S.-Canada border came in a fit of rage over his ongoing trade war with Ottawa and echoed a similar move from early in his second term when he attempted to unilaterally rename the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America."
While the president does have the authority to direct how the government recognizes the names of places and landmarks, he cannot force Canada or individual citizens on either side of the border to follow his preferred naming conventions.
The same goes for use of the term "super intelligence." He can direct the government to use it but he cannot force Americans — or anyone else — to use his preferred terminology.
The Independent has reached out to NVIDIA, Palantir, Meta, OpenAI, Google, Tesla and Anthropic regarding whether the companies have any plans to use the president's new terminology in promotional materials or other customer communications; none responded.
But the White House has touted a short list of tech CEOs who'd used the phrase, including Elon Musk and NVIDIA's Jensen Huang.
Complicating the matter, the word superintelligence already means an AI system that surpasses human intellect and ability across multiple domains in couding reasoning, social skills and scientific research — a step toward the kind of rogue AI that many fear, sparking the calls for guardrails and kill switches.

articles.title_orig: Europe And China Confront Growing Trade Tensions
articles.title_zh: Europe And China Confront Growing Trade Tensions
articles.content_orig:
Europe’s top trade negotiators are meeting with Chinese officials in Beijing this Thursday and Friday, October 8th and 9th, to discuss the European Union’s growing trade deficit with China, which runs at €1 billion per day, as well as other agenda items, according to The New York Times.
Since June, the EU and China have been locked in tense trade negotiations, with the EU concerned about the overwhelming flood of Chinese imports, which, according to Politico, is putting pressure on domestic manufacturers and forcing plant closures and layoffs. “I think our Chinese partners understood that this has direct implications on the future of emblematic European companies,” Maroš Šefčovič, European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security, said.
Additionally, according to Reuters, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament last month that the trade imbalance had reached a tipping point and that Europe would use all the tools at its disposal to rebalance the relationship.
The forthcoming meetings will include talks regarding China’s growing automobile export industry to Europe. Imports of plug-in hybrid automobiles into the EU have increased by 86%, with a 20% decline in prices, while imports of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) have risen by 40%, according to Reuters.
Among other items on the agenda is the renewable energy industry, specifically wind turbines, as well as Europe’s growing dependency on China for rare earth minerals and China’s increasing restrictions on their export. These minerals are crucial to the production of automobiles, drones, lasers, semiconductors, jetliners, electronics, and other advanced technologies.
As the EU and China approach a crucial turning point this week, significant economic consequences loom for both sides. For the EU, the primary concern is preventing further deindustrialisation and the potential loss of large numbers of domestic jobs. For China, the challenge lies in restructuring its economic model and reducing its reliance on exports to prevent the closure of key international markets and avoid contributing to a broader global economic crisis. While the EU is making every effort to reach a fair trade deal, as shown in its leaders’ various public statements, the disadvantages pose a notable risk. A potential trade dispute between Europe and China is not improbable and, if it occurs, could devolve into a trade war.
The success of this week’s negotiations will depend on the EU demonstrating political determination to implement concrete policies and measures to protect its economic interests. Taking such action could strengthen the EU’s negotiating position and encourage Chinese leadership to pursue a meaningful agreement, rather than risk the introduction of further measures, as noted by the Friends of Europe think tank. Ideally, a substantial trade deal could provide lasting economic benefits for both sides. Regardless of the outcome of these meetings, one thing is certain: Europe’s relationship with China is changing.

articles.title_orig: John Bisset, Engineer and Educator, Has Died
articles.title_zh: John Bisset, Engineer and Educator, Has Died
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › Headlines
John Bisset, who dedicated his career to the broadcast industry as a skilled engineer, consultant, sales executive and educator, and who authored Radio World’s popular column Workbench, has died after a period of illness. He was 73.
He spent 55 years in the industry. In his later career, Bisset served a who’s who of equipment manufacturers, including Harris Corp., Dielectric, Broadcast Electronics, Nautel, Tieline, Elenos and Telos Alliance.
His technical knowledge made him uniquely qualified to understand product design, but his ability to communicate, his hallmark, not only made him an asset in sales but as a teacher.
And that has been the hallmark of Workbench.
Every edition delivered hands-on, real-world engineering tips where readers learned something new. A testament to Bisset’s ability to build a vast industry network, ideas poured in from readers and contacts who wrote to him regularly.
Tips earned Society of Broadcast Engineers certification credit, again, a testament to Workbench’s standing.
“One of the fun things about this business is the long-term relationships you make, even though you may not talk to these people for years,” Bisset once wrote.
Radio World Editor in Chief Paul McLane said the column will continue, as Bisset wanted, with a new author to be announced later.
The first Workbench appeared in Radio World on Aug. 8, 1990. Bisset, who was Radio World’s technical editor at the time, began authoring the column on Nov. 7 of that year.
In his very first Workbench column, Bisset offered this piece of advice: “I’d like to encourage you to look around your plant to see what you’ve built that could help someone else. We all know of those little insignificant projects that may appear to be ‘just common sense.’ However, we’ve also all been in the position where we can’t see the forest for the trees.”
He authored approximately 920 Workbench columns over his career. Readers routinely told Radio World that Workbench was their favorite section of the publication.
Bisset told Paul McLane in 2020 that he was especially proud of the column’s popularity among programming and management readers. He understood the power of working the ladder.
“Make friends with your group’s personnel manager,” Bisset would write. “They can be an ally.”
Or, take them to your transmitter site, as Bisset once suggested in 2003. “Not only will it give them some perspective of the work you do, but you’ll earn a little more respect when they see the inside of a transmitter or phasor.”
There was, and still is, a resounding consensus among those who worked with him most of just how highly Bisset was regarded.
“He’s the same gentleman I have always known,” Marty Sacks of Telos Alliance told us in 2020. “The service he has provided to so many, including me, all these years through his Workbench columns have truly been a labor of love.”
In 2007, SBE honored Bisset with its Educator of the Year Award .
“John Bisset is an ‘engineer’s engineer,'” Frank Baptista wrote on his LinkedIn page following Bisset’s 2009 installation of an FM and HD Radio transmitter at UMass Dartmouth. “Anyone who has been a broadcast engineer for any length of time will know that he is considered one of the experts in the industry.”
He also understood his role as an advocate. A broadcast engineer, whether full-time or contract-based, is so often misunderstood. The tips and tricks included in Workbench sometimes needed the support of higher management to pull off.
[Email your thoughts about John Bisset so we can share. Send to [email protected] .]
“It is really important to let the people above you, the managers, the owners, know that you are taking care of their facility and are doing a good job with it,” he once told Kirk Harnack’s This Week in Radio Tech. “You’re saving the station money and you’re keeping it on the air at the same time.”
Some of the nuggets made us laugh . An almost understated simplicity was Workbench’s calling card. But every now and then, if you paid close attention, John would insert a prescient piece of wisdom that would resonate through any walk of life.
“Time. In this business, it can control us,” he wrote on May 9, 2007. “If time gets out of hand, it can destroy us.”
As a director of engineering told John early in his career : “’No radio or TV station is worth dying for.’ Your most important job is to work safely and return to your family at the end of the day.”
John often wrote in Workbench that he was fortunate to have been mentored by chief engineers as he worked his way up the ranks. Some of Bisset’s favorite memories included early AM radio improvement efforts and demonstrating Delta Electronics’ Splatter Monitor to the Federal Communications Commission with colleague Tom Wright.
Known as an accomplished chief and contract engineer, Bisset presented and moderated an all-day Radio Transmitter Workshop at the NAB Radio Show from 1997 to 2003, as well as three additional workshops at the spring NAB Show. He was also a frequent presenter at SBE Ennes Workshops around the U.S. and at chapter meetings.
Bisset co-founded Multiphase, a successful broadcast engineering service company, in 1990. He went on to serve as regional RF sales manager for Broadcast Electronics.
At Dielectric, he directed the completion of several product initiatives, including the Dielectric Pattern Viewer. During his tenure at Harris Broadcast, he earned three sales awards and sold 55 transmitters in a single year, setting a company sales record.
In a July 2018 Workbench, Bisset reflected on an early motivator of his fondness for tinkering with equipment.
“With the move by utilities to underground service distributions, you don’t see many aerial cable splicing tents anymore; but as a young boy, I watched a phone tech strap on his climbing spikes and belt and ascend the pole outside my house,” he wrote. “He assembled a platform and tent and crawled inside.
“As a little boy, I found this fascinating. I ran inside and ran a piece of string between the radiator and end table, and built a similar structure with my TinkerToys. A couple of tissues and tape completed my tent — and then I dispatched my plastic army men inside the tent to get to work.”
He was born Oct. 31, 1952 as John Paul Bisset. At age 10, he appeared on Willard Scott’s “Bozo the Clown” show in Washington, D.C. There he got his first taste of broadcasting.
John recalled going home afterward and, with the help of his father, rigging up his own version of Bozo’s TV studio, using cardboard boxes with pie tins as lights dangling from the ceiling. He used several boxes to model as television cameras, alongside empty fruit cans to serve as mock-up lenses.
As McLane detailed in a 2020 feature celebrating Workbench’s 30th anniversary , at age 12, Bisset constructed a pirate Top 40 radio station in his home, using money from his paper route to purchase equipment. He hooked a Lafayette mic mixer up to two turntables and fed a reel-to-reel deck into a Lafayette wireless AM transmitter, covering a two-block radius.
His first professional job came at age 16 at WFAX(AM) in northern Virginia, serving the Washington market.
“Program Director Roy Martin hired me as a summer relief announcer when I was 16,” Bisset recalled. “I worked there part-time through high school and college, and joined the full-time staff after graduation.” Around that time, he received training in technical writing from an influential teacher, professor Joey Horobetz.
Bisset said he was later inspired to become a Christian while playing religious programming on a station. “Becoming a Christian gave me tremendous encouragement,” he would say later.
He was eventually promoted to WFAX chief engineer. That same year, he and fellow engineer Henry Stewart launched a contract engineering business.
He earned an AAS in Broadcast Engineering Technology cum laude from Northern Virginia

articles.title_orig: AEM Brings Industry Leaders Together at World Dairy Expo to Talk Association Involvement and Program Value - AEM | Association of Equipment Manufacturers
articles.title_zh: AEM Brings Industry Leaders Together at World Dairy Expo to Talk Association Involvement and Program Value - AEM | Association of Equipment Manufacturers
articles.content_orig:
The dairy equipment industry faces no shortage of challenges, from emerging technologies and regulatory hurdles to shifting customer demands and evolving market conditions. Addressing those challenges often requires more than individual company expertise – it requires collaboration from across the industry.
That spirit of collaboration was on full display as AEM's dairy-focused committees gathered during the 59th World Dairy Expo held last week in Madison, Wisconsin. The meetings brought together dairy equipment manufacturers and industry leaders to discuss market trends, committee priorities, and the value of continued engagement in AEM programs and initiatives. AEM hosted its Dairy Equipment Engineering Committee , the Dairy Equipment Leadership Group , and the Dairy Equipment Statistics Committee for meetings during the event.
A highlight of the gathering was a member panel featuring representatives from dairy and agriculture-focused AEM member companies, who shared firsthand perspectives on the benefits of participating in AEM committees and Market Share Statistics programs .
One recurring theme throughout the discussion was the power of industry data to support smarter decision-making.
Attendees noted that participation in AEM's Market Share Statistics programs provides members with access to timely industry intelligence, helping companies better understand market dynamics and evaluate business opportunities. In addition to strengthening individual business planning, the collective data helps create a more complete picture of industry trends.
One member shared how AEM helped demonstrate the value of market intelligence as emerging technologies began gaining traction in the dairy sector.
"When we were struggling to break into an emerging area, AEM used real-world examples from other equipment sectors to show the value of industry data," said GEA Farm Technologies’ Adam Burns. "If organizations are wondering how data can help them, AEM can show people the data and show them how other industries are using it, and they will start to see that value."
Panelists emphasized that access to reliable market data becomes even more impactful when paired with external economic indicators and market intelligence through AEM’s Business Intelligence, allowing companies to make more informed strategic decisions.
Beyond market intelligence, members highlighted the importance of AEM committees as a forum for industry problem-solving.
As new technologies and equipment categories emerge, manufacturers often encounter common challenges, including product classifications, standards questions, and regulatory considerations. Rather than tackling those issues independently, AEM committees create an environment where members can discuss concerns, share experiences, and work toward common solutions.
"When members have questions about new equipment or emerging technologies, we can come together as an industry and find solutions instead of struggling alone," said DeLaval’s Chris Horton. "Trying to solve those challenges collectively benefits everyone."
That collaborative approach helps reduce duplication of effort while supporting the long-term health of both the dairy equipment industry and the producers it serves.
As the dairy industry continues to evolve, collaboration remains one of its greatest strengths. By leveraging data, sharing experiences, and working toward common goals, AEM members are helping build a stronger, more resilient future for dairy equipment manufacturers and the producers they serve. The conversations held in Madison demonstrated that when the industry comes together, the result is more than valuable insight. It is a collective commitment to advancing the success of the dairy sector for years to come.
For more information on AEM’s agriculture services, contact AEM’s Austin Gellings at agellings@aem.org . For more information on AEM Market Share Statistics, contact AEM's Jacquelyn LaFavor at jlafavor@aem.org .

articles.title_orig: Highest Mortgage Rates in 3 Years Chills the Housing Market
articles.title_zh: Highest Mortgage Rates in 3 Years Chills the Housing Market
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home more challenging at a time when housing prices are already high. Nam Y. Huh/AP hide caption
Carrie Goldstein's dream for a new home started with a family reunion at her cousin's home in Milwaukee. The home was old with character and she could walk anywhere from the front door.
"We were kind of in awe and drooling over her walkability," Goldstein says.
It was the lifestyle Goldstein wanted but lacked in her Cleveland suburb, which she says is also pretty walkable – with one major issue.
"There are lots of sidewalks," she says. "But you can't really go anywhere."
She brainstormed with her husband and realized nearby Rocky River was where they wanted to live. It was still a suburb, but with a quaint downtown and the option to walk to Lake Erie.
But as much as she wanted to move, one thing stopped her cold. The mortgage she would have to pay. Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home impossible for many people at a time when housing prices are also sky high.
Goldstein is running into a problem that's affecting many households at a time when people have already been struggling with years of high inflation: The rising cost of borrowing.
Carrie Goldstein stands outside her home on October 4, 2026. Home prices and mortgage rates prevent her from moving. Mike Goldstein hide caption
Bond markets influence all types of borrowing costs across the economy – and as yields have surged to their highest in decades, they've pushed up all kinds of interest rates paid by consumers, from loans for homes to cars and higher education.
And those rates are likely to continue moving up after the Federal Reserve in September raised interest rates for the first time this year – while signaling an additional hike could come this year.
Rate hikes from the Federal Reserve filter through the economy and are meant to slow down consumer and business spending by making people hesitant to take out a more expensive loan to pay for a car or a home – both essential purchases for many people.
"If you need to borrow, boy, it's really not a good time," says John Diamond, senior director of the Center for Tax and Budget Policy at the Baker Institute.
Buying a home is a key example of how households are affected when borrowing costs rise in the economy.
While mortgage rates were falling at the start of this year, they reversed upward after the U.S. war with Iran spooked the bond market by raising worries about inflation. As a result, mortgage rates, which are influenced by the bond markets, have surged this year.
For example, at the current 7.28% level for the average 30-year fixed rate mortgage, a person could end up paying about $900 more a month compared with the 3% pandemic-era rates for a median priced home.
As expected, fewer homeowners are willing or capable of making that financial leap, even if they have long since outgrown their current home. Existing house sales in August were down about 1.2% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors.
It's not just mortgage costs that are making Americans like Goldstein wince.
Alongside her dreams of owning a home in a walkable neighborhood, Goldstein is ready for a new car. Her old one is 11 years old, has 150,000 miles and plenty of quirks. The repair costs are approaching the point where they'll be more than the value of the actual car.
But a four-year loan for a used car is about three percentage points higher compared with the start of 2022, right around when auto loans began to shed their pandemic-era low rates and started climbing up.
"You can't go and get a car for $150 or $180 bucks anymore a month," she says about the car payments she would be facing.
Although so far the Fed has only delivered a modest quarter of a percentage point, it's adding to the higher borrowing costs at a time when households are already dealing with inflation and higher prices for other types of borrowing.
"It's added to higher mortgage payments. Higher student loan payments. Higher prices because of inflation," Diamond says. "That's what makes it really painful."
And that could mean that households could continue to delay any big purchases requiring a loan.
Goldstein is one of them. She says she can afford to wait on the car and house. But eventually she unsubscribed from real estate updates for that walkable suburb.
"It just became more and more disheartening when I did the math," Goldstein says. "It's just not in the cards."

Harvard, Yale, Stanford and MIT are among schools facing scrutiny over alleged visa abuse and Chinese influence on federally funded research
The Trump administration is launching an investigation into nine US universities over alleged J-1 visa fraud, with officials raising concerns about Chinese scholars and the Chinese government.
At a Thursday press conference, Anthony D’Esposito, inspector general of the US Department of Labor, announced what he called a “historic investigation” into J-1 visa fraud at Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, UC Davis, Caltech, Arizona State University and MIT. Subpoenas have been issued to the universities, officials said.
Standing alongside Vice-President J.D. Vance and other White House officials, D’Esposito singled out China, warning that the Chinese government need not break into US research labs if institutions leave their doors open.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq drops, weighed down by AI stock sell-off after OpenAI revenue details disappoint: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq drops, weighed down by AI stock sell-off after OpenAI revenue details disappoint: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Nvidia , Oracle , CoreWeave and other artificial intelligence names sank lower on Thursday after the market learned more details about OpenAI's revenue.
OpenAI told investors that it hit roughly $50 billion in annualized revenue at the end of September, CNBC confirmed, lower than the the $68 billion figure that was widely reported late last month. A person familiar with the matter said the $68 billion figure included gross revenue from OpenAI's partners, which helps investors make a more direct comparison with its chief rival, Anthropic .
The Financial Times was first to report the $50 billion figure.
OpenAI shared an update about its finances in an investor presentation, said the person, who asked not to be named in order to discuss the numbers. In addition to the $50 billion in annualized revenue, OpenAI touted 77% total run rate growth during its third quarter, as well as 107% run rate growth for its enterprise business during the same period, the person said.
The company is under pressure to justify its $852 billion valuation to investors as it gears up for what is widely expected to be a blockbuster IPO. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with regulators in June, and executives have signaled that the company is eyeing a 2027 debut.
In the interim, OpenAI is engaging in early stage discussions with investors about a potential new funding round. The company could raise around $30 billion, as CNBC previously reported, but that figure could change. The round is being driven by investor demand and no term sheet has been finalized yet.
OpenAI closed a historic $122 billion funding round in March, and CFO Sarah Friar told CNBC last week that it is still "very well capitalized."

articles.title_zh: US freezes Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys green-card applications over alleged fraud
articles.content_orig:
The United States government is suspending several major tech companies, including Adobe and Microsoft, from a programme that gives skilled foreign workers a path to permanent residency amid allegations of fraud.
The move comes as the White House ramps up pressure on companies to hire more Americans. “Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” US Vice President JD Vance said at a news conference on Thursday.
Vance claimed that the Redmond, Washington-based tech giant laid off 6,000 American workers while obtaining 6,300 H-1B foreign work visas and almost 3,000 permanent residencies known as green cards.
“You cannot lay off American workers and replace them with foreign indentured servants,” Vance said.
Across the technology sector, there have been more than 131,000 layoffs in 2026 alone, according to Layoffs.fyi, which tracks job cuts across the tech and startup industries.
“When someone comes in, they are completely subordinate to that company. If they lose that job, they have to leave the country.”
Microsoft pushed back on Vance’s claims in a blog post, saying that “80 percent of the visas were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees.”
“The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country,” the company said in the post.
Microsoft is No 5 among US employers when it comes to using H-1B visas, according to data from US Citizenship and Immigration Services. Amazon is No 1.
Adobe did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling also said that several major information technology firms will be suspended from the programme as well. Among them are Indian tech giants Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services.
The H-1B programme has long been a target of supporters of US President Donald Trump who say that the programme undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse.
H-1B visas are meant for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find US workers to fill. Technology companies are the biggest users, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India.
The Department of Labor also said it had uncovered $22bn worth of visa fraud.
“Today we are protecting something far more valuable than any dollar amount. We are protecting the American worker,” Sonderling said.
The news came hours before Trump was to honour Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. India-born Nadella was one of six business leaders to be awarded on Thursday. Five of the leaders were foreign-born, including Tesla boss Elon Musk and Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
During the news conference, officials also announced a crackdown on alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine universities, including MIT, Harvard, Yale, Stanford and Cal State, amid allegations that they brought in international students to undercut US wages. A J-1 visa allows foreign nationals to enter the US temporarily for education or cultural programmes. Universities use these visas to bring in international PhD candidates or scholars.
Vance claimed that when schools employ an American as a researcher, that person earns $20,000 more than someone brought in under a J-1 visa.
Al Jazeera asked for data supporting this claim, but the White House did not respond.
Microsoft’s stock slumped 1.5 percent on the heels of the news, while Adobe was up 2.1 percent in late day trading on Thursday.

articles.title_orig: Curtis Flowers, Mississippi man wrongfully convicted after being tried for the same killings 6 times, dies at 56
articles.title_zh: Curtis Flowers, Mississippi man wrongfully convicted after being tried for the same killings 6 times, dies at 56
articles.content_orig:
Curtis Flowers, a Black man from Mississippi who was wrongfully convicted multiple times when he was tried six times for the same crime by the same prosecutor, has died. He was 56.
Flowers' family confirmed that he died Wednesday at his home in Winona,  Mississippi, attorney Rob McDuff told CBS News on Thursday.
No cause of death was given, said McDuff, who was part of Flowers' legal team. CBS News has reached out to the coroner.
Flowers' struggle with the justice system began in Winona, Mississippi, on a July morning in 1996, when the owner of Tardy Furniture, a bookkeeper, a delivery man and a 16-year-old were shot in the head execution-style.
Flowers briefly worked at the furniture store that summer, but he was let go after he stopped showing up after only three days. Police questioned him after the murders, but didn't arrest him at the time. Flowers later moved to Texas to live with his sister, and he was arrested there in January 1997. He had no prior criminal history.
McDuff previously called Flowers' case "unprecedented in the history of the American legal system."
He told "60 Minutes" in 2021 that the first three convictions against Flowers were overturned "because of the prosecutor's misrepresentation of the evidence to the jury and because of his discrimination in the selection of the jury."
The murder weapon was never found, and there was no DNA or fingerprints linking Flowers to the crime.
In the first trial, an all-White jury convicted him after just an hour of deliberation. Flowers, then 27, was sentenced to death.
His conviction was appealed and overturned. But he was tried five more times for the same crime by the same prosecutor. He had three more convictions overturned on appeal, in addition to two mistrials.
The prosecutor was District Attorney Doug Evans, who in 2010 finally got a conviction to stick in trial six, and Flowers returned to death row.
Then reporters at American Public Media's podcast "In the Dark" looked into the case. Their investigation led witnesses, including one who said Flowers had confessed, to recant their stories.
"In the Dark" reporters and producers also analyzed decades of court data that revealed Evans had a history of excluding Black people from juries at a disproportionate rate. Across all of Flowers' trials, 61 of the 72 jurors were White. All 61 voted to convict.
In 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that Evans and the state of Mississippi had violated Flowers' constitutional rights and overturned his conviction yet again. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that there was a "relentless, determined effort to rid the jury of Black individuals." Six months later, Flowers was released on bail, leaving jail for the first time in 23 years.
"And I'm telling you, I felt like I was floating. I was just ready to go," Flowers told CBS News in 2021.
Sharyn  Alfonsi contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Video: China Coast Guard Uses Water Cannon During Philippine Medevac
articles.title_zh: Video: China Coast Guard Uses Water Cannon During Philippine Medevac
articles.content_orig:
By The Maritime Executive 2026-10-08 14:50:00
The Philippine Coast Guard has reported another dust-up at Second Thomas Shoal, where the Philippine Navy maintains an outpost aboard a deteriorating shipwreck in order to deter Chinese expansion within Manila's exclusive economic zone.
Second Thomas Shoal has been an on-again, off-again flashpoint for tensions between Philippine and Chinese forces in the Spratly Islands since at least 1999, when the Philippine Navy intentionally grounded the WWII-era landing ship BRP Sierra Madre on the reef to serve as a base. The service has maintained a small detachment of marines on board the wreck ever since, and the periodic resupply and rotation missions to and from the shoal are a recurring source of friction. In times of heightened diplomatic tension, the China Coast Guard has often attempted to prevent PCG personnel from reaching the station, periodically adopting forcible methods like aggressive maneuvering and water-cannoning.
The latest encounter occurred on October 8, according to PCG spokesman Jay Tarriela. A Navy servicemember aboard BRP Sierra Madre was in need of medical attention and required evacuation from the station, and the PCG was tasked with mounting a medevac mission. On Thursday morning, the patrol vessel BRP Cabra departed Lawak and got under way for Second Thomas Shoal. At about 0730 hours, Cabra arrived at a position about nine nautical miles away from the reef, where it encountered a familiar presence: China Coast Guard cutter CCG 5306. The CCG crew turned on their water cannon and closed the distance to Cabra, approaching to within 400 yards, Cabra's crew reported. The Chinese cutter's maneuvering prevented further progress towards the Philippine base.
In order to avoid getting hit by the water cannon, BRP Cabra stayed about 13 miles offshore and waited. The crew had hoped to conduct a rendezvous and transfer closer to the patient, but this was not possible because of the Chinese presence, Tarriela said.
By early afternoon, the situation had not changed. To adapt, Cabra's crew launched a team in its RIB boat, and the BRP Sierra Madre station dispatched two inflatable rubber boats with the patient and escort personnel. They met up about four nautical miles off the reef and transferred the patient between boats. Throughout the evolution, CCG small boats and cutters harassed the PCG boat crews, Tarriela said, using "dangerous" maneuvers. Other Chinese vessels involved or in the area included CCG cutters 5009 and 21585, plus the PLA Navy frigate Yongzhou (628) and one maritime militia fishing vessel.
After bringing the patient safely aboard, the Cabra's crew provided him with a checkup and with IV fluids, then got under way to deliver him to shore for a higher level of care.
According to the PCG, the CCG's interference delayed the medevac for hours and created danger for Philippine personnel and the patient. In a statement, Tarriela also highlighted the root of the longstanding sovereignty dispute: China claims a right to control navigation within the western Philippine EEZ, despite a 2016 international arbitral ruling to the contrary.
"When a life is at stake, there should be no water cannon, no obstruction, and no delay. Saving a sick or injured person at sea is a basic obligation that every coast guard in the world is expected to uphold. We call on the CCG to value and respect humanitarian missions moving forward, and to act in a manner consistent with international law and the professional standards expected of any coast guard," PCG Commandant Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan said in a statement.
Get the latest maritime news delivered to your inbox daily.
As in prior incidents, the China Coast Guard claimed that it had permitted PCG units to access Chinese territory within the Philippine EEZ.
"China on Thursday allowed the Philippine Coast Guard vessel 4409 to evacuate an injured person from a Philippine vessel illegally grounded at [Second Thomas Shoal], permitting a small-boat transfer on humanitarian grounds, and the China Coast Guard (CCG) handled the operation in accordance with the law and provided necessary assistance," CCG spokesperson Jiang Lue told state-owned Chinese outlet Global Times.

articles.title_orig: China government bond yields fall as global yields surge
articles.title_zh: China government bond yields fall as global yields surge
articles.content_orig:
China's 10-year yield dropped to 1.7% on Wednesday, more than 3 percentage points below the equivalent U.S. Treasury note
China's government bond yields are moving in the opposite direction from those of nearly every other major economy, as a glut of savings and a sluggish domestic economy push prices higher and returns lower.
China's benchmark 10-year government bond yield touched 1.7% on Wednesday, its lowest point this year. The yield sits more than 3 percentage points below the 5.3% yield on the comparable U.S. Treasury note and well below 10-year benchmark yields in the U.K., France, and Japan.
"China is bucking the entire global trend," Lynn Song, chief economist for China at investment bank ING, told the Wall Street Journal .
Across most major economies, yields have been grinding upward, driven by investors reacting to mounting government debt loads and the energy-price shock stemming from the war in Iran, according to the Wall Street Journal. Optimism around artificial intelligence has also drawn money away from government bonds and toward AI labs and data center builders, adding upward pressure on yields elsewhere.
China faces a different set of pressures. Exports are strong, but the broader economy remains weighed down by weak consumer spending and a prolonged property slump. Capital controls trap household savings within the country, and real estate — once the preferred vehicle for Chinese savers — has lost its appeal. With few alternatives, those savings flow heavily into bonds, pushing prices up and yields down.
China's banking sector has amplified the trend. Faced with lackluster loan demand, Chinese banks have turned to bonds to build out their asset bases. Chinese banks' bond portfolios reached 29 trillion yuan (roughly $4.4 trillion) by August, a figure that represents more than twice what those institutions held just three years earlier, according to the Wall Street Journal.
"China still has a savings glut," Julian Evans-Pritchard, head of China economics at Capital Economics, told the Wall Street Journal. "A lot of it just ends up in the bond market."
The People's Bank of China has shifted its posture as well. In 2024, the concern among Chinese policymakers over depressed yields was serious enough that officials formulated a bond-selling program aimed at lifting them. This year, the central bank has been a net buyer instead — a signal, Evans-Pritchard told the Wall Street Journal, that Beijing now views lower borrowing costs as useful for struggling parts of the economy.
Low yields are not without consequences. Savers earn less on their holdings, which can weigh on overall consumption, and the subdued rate environment telegraphs weak growth expectations that give companies little incentive to expand their workforces or commit capital. The global bond selloff that has pushed yields to multi-decade highs in the U.S. and Europe has been driven by factors largely absent in China — persistent inflation, heavy government borrowing, and a technology-fueled investment boom.

articles.title_orig: Students Rally in France for Second Day of Mass Protests in a Week: Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Students Rally in France for Second Day of Mass Protests in a Week: Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Mark Landler Ségolène Le Stradic and Catherine Porter
Thousands of students and others angry about conditions in public schools rallied in one of the main squares in Paris on Thursday, as French officials looked for ways to ease a crisis that has threatened to swell into a nationwide wave of grievance.
In the evening, the French police moved to try to clear the square, Place de la Bastille, charging demonstrators and firing off tear gas canisters, while some people in the crowd pelted officers with debris. In some places the officers used a water cannon on protesters. At 7 p.m. local time, hundreds of young people who had refused orders to leave were sitting down in the square, singing the French national anthem.
“It’s shocking because it means we don’t have the right to protest,” said Orian Loupescande, 20, a business student, who was crying from tear gas.
The students have been protesting against overcrowded classrooms , a shortage of teachers and decrepit facilities. But with parlous public finances, the French government has offered students little remedy beyond continuing to suspend most classes so they can air their complaints.
One question confronting French officials is whether labor unions and other civic groups will now join the protests. So far, they have largely been contained to high school campuses, but on Tuesday , when union activists rallied with the students, marches drew an estimated 250,000 people across the country, according to the Interior Ministry. Unions have called for a third day of nationwide protests next week.
The French interior ministry estimated that 71,500 people took part in protests across the country, including 24,500 in Paris.
More than 150 high schools were closed around France because of the demonstrations as of midday on Thursday, according to the French education ministry. That was down sharply from Tuesday, when the ministry said that nearly 900 schools were shuttered because of the student protests.
France’s education minister, Édouard Geffray, earlier met with three major student groups in an effort to calm tensions. Mr. Geffray pledged there would be no job cuts at schools, addressing one of the students’ complaints — a shortage of teachers.
Solidarity from university students: The crowd of demonstrators in Bastille square included many university students who said they were moved to join the protests because of police violence against high schoolers that they had seen online. “We are used to seeing police in France beat people but they are normally adults,” said Kerra Underwood, 20, who is studying psychology. “These are kids.”
Paris protest: One of the wellsprings of the protests is the Paul Éluard high school , where crumbling buildings and staff shortages propelled student anger and led some of them to pull down a fence and set fires outside the campus.
A key suburb: Though the protests have affected schools across the country, they have been particularly intense in Seine-St.-Denis, a suburb north of Paris where there are unusually high levels of unemployment, poverty, immigration and teacher absenteeism.
Far-left in focus : The protest movement has been a double-edged sword for France Unbowed, France’s main far-left party, and its leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who is one of the most serious contenders for next year’s presidential election. Some of the party’s lawmakers joined blockades early on and were quickly accused by the center and right-wing parties, as well as the government, of stirring up tensions. The party has denied the accusations and criticized the government for adopting what it considered to be a heavy-handed police response.
The French interior ministry estimated that 71,500 people took part in protests across the country, including 24,500 in Paris. That’s a lot smaller than the figures it gave for the demonstrations on Tuesday — 266,000 nationally, and 56,000 in Paris. The unions have done their own counts in past days, which are much higher than the interior ministry’s, but they haven’t released new figures today. The students are planning another day of action next Tuesday.
The police are closing in now on protesters in Bastille square. They used tear gas on the crowd again and prevented some protesters from leaving on another side of the square. They also climbed the steps of the opera where many students and their supporters had gathered, including a young girl who was covered in blood, having apparently been cut on the brow. Part of the crowd has now decided to sit down in front of the police. They are singing the French national anthem, the Marseillaise.
I’ve covered protests in France for four years now, and almost always they end in chaos and cat and mouse chases between police and strangling protesters, some of whom are “black bloc” members throwing bottles and chunks of concrete at the police. The police have begun to push out protesters from the square now, lining up in phalanxes behind their shields and blasting tear gas canisters towards them. They’ve brought out a giant water cannon too.
Police are under an intense spotlight in this case, as most of the protesters are still minors and some have already been badly injured. I talked to a group of parents at the protest today who told me this is the first time they’ve started to attend their kids’ protests as shields and witnesses, to make sure their kids remain safe.
The police just charged at the crowd in Place de la Bastille again and used tear gas. Many of the protesters have no gathered around the Bastille opera, with rows of police officers and trucks blocking the rest of the square. Orian Loupescande, 20, a business student, was still crying from tear gas. He said he didn’t understand the police’s violence because many had come to demonstrate peacefully. “It’s shocking because it means we don’t have the right to protest,” he said.
Aubépine Dahan, a 54 year old mom and NGO worker, came to support student blockades including the one at the Sophie Germain high school in Paris, in which her daughter had taken part. “Even though the children attend a relatively privileged high school, we know that education has been severely undermined for years; there are not enough resources and that is a serious matter, for this is where the society of tomorrow is being shaped,” she said.
The police are now trying to disperse the protesters at Bastille square. An officer on a megaphone is directing people to take a specific route, and from the end of the square I could see that a police water cannon was used at one point. Some people are starting to disperse but a huge crowd remains.
The mood has changed on part of the square, where police have scuffled with protesters who were throwing plants, chairs and benches toward officers. The police just charged toward protesters and fired tear gas, sending dozens of people running. The confrontation with the police is, from what I can tell, concentrated to one end of the square. Elsewhere, the demonstration is continuing peacefully, with songs and chants.
It’s hard to explain how crowded the Bastille has become. People are flooding the streets, sidewalk and medians of nearby roads. Police are blocking some exits, making it impossible to leave. Many of the students I have spoken to say they intend to keep blockading their schools next week. They considered Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s speech last night an insult and a delay tactic.“His speech motivated us to keep blocking our school until the government stops refusing to listen to us and responds to our demands,”said Augustin Lassaab, 17. “We will not stop.”
The thing I have probably heard the most from people in the crowd today is “convergence of struggles.” That’s also what Juliette Decugnière and Andréane Pierzo, two twenty-year olds studying to become doctors, told me.
