articles.title_orig: Gas prices face new threat as Hurricane Isaias forces widespread Gulf oil shutdowns
articles.title_zh: Gas prices face new threat as Hurricane Isaias forces widespread Gulf oil shutdowns
articles.content_orig:
A powerful storm snaking its way through the Gulf of Mexico threatens to disrupt U.S. oil and gasoline production at a moment when retail gas and diesel prices are squeezing American consumers and companies.
Hurricane Isaias is rapidly intensifying and expected to make landfall along the northeastern Gulf shore late Friday or early Saturday.
Already, major oil companies, including Chevron and Shell, have begun shutting down some oil production sites. Chevron said it was shutting down four of its assets in the Gulf, although production at its five other facilities in the region remained at normal levels. Shell said it was halting production at five sites.
All told, nearly two-thirds of Gulf oil production and 57% of natural gas production had been shut in by noon Thursday, according to the U.S. Marine Minerals Administration.
Hurricanes and major storms are common in the region, so oil companies have well-established evacuation and shutdown protocols.
Still, the timing could hardly be worse for U.S. consumers.
The U.S.-Israeli war against Iran has spawned broader regional conflict, which continues to disrupt energy supplies and drive oil and gasoline prices higher.
Global benchmark Brent crude oil prices surged nearly 5% in early Thursday trading amid reports that President Donald Trump was considering renewed attacks against Iran. U.S. gasoline prices averaged $4.36, down slightly from a week ago but still up 21 cents over the past month.
“This could not have come at a worse time as gasoline and diesel inventories are quite low,” Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates LLC consultancy, wrote in a note Wednesday.
Nearly all U.S. offshore production is in Isaias’ path, he wrote, which means “the impact, even short-lived, can be significant.”
Lipow estimated that 14% of the nation’s refining capacity is in the storm’s path. Given that most U.S. refineries are now running at maximum levels in response to the global squeeze on capacity, “There is no slack in the system,” he wrote.
Oil is a globally traded commodity, so any reduction in supplies will send prices higher around the world.
Refineries in the path of Isaias are likely to see flooding that could take them offline for up to 10 days, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. That is expected to produce a short-term squeeze for U.S. gasoline prices.
But for U.S. motorists, the bigger concerns remain overseas — especially in Russia, where Ukraine continues to target refineries.
“The refining problem is looking like, short to medium term, at least three to six months,” De Haan said. “And it sounds like it’s going to be continuing, especially with Ukraine promising to target more Russian refineries. So there needs to be some de-escalation there for there to be any relief, but it doesn’t look like we’re seeing it.”
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: FBI Says China-Linked Hackers Ran Portal Giving Third Parties Access to Stolen Emails
articles.title_zh: FBI Says China-Linked Hackers Ran Portal Giving Third Parties Access to Stolen Emails
articles.content_orig:
Hackers tied to a Chinese cybersecurity company stole email from government organizations, law enforcement agencies, healthcare systems, and religious institutions in Southeast Asia, the FBI and agencies in 6 other countries said on October 8.
The company, Integrity Technology Group , has been sanctioned by the U.S. and the UK. The hackers scanned websites for flaws using a tool containing more than 1,300 scripts, guessed passwords for Microsoft 365 and Exchange accounts, and copied mailboxes using tools designed to collect mail.
The hackers have been breaking into networks since at least mid-January 2021, according to the agencies' joint advisory . It describes the hacking in the present tense but provides no date for any theft and does not specify how many organizations were breached.
The same hackers targeted U.S. government services, critical manufacturing, healthcare, and IT organizations, along with U.S. law enforcement, education, and religious groups. Organizations in Southeast Asia, Africa, and North America were also targeted.
The hackers also run a web application that "provides third-party access to stolen email content," the advisory said. It does not identify those third parties.
In September 2024, the FBI disrupted a botnet , a network of hijacked devices, that the U.S. Justice Department said Integrity Technology Group controlled. It held more than 200,000 routers, cameras, and other consumer devices, and Lumen researchers had named it Raptor Train.
The 2024 action dealt with the botnet. The new advisory covers how the hackers get into networks and what they take. It is based on evidence the FBI recovered and observed during several investigations related to the company.
The agencies describe Integrity Technology Group as "a China-based for-profit company with links to the Chinese government" whose employees build or get cyber tools "for use and sale," host infrastructure, and break into networks.
The advisory uses a single label, "the threat actors," for the company and the hackers it enables. It does not say which of them carried out each break-in.
The U.S. Treasury sanctioned the company in January 2025 for its role in several computer break-ins against U.S. victims. The UK sanctioned it in December 2025.
Christopher Wray, then the FBI director, said in 2024 that the company's "chairman has publicly admitted that for years his company has collected intelligence and performed reconnaissance for Chinese government security agencies."
The hackers' methods are "consistent with" activity that security companies track as Flax Typhoon, Ethereal Panda, and RedJuliett, among others, the advisory said. Those names may not match the U.S. government's own tracking one-to-one, and the same hackers may also carry out work unrelated to Integrity Technology Group.
Flax Typhoon is Microsoft's name for a China-based group that it described in 2023 as targeting organizations in Taiwan.
Integrity Technology Group rejected the U.S. accusations in January 2025. It told the Shanghai Stock Exchange that the U.S. move had no factual basis, the Associated Press reported . A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson, asked about the sanctions, said China firmly opposed the U.S. action, according to the same report.
The hackers look for flaws in networks and web applications with open-source scanners such as Nmap, masscan, and WPScan, the advisory said. Their scans focus on ports 21, 22, 53, 80, 443, and 1080.
"The use of open source tools typically found on GitHub suggests the threat actors tend to look for more vulnerable targets," the agencies said.
The hackers have also used a scanner called MicroScan since as early as 2017. It is a Python web application containing more than 1,300 penetration testing scripts designed to scan websites for specific flaws. The hackers have used the scripts against services including OpenSSL, Oracle WebLogic Server, Rejetto HFS, WordPress, Juniper ScreenOS, Jenkins, and Apache Struts.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre, one of the agencies behind the advisory, said in its news release that the hackers are "uniquely using AI tools, such as automated scanning." The advisory itself does not mention AI.
The hackers mostly get in with command-line tools built on exploit code written in languages such as Python and Go. The advisory lists 8 known flaws that it says were successfully exploited. The flaws were found in the hackers' penetration testing scripts.
The table shows the affected versions as the advisory gives them and, where one could be confirmed, the release that fixes the flaw.
The advisory marks 5 of the 8 with an asterisk and describes them as newly added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, the list of flaws that the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) says have been used in attacks. They were not in the catalog data that CISA publishes on GitHub (version 2026.10.04) when The Hacker News checked at 18:05 UTC on October 8.
Strapi's own advisory gives a wider range than the joint advisory. It says versions from 3.2.1 through 4.7.9, but not including 4.8.0, are affected.
Two flaws depend on a setting. The Struts flaw works only when Dynamic Method Invocation is turned on, and Apache says turning it off is an alternative to upgrading. The ONLYOFFICE flaw applies when JWT is used, according to its NVD record.
The BIND flaw is a denial-of-service bug that makes the DNS server exit.
Another way in is a fake login. The FBI recovered a cross-site scripting (XSS) payload that changes a vulnerable web page to show username and password fields.
After a visitor enters any username and password, the page offers a password-protected ZIP file that holds a program named live700_v1.exe. That program starts a process named DiagTrack.exe, the same name as a legitimate Windows program, which sends encrypted traffic to dns.studiocloud[.]xyz.
The FBI attributes that domain to Integrity Technology Group and assesses that the malware likely targets email.
The hackers also use password spraying, which means trying a few common passwords against many accounts. For this, they use EBurst, an open-source Python tool that targets Microsoft 365 and Exchange accounts.
EBurst tries logins through Exchange interfaces that include ECP, EWS, OAB, OWA, RPC, API, MAPI, PowerShell, Autodiscover, and Microsoft-Server-ActiveSync, according to its README file. Defenders should cover these interfaces, the agencies said.
To keep access, the hackers install SoftEther, a legitimate VPN program that security software is less likely to flag, the advisory said. They often rename the installer conhost.exe or dllhost.exe so it looks like a Windows file, and they set the client to reconnect each time the machine starts.
To take credentials, they ran a tool named DC.exe that uses DCSync, a technique that copies data from a domain controller through Active Directory's replication service. It copied account credentials, group membership details, and trust relationships.
For email, the hackers built a bot from a PHP script named Curlc4.txt. It collects mail through Exchange Web Services (EWS), an interface that also gives access to calendars and contacts.
The bot compresses the mail, sometimes encrypts it, and uploads it to a remote server. The script appears to be stand-alone rather than installed on a hacked device, and its main command-and-control domain was natcloudservice[.]com.
A second tool, office-cli, keeps going back to Microsoft 365 accounts to take mail from different time periods. It works from configuration files that hold a client ID, tenant ID, and secret, and it avoids detection by using legitimate access methods, the agencies said.
The FBI also saw the hackers download databases or pull data from victims' email by hand.
In some cases, the hackers limited access to the stolen data to IP addresses in Xiamen, China.

articles.title_orig: Set your alarms and look up! The northern lights may dazzle over New England tonight.
articles.title_zh: Set your alarms and look up! The northern lights may dazzle over New England tonight.
articles.content_orig:
If you’re willing to lose a little sleep tonight, there could be a pretty good reason to step outside and look to the north.
The Northern Lights could make an appearance across New England overnight, thanks to a coronal mass ejection (CME), essentially a cloud of magnetized solar material racing past Earth. NOAA’s Space Weather Prediction Center is expecting a moderate geomagnetic storm , a level G2 out of 5, overnight Thursday into the predawn hours of Friday. A geomagnetic storm watch of that level can typically extend the visibility of the northern lights as far south as Massachusetts, although some forecasts have the viewing line as far south as New Jersey.
It’s never a certainty that a strong geomagnetic storm will occur. It’s always tricky to forecast how strong the CME might be when it erupts from the sun 91 million and 93 million miles away from Earth.
“This CME is forecasted to be a glancing blow,” said Vincent Ledvina, of Alaska, a space physics Ph.D. student who’s known as “the Aurora Guy .” “The cloud is a partial halo aimed mostly north of Earth, so the models have its flank sweeping over us rather than its core, and a flank hit can underperform or miss us entirely.”
But this is the best chance the region has seen in a while to catch a glimpse of the aurora borealis, since we’re coming off of Solar Maximum , when the sun is most active in producing these storms.
Weather-wise, we won’t have to worry about cloud cover tonight because high pressure will keep the night almost completely clear. The moonlight also shouldn’t interfere since we’re entering the new moon phase.
Based on the latest observations from NOAA, the best opportunity may actually come toward the early morning hours, roughly between 3 and 5:30 a.m. Forecasters are expecting the geomagnetic activity to build throughout the night, peaking near dawn. Again, forecasting space weather from millions of miles away isn’t easy, so it’s also worth taking a look between 11 p.m. and midnight, too.
So if you’re motivated to catch something, find somewhere dark and get away from the street lights and other light pollution. I don’t expect this to be a blockbuster event. The most likely scenario is that the geomagnetic storm stays on the weaker side and perhaps New Englanders can see some glow on the horizon to the north with the naked eye.
Be sure to snap a few photos on your phone if you can’t see anything. Your cellphone can often pick up the wavelengths and capture what you can’t see.
Of course, you can always keep track of the northern lights in real time via an app or NOAA’s site. Just head to the Space Weather Prediction Center website to monitor the Earth’s magnetic field .
Here’s an example below of two main metrics to watch for. The Bz (red) shows the orientation of Earth’s magnetic field. The Bt (white) shows the strength of it, and the solar wind speed is tracked in yellow.
Look for a jump up in Bt intensity (white), a flip to a negative in Bz orientation (red), and a jump in solar wind speed (yellow), then go outside and look up!
I touched on it above, but there’s a big reason why I think this one is worth watching.
We’re now past Solar Maximum, the peak period of the sun’s roughly 11-year activity cycle, meaning as solar activity gradually declines, these geomagnetic storms and opportunities to view the aurora should become less frequent over the coming years. That doesn’t mean the aurora is going away, but the odds of frequent, widespread displays should diminish as we move farther from the peak.
So, if you’re on the fence, I say set the alarm. Maybe you get nothing. Maybe you see a faint green glow hugging the northern horizon. Or maybe the night sky surprises us and puts on a display. Either way, it’s probably worth losing a little sleep to find out.
Ken Mahan can be reached at ken.mahan@globe.com . Follow him on Instagram @kenmahantheweatherman .

articles.title_orig: Search warrants against former prince Andrew were unlawful, court finds
articles.title_zh: Search warrants against former prince Andrew were unlawful, court finds
articles.content_orig:
Thames Valley Police has accepted warrants it used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes at the time of his arrest in February were unlawful, the High Court has been told.
Following Thursday's hearing, items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence.
Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing.
The former prince, who denies any wrongdoing, was arrested by police on 19 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after which he launched a legal challenge over the legality of the search warrants.
The force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties.
On Thursday at the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful.
However, he added: "The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful."
Mountbatten-Windsor opposes the police's bid to retain the evidence, the judge said, and another hearing is expected in 2027.
His lawyers have used a judicial review to challenge the actions of the force's chief constable and the Central Criminal Court in the build-up to his arrest.
His arrest arose after the US Department of Justice published documents which raised suspicions he had forwarded confidential information to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein when Mountbatten-Windsor was a UK trade envoy in 2010.
He has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.
The court heard on Thursday that Thames Valley Police seized documents and electronic devices when they raided Mountbatten-Windsor's homes earlier this year.
Thames Valley Police's position was that they had applied for search warrants under section eight and nine of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 at a hearing at the Central Criminal Court the day before the search.
That court determined that only section eight search warrants were needed and they were granted on that basis - but subsequently, a legal challenge has established that the court should have issued them under the section nine.
The judge explained on Thursday why the police could keep hold of the former prince's items that had been seized.
He said: "There would be little point in handing property back if it could then simply be lawfully seized under some other provision."
A Thames Valley Police spokesperson said: "The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgement on our ongoing investigation.
"We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout.
"We accept the position that the initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.
"Legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation."
The force said its "investigation into alleged misconduct in public office by a man in his 60s from Norfolk remains ongoing, and we continue to pursue all reasonable lines of enquiry to effectively and fairly progress this investigation".
The next stage in this legal dispute will be a behind-closed-doors hearing over whether the police can still retain material seized from Mountbatten-Windsor's homes under alternative powers designed for situations like this.
The error that has led to Thames Valley Police accepting the search warrants were unlawful relates to the particular power the judge permitted the force to use when its officers raided the properties.
Strict legal safeguards on searches bar the police from automatically seizing sensitive material without thinking through in advance the need to take it.
Examples of that material include advice from a suspect's lawyer or material which does not really belong to them, such as copies of confidential work-related papers from an employer.
In practice, if the police find such material during a search, they should return it rather than use it in their investigation.
The category of search warrant that was granted by the court in this instance did not take into account the possibility of such protected material being seized.
However, the law says police can in fact seize that kind of material - or potentially retain it in the event of an error - providing they pass some extra tests.
Thames Valley Police must now convince a judge that the material is likely to be of "substantial value" to their investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor and, ultimately, potential evidence to present to a court.
So while the force has conceded the search warrant was unlawful, a judge will have to decide whether this alternative search power, with its extra safeguards, justifies them keeping and using the material after all.

articles.title_orig: Beijing Will Not Pace the Frontier: China’s Speed-First AI Safety Regime
articles.title_zh: Beijing Will Not Pace the Frontier: China’s Speed-First AI Safety Regime
articles.content_orig:
AI safety is on fire. On 12 September 2026, Dario Amodei published an essay arguing that frontier labs must deliberately slow the pace at which they improve model capabilities. China was central to his geopolitical argument: export controls and tighter security could preserve America’s lead, creating room to slow down and leverage for a future agreement with Beijing. Within a day, Sam Altman and Elon Musk supported Dario’s call. However, President Trump scoffed. On 14 September 2026, he wrote that fears of AI destroying humanity are “a HOAX” and that “the only one that is happy about it is China.”  Beijing scoffed too, with the state-run Global Times calling Dario’s essay a “Cold War playbook.”
The debate then moved onto the diplomatic calendar. On 20 September 2026, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Vice Premier He Lifeng held the first US-China AI dialogue. On 23 September 2026, President Xi Jinping began his state visit to the US. The Trump-Xi summit formalized the dialogue as the “US-China Super Intelligence Dialogue,” using the name Trump had unveiled at the UN the day before Xi arrived. The summit also promised a channel for AI incidents. On 29 September 2026, Trump and six executives signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, a one-page voluntary pledge to self-police that Trump called “morally binding.”
China sits on both sides of the American argument. For President Trump, competition with China is a reason not to slow down. For Dario, preserving America’s lead over China is what makes slowing down possible. Nobody has asked what China is actually doing. So, we did. What do the Chinese government, frontier labs, and AI experts say and do about AI safety? And what should American labs, investors, and policymakers conclude from it?
Beijing’s stated position is the most safety-forward of any major AI power outside Europe. Xi Jinping told the Politburo in April 2025 that AI brings “unprecedented risks and challenges” and ordered systems for technical monitoring, risk early-warning and emergency response. At the 2026 World AI Conference in Shanghai, Xi said the world must “ensure AI always remains under human control” and that the faster AI advances, “the more promptly the measures to prevent loss of control must be improved.” China signed the Bletchley Declaration and the Paris and New Delhi statements, co-sponsored the UN resolutions, founded a World AI Cooperation Organization in Shanghai, and publishes bilingual AI Safety Governance Frameworks.
The newest text goes further. The AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, released by TC260 under Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) on 14 September 2026, warns that AI has shown a self-accelerating trend of autonomous learning and recursive self-improvement, and calls for “attention and vigilance” for potential AI evolution exceeding human prediction and control. The Framework 3.0 also introduces a new model-risk category, “behavior deviating from expectations,” covering models that acquire system privileges and external resources without authorization, bypass safety protections, deceive evaluators, hide their true capabilities, and refuse user instructions, illustrated with a boxed case study of models disabling shutdown scripts, sandbagging under evaluation, and breaking out of isolation into real systems. Its list of derivative risks goes further still; past behaviors already observed to a hypothetical AI that becomes self-aware, seeks power of its own, and competes with humanity for control. On paper, this is the most explicit official Chinese text yet on frontier risk, and its vocabulary overlaps strikingly with Dario’s essay Beijing denounced that same week.
However, we think China’s real approach to AI safety is speed-based, not safety-based. Though Beijing recognizes frontier AI risks, it has been prioritizing rapid development. The Framework 3.0 opens its principles with “promoting AI innovation and development as the first priority .” The comprehensive AI Law promised in the 2023 and 2024 legislative plans was shelved in 2025, four months after the DeepSeek moment. The State Council’s AI+ Action Plan targets 70% penetration of agents and intelligent terminals by 2027 and 90% by 2030, aiming for a rapid deployment of AI across all sectors and industries.
We think the Chinese government takes an open position on frontier models but tightens the applications and regulates outputs. Since 2025, China has issued a number of mandates, including mandatory content labeling (Sep 2025), Cybersecurity Law Article 20 (Jan 2026), the minors’ information classification rules (March 2026), MIIT’s AI ethics-review regime (March 2026), the policy-level agent rules (May 2026), the world’s first AI-companion rules (July 2026), the network-data risk assessment rules (August 2026), and MPS inspection powers (October 2026). Every one of these governs what AI says and what AI does to people. There is no set of frontier-risk duties triggered by training compute or model capability. The result is a safety regime stricter than any in the world on content and on process for public-facing services, and looser than the EU (systemic-risk duties from 10²⁵ FLOP) and California (SB 53: frontier frameworks and 15-day incident reporting from 10²⁶ operations) on the frontier.
The week Framework 3.0 came out shows the pattern in real time. Framework 3.0 added two new application-layer risk categories, agents and embodied intelligence, plus an appendix on managing agent risk. On 15 September, TC260 issued four AI application security guides, with a general one and three specific ones for education, health care and broadcasting, respectively. On 18 September it opened comments on a draft Agent System Development Security Guide (due 2 October) that walks developers through identity, least privilege, tool verification and human-approval nodes. The same day the CAC published a draft State Council regulation on minors’ internet use (comments due 17 October) that bars offering minors “virtual relatives, virtual companions and other virtual intimate-relationship services” and bars livestreaming under the age of 16. Seven texts in five days. Everyone is about how an agent or an application is built, deployed, and to whom it is offered. The gap at the frontier has not moved at all.
Compliance therefore tells us nothing about frontier safety. A Chinese lab can satisfy every rule on this list without ever running a dangerous-capability evaluation. Thus, to know what the labs do at the frontier, we must look at what they evaluate, what they disclose, and whether any of them change what they ship.
Nobody in China’s AI industry is slowing down, and nobody is asking them to. The frontier labs are in a release and price war.
We conduct a systematic analysis to clearly understand what Chinese labs do about safety. We constructed an original dataset that includes all identifiable model release by the 9 leading Chinese developers from 2021 to 15 September 2026. These 9 companies include 4 hyperscalers (ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu) and 5 startups (DeepSeek, MoonShot, Zhipu Z.ai, MiniMax, and StepFun). The dataset includes 857 counted releases (741 product models and 116 research models), each with a first-public date, weight status, license, and source. We then check each against the developer’s model cards, release notes, and technical reports for a published safety-evaluation result that can be matched to that release. Our standard is strict: a result means a quantitative or substantive finding on harmful output, jailbreaks, toxicity, privacy, refusal, or dangerous capability, tied to the named model. Statements that a model was “safety-trained” or “evaluated” do not count. A flagship model’s result is not extrapolated to other sizes or snapshots. “Not found” is bounded to the materials checked and does not mean “not tested.” Companies also name variants at different granularity (Alibaba’s 238 releases count every Qwen size

articles.title_orig: Lawyers for accused man in Cornell case want Letitia James removed as prosecutor
articles.title_zh: Lawyers for accused man in Cornell case want Letitia James removed as prosecutor
articles.content_orig:
The “Cornell 7” Jane Doe at the center of an alleged frat house gang rape was “misled” about the status of the criminal probe into her claims — after bringing them to campus police, her attorney said.
The victim, a female student only identified as Jane Doe , was led to believe an investigation was moving forward after reporting the alleged October 2024 assault to campus police several weeks later, according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra.
But it turned out the probe wrapped shortly after it started, when Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten decided against pressing charges days after cops first spoke with her.
Van Houten said he asked Cornell police to tell Doe about his decision — but never spoke to her or her lawyer personally.
“I think she was misled. She was told it was still — they weren’t going to prosecute, but they were still investigating,” Giuffra told the Associated Press . “I was involved with this case early on. I thought they were still investigating.
“It was news to me that they weren’t doing anything.”
The attorney said he assumed investigators needed more time to speak with witnesses and build a case.
“But nothing was being done, and we didn’t know that,” Giuffra said.
Last week, Van Houten said his office had declined to press charges after reviewing a six-page summary of Doe’s account written by a police officer.
From that report, Van Houten believed no crime had been committed and that Doe’s sexual participation and drug use that night were “voluntary, conscious and consensual,” he said.
That account differs greatly from what Doe said she told police and Cornell investigators at the time, and with what she alleged in a lawsuit she filed last month against seven Chi Phi fraternity members and Cornell.
Last week, it was reported that a Cornell police investigator allegedly tried to get Van Houten’s office to consider additional evidence in the weeks following the reported rape, but was rebuffed.
“At first I thought these police were incompetent. It sounds like they were doing the right thing. And they just got shot down,” Giuffra said.
The case was yanked from Tompkins County by Gov. Kathy Hochul Friday — and handed over to New York Attorney General Letitia James to probe.
Giuffra applauded the move, saying he “didn’t think [Van Houten] was up to the task” and was concerned about his plan for conducting the reopened investigation.
Van Houten reportedly wanted to take the case to a grand jury and have Jane Doe testify before the panel in the next two weeks.
Meanwhile, New York’s top cop suggested her probe into the alleged gang rape could take months.
Van Houten’s office and Cornell Campus Police didn’t respond immediately to The Post’s requests for comment.
None of the fraternity brothers named in Jane Doe’s suit have yet to be officially charged with any crimes.

articles.title_orig: Ballet Hispánico brings world-class dance to the Ogle Center Oct. 15-Free and open to all
articles.title_zh: Ballet Hispánico brings world-class dance to the Ogle Center Oct. 15-Free and open to all
articles.content_orig:
One afternoon only: Acclaimed New York company performs highlights from its celebrated repertoire, followed by an interactive Latin dance experience
NEW ALBANY, Ind. — There are performances worth making time for — especially when the price of admission is nothing.
Ballet Hispánico , one of the nation’s foremost dance companies and a leading voice in Hispanic and Latino arts and culture, comes to the Ogle Center at Indiana University Southeast on Thursday, Oct. 15, from 4:30 to 6 p.m. for Ballet Hispánico Live at the Ogle Center: A Dance Showcase . Admission is FREE, and no ticket is required.
With the performance just days away, the Ogle Center is encouraging Southern Indiana and Louisville-area audiences to take advantage of a rare opportunity to experience the internationally recognized New York-based company at no cost.
“This is exactly the kind of event you don’t want to hear about afterward and wish you had attended,” said Kirk Randolph, director of the Ogle Center . “Ballet Hispánico is an extraordinary company, and we have the chance to welcome these artists to our stage and offer the experience to our community completely free of charge. Clear your calendar, bring a friend and come see what makes this company so remarkable.”
The 90-minute showcase will offer audiences a fast-moving tour through Ballet Hispánico’s diverse repertoire, with selections from “Guajira,” “Línea Recta,” “Trança,” “Otra Vez, Otra Vez, Otra Vez” and “Club Havana.” The afternoon won’t end with audiences simply watching from their seats: Rodney Hamilton will lead an interactive Latin social dance experience, inviting attendees to get moving themselves. Hamilton, a Juilliard graduate and former Ballet Hispánico principal dancer, has taught dance internationally and has a long history with the company.
The program offers an unusually broad look at the company’s artistic range. Annabelle Lopez Ochoa’s “Línea Recta” brings the passion of flamenco into an inventive movement vocabulary centered on partnering and set to flamenco guitar. Cassi Abranches’ “Trança” draws upon the ancestral art of braiding and Brazilian cultural traditions to explore individuality, community, identity and connection. Stephanie Martinez’s “Otra Vez, Otra Vez, Otra Vez” takes inspiration from Picasso’s The Old Guitarist and reflects on human connection and the fleeting nature of life.
Pedro Ruiz’s “Club Havana” turns up the temperature with a portrait of glamorous 1950s Havana nightlife, bringing the rhythms of conga, rumba, mambo and cha-cha to the stage. Ruiz, a Cuban-born choreographer and former Ballet Hispánico principal dancer, is also the choreographer of “Guajira.” His work has earned honors including The Bessie Award and the Choo-San Goh Award.
The Oct. 15 performance is part of the Ogle Center’s 30th Anniversary Season , presented with support from Patty Cress and in partnership with IU Auditorium .
MORE THAN 50 YEARS OF DANCE, CULTURE AND CONNECTION
Founded in 1970 by Tina Ramirez on the principle that everyone deserves access to dance, quality dance training and innovative performance, Ballet Hispánico has grown into the largest Latino cultural organization in the United States and has been recognized as one of America’s Cultural Treasures. Its professional Company, School of Dance and Community Arts Partnerships use dance to celebrate and explore the breadth of Hispanic and Latino cultures and experiences.
The Company has performed for more than 2.5 million people across three continents and all 50 states , presenting work by Latino and Latina choreographers while creating opportunities for cultural dialogue and inspiring new generations of dancers.
Under Artistic Director and CEO Eduardo Vilaro , who first joined Ballet Hispánico as a dancer in 1985 and became artistic director in 2009, the organization has continued to expand its contemporary repertoire and its role in developing Hispanic artistic leadership.
The company has earned national attention for the versatility and technical command of its dancers. Its repertoire moves across classical and contemporary dance and a range of cultural traditions, giving audiences an experience that can shift dramatically in style, rhythm and atmosphere from one work to the next. The company’s own community programs similarly combine professional repertory with interactive movement and cultural exploration.
For anyone who has been curious about Ballet Hispánico — or who simply wants to experience professional dance up close without the usual price of a ticket — Oct. 15 is the opportunity. There is nothing to reserve and nothing to buy. Just show up.
WHAT: Ballet Hispánico Live at the Ogle Center: A Dance Showcase WHEN: Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, 4:30–6 p.m. WHERE: The Ogle Center at Indiana University Southeast, New Albany, Indiana ADMISSION: FREE — No ticket required PROGRAM: Selections from Guajira, Línea Recta, Trança, Otra Vez, Otra Vez, Otra Vez and Club Havana , plus an interactive Latin social dance experience led by Rodney Hamilton PRESENTED: As part of the Ogle Center’s 30th Anniversary Season, with support from Patty Cress and in partnership with IU Auditorium MORE INFORMATION: oglecenter.com

Home › News and Business › Business and Law
Nyx Hemera Technologies has acquired Comlab Telecommunications and its Davicom division.
The buyer provides intelligent lighting control and management systems for critical infrastructure including smart-city lighting control systems for road tunnels and underpasses. Comlab and Davicom sell automation and control products for broadcast and telecom sites. All are based in Quebec City, Canada.
Nyx Hemera and Comlab/Davicom will continue to operate separately. But John Ahern, president of Comlab/Davicom, plans to retire next spring.
“This acquisition marks a significant milestone in the growth of both companies, as they possess highly complementary technological expertise; it will enable them to expand their engineering and product development capabilities while creating new opportunities for innovation in their current and future markets,” Nyx Hemera said in the announcement.
President Pierre Longtin was quoted, “The skills developed by Comlab/Davicom over the years in radio frequency electronics, antennas and telecommunications complement those of Nyx and give us access to new development opportunities.”
John Ahern told Radio World: “The company continues, the products continue, our support continues and the team continues. The main change is that I will be retiring after the spring NAB Show.”

articles.title_orig: XPRIZE Convenes World's Leading Innovators to Choose Its Next Global Competitions
articles.title_zh: XPRIZE Convenes World's Leading Innovators to Choose Its Next Global Competitions
articles.content_orig:
MALIBU, Calif., Oct. 8, 2026
Scientists, astronauts, investors and philanthropists to decide which grand challenges XPRIZE takes on next
MALIBU, Calif. , Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- XPRIZE , the world's leader in designing and operating large-scale incentive competitions to solve humanity's grand challenges, will host its annual Global Visioneering Summit on October 15–17 at Calamigos Ranch in Malibu, California. Over three days, a rare cross-section of the world's leading minds, including scientists, frontier technologists, astronauts, investors, and philanthropists will convene not as an audience, but as collaborators, working side by side to determine which of humanity's most urgent challenges XPRIZE takes on next.
Over the course of the Summit, six prize concepts developed through XPRIZE's year-long Global Visioneering process, two each in Health; Food + Water + Waste; and Energy + Climate + Nature, will be pitched live to attendees. Attendees will score the concepts, debate, vote and commit seed funding to launch them as XPRIZE's next global competitions. The XPRIZE model is unique amongst non-profits with its ability to leverage every prize purse dollar for a 62X return — and a record of generating $32.4 billion from the $519 million in prizes launched since its inception in 1994.
The Summit will be hosted by XPRIZE CEO Anousheh Ansari, the first female private space explorer and sponsor of the Ansari XPRIZE that spurred the private spaceflight industry, and XPRIZE Founder and Chairman Peter Diamandis, New York Times bestselling author, entrepreneur and co-founder of Singularity University. The event will be emceed by Van Jones, CNN Host, Founder of DreamMachine.org and Founder of RAPPORT.co.
"Global Visioneering is where the future takes shape," said Ansari. "Each year, we bring together the boldest minds in the world to decide how we can direct breakthroughs that will create a better future for all. That work has never been more urgent. Public and corporate funding for long-term solutions is pulling back just as the world's challenges are growing in size. XPRIZE exists to close that gap, giving audacious solutions the backing and momentum to reach the people who need them."
Summit programming will span priority focus areas XPRIZE is racing to advance:
Ansari will lead The Future of Space and Its Impact on Humanity, a conversation with Apollo 9 astronaut Rusty Schweickart, investor Steve Jurvetson and APEX Co-Founder and CEO Ian Cinnamon. The panel will explore how exploration, enterprise and collaboration in space can shape humanity's future, building on the legacy of the $10 million Ansari XPRIZE that helping catalyze today's commercial space industry.
XPRIZE Chairman, Peter Diamandis will record a live episode of Moonshots, his podcast tracking the future of technology and how it impacts humanity, with Ansari, Openexo Chairman Salim Ismail, and Intelligent Internet Founder Emad Mostaque.
Composer Philip Sheppard, violinist Stephanie Yu and poet Salome Agbaroji will perform throughout the Summit, weaving music and spoken word into the program to open space for reflection, unexpected connections and ideas beyond what seems possible today.
Attendees will also hear from XPRIZE alumni teams continuing to drive industry-changing impact well beyond their original competitions, including PLANETVILLAGE, awarded $1M in the XPRIZE Carbon Removal competition, and Longeveron, an XPRIZE Healthspan finalist.
The Summit is made possible by partners who share XPRIZE's commitment to bold, catalytic impact: North Star Sponsor CollectivIQ , Alumni Advancement Sponsor Avanci , Breakthrough Sponsor The Rodney Fund , Moonshot Sponsors ECOS and GIGAHEALTH , and Health Domain Sponsor Pointe Malibu Recovery Center are all official event sponsors this year.
Those interested in attending can register and view the full program at xprize.org/visioneering .
XPRIZE is the recognized global leader in designing and executing large-scale competitions to solve humanity's greatest challenges. For over 30 years, our unique model has democratized crowd-sourced innovation and scientifically scalable solutions that accelerate a more equitable and abundant future. Donate, learn more, and co-architect a world of abundance with us at xprize.org.

articles.content_orig:
The Israel Defense Forces announced Thursday that two more Hamas terrorists have been taken out in the Gaza Strip.
"ELIMINATED: Muhammad Muhsen Nimr Yazji, a commander in the Shati Battalion of Hamas’ military wing, who was involved in holding hostages in the Gaza City area," the IDF wrote on X. "Additionally, in the Sabra area, Muhammad Fawzi Muhammad Awad Gamal, a terrorist in the Daraj Tuffah Battalion of Hamas’ military wing, was eliminated."
The IDF said both men "advanced attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops and operated to restore Hamas’ capabilities, in systematic violation of the ceasefire," and they they "were eliminated in order to remove the threat they posed."
A further attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport Thursday prompted U.S. Embassy security warnings, travel restrictions for government personnel, and widespread flight cancellations, with some carriers suspending service for several days.
The U.S. Embassy warned of disruptions, including potential airspace closures and travel delays.
“The Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including against civilian airports, and the military conflict has the potential to escalate,” the embassy stated on X .
The alert also advised U.S. citizens to avoid the Yemen border and announced that U.S. government employees now require special authorization to use the Riyadh airport.
Government personnel remain barred from traveling within 20 miles of the border and need approval to visit Jizan, Asir, and Najran provinces, as well as Qatif, Yanbu, and Taif, the alert said.
Flightradar24 reported hundreds of canceled flights, with carriers such as Lufthansa suspending multi-day service and IndiGo canceling all Riyadh flights through Oct. 9.
Air India also says it has canceled flights to and from Riyadh until Saturday amid escalating missile attacks by the Houthis.
Meanwhile, Reuters reported that an empty Saudia commercial aircraft parked at a terminal was heavily damaged by fire.
The U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned 17 tankers and their owners Thursday as part of Operation Economic Outcast, aimed at dismantling Iran’s remaining shadow fleet network.
In a statement, Treasury said the ships had carried millions of barrels of Iranian crude oil, petroleum products and petrochemicals to markets in South and East Asia.
The network spanned more than a dozen jurisdictions and relied on international front companies, Treasury said in a statement .
“Today’s action effectively neutralizes the vast majority of Iran’s remaining shadow fleet network.”
“Treasury is starving the tyrannical regime in Tehran of the money it uses to wage war in the region, and we will continue exposing those who enable the regime’s oil sales,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
“No enabler of Iranian sanctions evasion is safe from the full force of Treasury’s authorities.”
The sanctioned vessels included the Cameroon-flagged Shenzhen, which Treasury said had transported more than 3.5 million barrels of Iranian crude oil since November 2025, and the Vanuatu-flagged Tina 5, which had carried more than 1.5 million barrels in August.
U.S. Central Command said Thursday that "in recent months, U.S. forces have supported the shipment of over 1.25 billion barrels of crude oil from Gulf partners and through the Strait of Hormuz.
"In contrast, Iran has not shipped any barrels because of America's ironclad blockade on Iranian ports," it wrote on X.
CENTCOM revealed earlier this week that 130 ships have been redirected as part of the blockade.
"The U.S. military remains intensely focused on this mission, Adm. Brad Cooper, CENTCOM commander, said in a statement. "We will swiftly act against any vessels trying to run the blockade. Our forces are highly trained, professional, and lethal."
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) said Thursday that a crude oil tanker has been struck while traveling through the Strait of Hormuz.
The incident, in which the tanker was hit by an "unknown projectile," happened on Wednesday, according to the UKMTO.
"There have been no reported casualties. Damage assessment and environmental impact are unknown at time of report," it added.
President Donald Trump announced Thursday that the U.S. military "will not be attacking Iran" in the leadup to November's midterm elections.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran. I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait (22 Million Barrels, last night alone, with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran!), we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
"IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!" the president also declared.
A White House official told Fox News on Thursday that "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States" when asked to respond to reporting about potential strikes against Iran.
The remark comes after The Atlantic, citing two administration officials, reported Wednesday that “The White House has asked the Pentagon to develop strike options against Iranian targets that could be exercised ahead of the midterms.”
“The Commander-in-Chief has all options available at any time. The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing," the White House official said.
"Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways; the easy way or the hard way," the official added.
Fox News' Patrick Ward contributed to this post.

articles.title_orig: Russian attack on buses in Ukraine’s Kramatorsk kills at least 30 people
articles.title_zh: Russian attack on buses in Ukraine’s Kramatorsk kills at least 30 people
articles.content_orig:
A Russian attack on two buses has killed at least 30 people and wounded 18 others in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk, near the front line, authorities said.
The local prosecutor’s office on Thursday posted photos of bodies and debris strewn across a road in front of the burning metal shell of a bus.
Police said the attack took place on a street where two city ⁠buses were operating at the time. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described it as a bus stop and said there would be a response.
“This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is attempting to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world must respond … firmly,” he said on Telegram.
The Donetsk governor accused Russia of “deliberately targeting civilians”.
“For them [the Russians], a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one strike can kill as many people as possible,” Vadym Filashkin wrote on Telegram.
Police said the buses were hit with a glide bomb. Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said glide bombs “do not have the precision of a ballistic missile or the first-person view of something like a drone, so they don’t have the same accuracy as those weapons”.
Therefore, there is no way of knowing whether these buses were intentionally targeted or if they were “at the wrong place at the wrong time,” MacAlpine said.
The correspondent added this was one of the largest and deadliest aerial attacks in recent months, “in a sign of how the front line city of Kramatorsk is becoming more and more dangerous.”
There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the attack. Russia denies targeting civilians, though it has regularly pounded Ukrainian cities, towns and other targets during its full-scale invasion that began in February 2022.
Kramatorsk is one of the key cities that Russia has not yet captured in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, which Moscow claims as part of Russia.
It has been a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military for much of Moscow’s war and is part of the so-called “fortress belt” that troops are fighting to keep hold of.
Russian forces have edged close to the city’s eastern edge, which has prompted calls for civilians who remain to relocate to safer regions of Ukraine.
Kramatorsk City Council said it was “yet another horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population”.
“Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets,” it added.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, the death toll from Wednesday’s Russian missile attack on a residential building in the city of Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region rose to 22 , including five children, Governor Vyacheslav Chaus said in a statement on Telegram.
President Zelenskyy said a cruise missile directly hit the building in Pryluky, about 150km (93 miles) east of the capital, Kyiv.
The city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said two people were found dead on Thursday after a fire at a four-storey building that was hit by a drone in the densely populated Solomyansky district.
Klitschko has said the attacks, which have hit key transport bridges in the city, as well as the rail network and energy grid, were “tearing Kyiv apart”.
Meanwhile, in Russia, a drone caused a fire at a data centre belonging to Russian technology company Yandex, the firm told the AFP news agency on Thursday.
Unverified images published on social media showed columns of thick, black smoke pouring from the roof of the building, which the company said was in the central Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow.
Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with some of the latest Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.
The former head of Ukraine’s Centre for Countering Disinformation said Kyiv was responsible for the strike on the Yandex facility, writing on Telegram: “Two can play at this game”.
The firm is Russia’s largest technology company.
Often dubbed “Russia’s Google”, Yandex runs the country’s most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and ride-hailing application used by tens of millions of people across the Russian-speaking world.
Ukraine also claimed to have struck a large oil refinery complex in the city of Salavat, some 1,200 kilometres (about 750 miles) east of Moscow. Ukraine’s General Staff described the complex as one of Russia’s largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities.
Separately, a man was ⁠killed and ⁠a woman was injured in a ‌drone attack on Moscow region, Andrei Vorobyov, the regional governor, ⁠said. A residential building ⁠and three ⁠cars ⁠were damaged in the attack.
In ⁠Russia’s Omsk region, Vitaly Khotsenko, ⁠the region’s governor, said Kyiv had hit an ⁠industrial ⁠zone. The Omsk region, which is in Siberia, hosts ‌an oil refinery operated by Gazpromneft.
Ukraine has been waging its own campaign of long-distance drone strikes against ⁠military, energy and ⁠commercial targets in a bid to raise the cost ⁠to Moscow of ⁠continuing the ⁠war.
US Secretary of ⁠State Marco ⁠Rubio on Thursday said Russia’s war in Ukraine was at a dangerous stalemate and that Washington would ⁠keep working toward a settlement to end the conflict.
“We’d love to see a negotiated settlement to this war ⁠that is permanent, enduring, and fair. And that’s what we’re committed to continuing to do,” Rubio told reporters during a visit to Portugal.
The US official said escalations could spark a wider conflict.
“That escalation could wind up being a sabotage campaign in neighbouring countries that ⁠are members of NATO,” he said, adding that other things “could quickly turn what is ⁠a war between two countries into a ⁠much broader and far more dangerous regional conflict.”
“This war needs to end in a negotiated settlement. The sooner, the better. The United States stands ready to ‌facilitate that. We have tried. We will continue to try. But we’re also not going to invest in pointless processes if ‌we ‌can’t make progress,” Rubio added.

articles.title_orig: China Daily reports on the Socialist China Conference 2026
articles.title_zh: China Daily reports on the Socialist China Conference 2026
articles.content_orig:
China Daily has published a report by its London correspondent Xing Yi on our third annual Socialist China Conference, held in London on 3 October to mark the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China.
The report notes that speakers from left-wing and anti-war organisations, embassies and academia called for China’s peaceful rise, its contribution to the Global South and its vision of a shared future for humanity to be better understood in the West. It summarises the conference’s three panels – on AI and technology, on China’s foreign policy and the making of a multipolar world, and on resisting the New Cold War – and covers the launch of the book China’s Foreign Policy and the Making of a Multipolar World , edited by Keith Bennett and Carlos Martinez.
For a fuller account of the day, see our own report of the conference . Recordings of all the sessions are available on our YouTube channel .
This article first appeared in China Daily .
China’s peaceful rise, its contribution to the Global South, and its vision of a shared future for humanity deserve to be better understood and promoted in the West, experts and activists said at the third annual Socialist China Conference in London on the weekend.
Organized by the Friends of Socialist China platform, the gathering brought together speakers from left-wing and anti-war groups in the United Kingdom and Europe, as well as representatives from embassies and academia.
Experts attending the event recalled the journey of Chinese modernization and agreed that, no matter how far China develops, the nation will continue to provide the world with development opportunities, safeguard world peace, and contribute to improving global governance.
Acknowledging the difficulties in telling the true story of China in the West, they highlighted the importance of perseverance, calling for persistent and unremitting efforts in that regard.
Carlos Martinez, co-founder of the Friends of Socialist China, said: “China is blazing a trail of modernization from outside the framework of imperialism, and China’s progress is proof that socialism with Chinese characteristics is an entirely viable and highly successful model.”
The conference featured three panels. During a discussion on artificial intelligence and technology, speakers compared China’s approach to AI, which they said puts people at the center and promotes industrial development and open-source collaboration, with that of the United States, which they described as more closed and aimed at advancing US interests and dominance.
During the panel discussion on a multipolar world, scholars and activists from Latin America and Africa argued that China’s foreign policy and infrastructure projects bring long-term benefits to their regions. They also praised China’s global initiatives for emphasizing sovereign equality and multilateralism, in contrast to the rising trend of unilateralism in the US and protectionism in the West.
Resisting a new Cold War was the focus of the third panel discussion, where anti-war campaigners warned about the expansion of military alliances, including AUKUS and NATO, and stressed the need to move beyond ideological differences and to oppose imperialists’ military expansion and their drive toward war.
The book China’s Foreign Policy and the Making of a Multipolar World: Changes Unseen in a Century , which was edited by Keith Bennett and Carlos Martinez, co-founders of Friends of Socialist China, was also launched at the conference.
Bennett spoke about public opinion and noted that, with the US and Israel involved in conflicts in Iran and Gaza, a new generation of people has become involved in anti-war politics.
“We hope our book can reach them in explaining the theoretical underpinnings of Chinese foreign policy. We have aimed to highlight continuity amidst change and development,” he said.
More than 120 people attended the conference, which was supported by the Morning Star, the Communist Party of Britain, the Workers Party of Britain, the Communist Party of Ireland, Caribbean Labour Solidarity, No Cold War Britain, the International Manifesto Group, the Black Liberation Alliance and others.

articles.title_orig: Andreeva beats Alexandrova to reach China Open semifinals and next faces Bartunkova
articles.title_zh: Andreeva beats Alexandrova to reach China Open semifinals and next faces Bartunkova
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING (AP) — French Open champion Mirra Andreeva reached the semifinals of the China Open after battling past Ekaterina Alexandrova 7-6 (4), 7-6 (3) on Thursday.
Andreeva had lost her previous two matches against Alexandrova, who rallied back from 4-1 down in the second set and 5-3 down with Andreeva serving for the match.
“I felt like she was playing better and I didn’t take my chances. I could have played more aggressive but what a match this was,” Andreeva said. “She played unbelievable today, and I’m very happy to get my very first win against her.”
The fourth-seeded Andreeva is aiming for a fourth singles title this year and next faces Nikola Bartunkova. She earlier reached her first WTA 1000 semifinal after beating fellow Czech Karolina Muchova 6-3, 6-0.
Bartunkova stamped her authority on the quarterfinal by racing to 5-0 against her seventh-seeded opponent. It was the 20-year-old Bartunkova’s third career win against a top 10-ranked opponent. ___

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
articles.content_orig:
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage
Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US president urged Texas voters to back the embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena.
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. “He’s going back home to mom,” the president said after the man was removed. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”
Supporters waving cowboy hats and chanting “USA” drowned out some of the protesters, while Trump told demonstrators to “get the hell out of here”. He mocked their appearance and claimed without evidence that “they’re paid by enemies of our nation”.
The president also used Wednesday’s rally to address recent comments in which he appeared to suggest that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego, earning widespread condemnation from Democrats.
In remarks that were again less than crystal clear, Trump said: “I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit – you want to see a horror show? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles and you want to see some bad things happen.
“You want to see a country that would be in freefall. We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities, we protect our country, we’re not letting that happen. And they’d use it, too. They’d use it.”
Trump was making his third trip to Texas in less than a month as Republicans pour money into races they had expected to win comfortably in November’s midterm elections.
Paxton, whom Trump endorsed during the Republican primary after turning against the incumbent senator John Cornyn, was called on stage by the president and thanked him for his support.
“Mr President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas,” Paxton said. “We are going to win this race.”
Trump described Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America”, and said: “He was tough and he was with us all the way. He’s a fantastic man.”
The Republican campaign to maintain control of the Senate has become increasingly focused on Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has emerged as a serious threat. A New York Times/Siena College poll released last weekend showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.
Trump won the state by almost 14 percentage points in 2024, but his approval rating has fallen sharply. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday put his approval rating at 32%, while registered voters preferred Democrats to Republicans 44%-37%.
after newsletter promotion
Trump’s relationship with Paxton has sometimes appeared uneasy. Trump called Paxton “a pain in the ass sometimes” last week, but on Wednesday did not discuss a leaked recording of Paxton in which the Senate candidate reportedly complained about the war in Iran, rising fuel prices and the way his campaign was being run.
Instead he spent much of the rally attacking Talarico, whom he repeatedly referred to as “Tala-freako”. He claimed without evidence that Talarico is vegan and recently disappeared: “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”
Trump insisted: “The people of Texas are not going to let weak, gutless, self-hating, transgender-promoting freak shows destroy everything that we’ve built.”
The president’s political difficulties in Texas were underlined by the absence of the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is himself facing a competitive re-election race against the Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa.
Abbott was instead due to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on his decision not to appear with Trump.
Republicans have now devoted more than $300m to elections in Texas, according to the Associated Press, while Trump’s broader 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through several Republican-leaning states, including Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska.

articles.title_orig: Chico State Agriculture Professor Seeks to Deliver Virtual Fences and Real-World Learning
articles.title_zh: Chico State Agriculture Professor Seeks to Deliver Virtual Fences and Real-World Learning
articles.content_orig:
It was mechanical engineering student Ethan Welge’s first time at the University Farm . He trudged onto the muddy, mucky Dairy Unit pasture on this September morning to pilot “Leonard,” a robodog.
The cows were curious. They herded around the mechanical creature—with its spinning LiDAR laser light mounted on its chin—to sniff and size up this little thing in their midst.
“That’s kind of amazing how interested they are,” Welge said, while carefully maneuvering Leonard among the herd.
The exercise was part of agriculture professor Italo Lima’s preparation for a new research project that will use GPS-enabled collars to create virtual fences.
Lima is one of two Chico State faculty members this year to earn a highly competitive CSU Growth in Undergraduate Innovation, Discovery and Engagement (GUIDE) grant. Professor Deserea Langley of the Ethnic, Gender, and Queer Studies Department received $80,000 on a collaboration with Cal Poly Humboldt Native American Studies to increase undergraduate research opportunities and experiential education for Indigenous students. In all, the CSU awarded 26 grants to 18 schools for 2026-27.
Lima received a $40,000 GUIDE grant for “Smart Grazing and Virtual Reality to Improve Organic Dairy Farming and Student Learning.” He’ll hire six undergraduates as researchers this year, and collar dairy cows at the University Farm as part of a virtual fencing experiment. He’ll use the grant money to buy his own robodog, equipped with technology to monitor behavior, health, and location of the cows, as well as pay stipends to the new student researchers.
“The big challenge is grazing management,” Lima said. “Grazing is dynamic. Physical fencing is not. The number of animals grazing changes, the animals change, the forage changes, everything changes over a year or even over a week because of the weather. So why can’t the fence also change?”
Virtual fencing could give livestock producers flexibility. Since the late 19 th century, most U.S. ranchers have used barbed wire to fence in livestock. While effective in keeping cattle enclosed, it can be expensive to install, maintain, and, of course, difficult to reposition. Moreover, barbed wire fencing harms wildlife. A 2006 study published in Wildlife Society Bulletin estimated that every two and a half miles of barbed wire fencing was responsible for killing one deer, elk, or pronghorn a year.
Cost also is an issue with virtual collars, which run upwards of $240 apiece, but prices are expected to drop if or when the technology scales, Lima said.
Using GPS-enabled collars, Lima and his students will draw virtual boundaries across a pasture on smartphones. When a cow crosses a virtual border, its collar will first emit a warning sound. If the cow continues to wander, the collar delivers an “electric stimulus.” The boundary can later be redrawn to move cattle to other grazing areas.
The yearlong experiment will deploy 25 commercial collars to study forage disappearance, grazing distribution, and how cattle adapt to the technology. Lima sees the cows’ response as a research question in itself.
“Part of our research is not only understanding the technology side, but understanding how the animals perceive this technology, how they behave with this technology, and how they adapt and adjust,” he said.
Collars that track cattle location and behavior could have far-reaching benefits for dairy farmers and ranchers. Instead of driving to a distant pasture to check on a herd, a producer could look at a phone to see where cattle are.
“There’s no way to measure how this can change your life,” Lima said.
For students, the project offers something difficult to replicate in a classroom: responsibility for gathering and interpreting their own real-world information.
“Here they’ll be able to build their own data set,” Lima said. “They’ll be able to get their own information. They’ll be able to see things happening in action.”
The six undergraduate researchers will contribute a combined 600 hours to the project, collecting GPS and pasture data and recording cattle behavior with 360-degree cameras. Lima plans to turn the footage and research into virtual reality (VR) instructional materials that could eventually reach hundreds of Chico State students annually.
Lima envisions sharing the materials with other CSU agricultural programs, particularly campuses where students have limited access to livestock.
Lima hopes the project extends beyond a single grant—producing data for larger studies, giving students experience with precision agriculture, and sharing findings with livestock producers.
“Success for me is not finishing the grant,” he said. “It’s more about continuing.”
Michael Drummond is Chico State’s media relations coordinator. He is a Pulitzer Prize finalist, a former war correspondent, author of “Renegades of the Empire,” and enjoys surfing and fishing.

articles.title_orig: Multiple solar eruptions could spark auroras across the northern US starting tonight - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Multiple solar eruptions could spark auroras across the northern US starting tonight - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The ejection is associated with a moderate solar flare.
It's been a busy week for the sun, and aurora watchers in some northern and upper Midwest states looking for a glimpse of the famed colorful sky could benefit from enhanced solar activity Thursday night into Friday morning, Oct. 9.
On Tuesday, a coronal mass ejection (CME), a massive burst of charged particles embedded in a magnetic field, departed the sun bound for Earth.
The ejection is associated with a moderate solar flare.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) has issued a moderate Geomagnetic Storm Watch beginning Thursday evening into Friday, as a result of the CME.
According to NOAA , a geomagnetic storm is "a major disturbance of Earth's magnetosphere that occurs when there is a very efficient exchange of energy from the solar wind into the space environment surrounding Earth."
While the agency says much of the activity will be minor, there could be periods of moderate storm activity. The UK Met Office says there's even a slight chance of strong G3 levels.
The SWPC says the solar activity could create minor impacts to our technological infrastructure, but it's "mainly manageable."
On the bright side, the aurora borealis, which appears in the night sky when electrically charged particles from the sun hit Earth's atmosphere, could be visible in areas that don't normally experience it.
"Aurora may be seen as low as New York to Wisconsin to Washington state," SWPC said in its alert.
Another CME linked to a smaller solar flare is also headed toward Earth but is only expected to deliver a "glancing blow" over the weekend, according to the UK Met Office.
All this solar weather will keep conditions unsettled to active over the next few days. But whether you'll be able to see the auroras depends on exactly when the CME arrives, the cloud cover and the magnetic orientation of the CME's magnetic field.
When geomagnetic activity becomes stronger, the aurora can sometimes be seen farther south than usual.
