articles.title_orig: “We need to see China as it actually is” – China Daily hosts ‘Vision China’ in London
articles.title_zh: “We need to see China as it actually is” – China Daily hosts ‘Vision China’ in London
articles.content_orig:
Intended to showcase vibrant and vivid examples of people-to-people links, China Daily organised a ‘Vision China’ event, held at the global headquarters of the Institution of Civil Engineers in central London, on September 17, with the theme, ‘Listen to Each Other, Open New Horizons’.
With opening addresses by Qu Yingpu, publisher and editor-in-chief of China Daily, and Zhao Fei, chargé d’affaires ad interim of the Chinese Embassy in London, the event also heard from renowned British Sinologist Frances Wood, who is also a vice president of the Society for Anglo-Chinese Understanding (SACU). For Frances, mutual learning was not just a ‘good-to-have’, but also central to her nearly 35 years of work at the British Library, which involved the conservation and digitisation of some 7,000 complete manuscripts and 6,000 fragments of ancient scrolls from Dunhuang, in northwest China’s Gansu province, dating from the third to the 10th century CE.
Michael Spence, president and provost of University College London (UCL), noted the contributions of the college’s 15,000 Chinese students and its many more Chinese alumni, as well as its role in promoting Chinese language learning in schools across the country. Listing some daunting global challenges – from fighting climate change to governing artificial intelligence – Spence said he does not see any “reasons for pessimism”, because what British and Chinese students, scholars and researchers have already achieved through collaboration is “proof of what is possible”.
Other speakers included Chen Junyan, winner of the second prize at the Leeds International Piano Competition in 2024, Mike Longhurst, a fellow of the Royal Photographic Society, and Richard Trainor, provost of the Rhodes Trust at the University of Oxford.
Also addressing the event was Ondřej Dostál, a member of the European Parliament from Czechia (Czech Republic), who began by noting with reference to his country’s socialist period: “I was born in Czechoslovakia, which was never a colonial power, but always helped the developing countries across the world with technologies and education.”
Referring to how times are changing, he continued: “When I was eight, we had elections and I remember seeing posters: ‘With the Soviet Union. Forever and never otherwise.’ When I was eleven, the Soviet Union was no more.”
Disillusioning experiences followed with the United States and the European Union, however: “I first visited China in 2008 to attend a conference on health law.
“After I was elected to the European Parliament, I decided to visit China again. I had the honour of being the only Member of the European Parliament present at China’s Victory Day parade commemorating the 80th anniversary of the victory over fascism. [On September 3, 2025.] And, just over a month ago, on 15 August, I laid flowers at Chairman Mao’s statue in Shaoshan, and saw, not only in the museum, but also in real life, what China has achieved over a mere three generations.
“I saw the incredible development of China in cities such as Shanghai, Hangzhou, Changsha and Ningbo. I saw how China has become the world’s leader in innovation, patents and high-quality productive forces and in technologies that will shape our future.”
But there is still “an enormous gap between the real China and perceptions of China in the West”.
Dostál thinks there are two reasons for that:
He argues: “We need to understand China as it actually is. Its achievements and its contradictions. Its history and its aspirations. Its government and its people.
“Only when we see China as it actually is, can Europe formulate a China policy based on reality rather than projection.”
We reprint below the text of Mr Dostál’s speech, which has been lightly edited by us. It is preceded by China Daily ’s report of the event, written by its journalists Xing Yi and Wang Huazhong.
Sep 19 ( China Daily ) – Engagement with China fosters a deeper understanding of the country and encourages more people from abroad to visit China, meet its people and experience its culture, said experts in education, art and music on Thursday.
They made the remarks during a Vision China event held at the global headquarters of the Institution of Civil Engineers in central London, the United Kingdom. The event, themed “Listen to Each Other, Open New Horizons”, aimed to inspire its audiences to engineer a cultural bridge to overcome boundaries with an inclusive mindset.
The London edition of Vision China followed a recent phone conversation between President Xi Jinping and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. It underscored their consensus on the importance of communication and exchanges in developing bilateral relations.
During the phone call, Xi urged China and the UK to seek common ground while reserving differences and make their mutually beneficial cooperation even stronger. Burnham expressed the UK’s readiness to advance bilateral cooperation across all fields and strengthen people-to-people exchanges.
Qu Yingpu, publisher and editor-in-chief of China Daily, which hosted Thursday’s event, said via video call that “by heeding this shared vision, China and the UK can also encourage the wider international community to bridge differences and work together”.
Even though advancements in technology have made communication quicker and easier, “we still need closer exchanges to break preconceptions that often shape how we see one another”, Qu said.
He called on everyone to see, meet and listen, in order to build better understanding through empathy and carry forward friendly relations. “We need to open new horizons for international cooperation and development, and make greater contributions to building a community with a shared future for humanity,” Qu added.
Zhao Fei, charge d’affaires ad interim of the Chinese embassy in the UK, also gave a speech.
Ondrej Dostal, a member of the European Parliament representing Czechia, said that he has traveled to China several times and has seen how the nation has effectively become the world’s most significant innovator and producer, which is more than mere technological prowess.
For many people in the West, “perceptions have simply failed to keep pace with reality” and there is an “enormous gap between the real China and perceptions of China”, he said, referring to the intentional smearing of China in Western political discourse and media, which is designed to prevent engagement with the country and contain its rise.
“Therefore, a great deal of work is ahead of us in explaining China’s vision to Europe and to the world,” Dostal said, noting that Europe and China face “too many common challenges to allow misunderstandings to define our relationship”.
“Only when we see China as it actually is can Europe formulate a China policy based on reality, rather than projection. Only then can we move beyond outdated stereotypes and manufactured threat narratives. Only then can we move beyond rivalry and finally embrace partnership — and, I hope, friendship,” he added.
For renowned British Sinologist Frances Wood, mutual learning is not just a good-to-have, but also central to her 30 years of work at the British Library, which involves the conservation and digitization of some 7,000 complete manuscripts and 6,000 fragments of ancient scrolls from Dunhuang, Northwest China’s Gansu province, dating from the third century to the 10th century.
She recalled how British and Chinese conservators worked together to repair the fragments, forging friendships and a family-like bond along the way.
“After decades of hard work, we had a lot to show for it — over 7,000 ‘new’ manuscripts transformed from ‘debris’, and the publishing of a series of academic books,” Wood said.
For Chen Junyan, winner of the second prize at the Leeds International Piano Competition in 2024, listening is not a metaphor. “It is what we do,” she said, adding that music education in Shanghai and London taught her that listening helps broaden one’s horizons.

articles.title_orig: Spanish politicians trade blame after death of octogenarian at heart of housing protests
articles.title_zh: Spanish politicians trade blame after death of octogenarian at heart of housing protests
articles.content_orig:
MADRID — María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her longtime Madrid home sparked nationwide protests across Spain and unleashed a political crisis , died on Wednesday while hospitalized.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez led the way on social media offering his condolences after housing activists and Abascal’s lawyer announced her death. Known widely as “Maricarmen,” she had become a symbol for renters struggling with Spain’s housing affordability crisis.
“All my love to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones,” Sánchez said in a post on X. “A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today. Rest in peace.”
Elderly Madrid resident who was forcibly evicted dies at 87
The emotions ran into anger on the street among the protesters gathered near Spain’s Parliament who chanted, “Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on!”
Iciar López, a 32-year-old psychologist, shared her feelings with The Associated Press at the protest in Madrid.
“A great deal of sorrow. And above all, the thought that she is the cause, the head of this whole revolution that has happened, and that she can’t see it,” she said. “It makes me very sad that she can’t see if anything comes of it, if there is any result from all that she has fought for, as well. That’s what angers me the most, honestly.”
Spaniards increasingly frustrated by housing costs periodically march in major cities demanding action from lawmakers. But a fresh wave of indignation has swept Spain since Sept. 23, when Maricarmen, who used a wheelchair, was carried on a stretcher from her home of seven decades after police cordoned off the street and removed protesters. She was taken to a hospital because of her fragile health.
Televised images of the eviction prompted thousands of people to protest in Madrid and other cities across the country.
Maricarmen’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, did not disclose the cause of death when she confirmed it to Cadena Ser radio. Duro said that she and the activists were all devastated.
“Maricarmen’s case, which captured media attention and traveled around the world, leaves us the image of the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the impact they can have on people’s health,” Duro said.
She had been expected to return home after leaving the hospital. The real estate company that evicted her in order to rent the property at a much higher price eventually caved in under immense public pressure and agreed to let her return to the apartment.
“Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return home, this solution came too late,” the Madrid Tenants’ Union said in a statement Wednesday. “It was an entirely avoidable situation following a harrowing ordeal.”
The average rent for Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, according to the real estate website Idealista. Spain’s government said that 26% of Spaniards who rent housing spend an average of 40% of their income on rent and utilities, compared with the European Union average of 18% of renters who do so.
Protesters camped in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square held a minute of silence after learning of her death.
Maricarmen spent almost her entire life in her apartment, where she first lived with her parents and brother. She later worked as a secretary for the board of a pharmaceutical company, Spanish daily El País reported. She said both her parents died in the apartment.
After retiring in 1998, she spent her days walking around the neighborhood, doing errands and taking care of the precious items in her home. The paper reported that black-and-white family photographs were among the only things she had brought with her to the hospital.
“Maricarmen only wanted to die in her home. She wasn’t asking for anything else,” Eugenio Melchor, 22, said at the protest in Madrid. “She was dying in her home and she almost did. They have killed her. I mean, there’s no other word for it, and I hope those responsible for this pay and go to trial.”
Maricarmen’s plight galvanized a social movement, prompted Spain’s unions to announce a general strike next month and intensified pressure on political leaders. Sánchez called an early election Monday after his government failed last week to push emergency housing measures through Parliament. He now hopes the issue will reinvigorate his Socialist Party and help him form a new government after the Nov. 29 election.
Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez also expressed condolences, writing on X: “I deeply lament the death of Maricarmen. My condolences to those who accompanied her and fought by her side until the end.”
Conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who hopes to unseat Sánchez and his left-wing coalition, also offered condolences.
“I want to express my condolences to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones. No campaign, no party, no use for political advantage,” the Popular Party leader wrote. “When faced with the death of a person, we must only show respect.”

articles.title_orig: From coast to coast: China’s national day marked in Canada
articles.title_zh: From coast to coast: China’s national day marked in Canada
articles.content_orig:
In the following article, Arnold August, Canadian author, political activist and an active contributor to the work of Friends of Socialist China, takes the recent celebration of the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China as an occasion to assess the prospects for both enhanced bilateral relations and greater people-to-people friendship.
This year’s anniversary found echoes right across the vast land of Canada, from Prince Edward Island in the Atlantic to British Columbia facing the Pacific. Arnold lays particular emphasis on the role of Canada’s Chinese community, who, often in the face of discrimination and oppression, have, particularly since mass settlement began in the 1850s, made such an important contribution to building and developing their adopted nation and at the same time acting as the sturdy bridge of friendship back to their ancestral homeland.
He also assesses the recent positive developments in the relations between Canada and China, following a somewhat grim period, and especially since Prime Minister Mark Carney’s visit in January this year. Ambassador to Canada Wang Di provides a comprehensive survey of the present state of the relationship in an article contributed to a special supplement of The Hill Times . The Ambassador’s article is reproduced in full in the body of the article below.
Finally, Arnold notes: “Should this new situation mean we should still be careful not to overestimate Canada’s current positive role, since there are always pressures to throw a wrench into this present trend? Yes, it is right to be cautious. On the other hand, should one underestimate the Carney government’s role? The answer to this is no.”
More than 400 guests attended the Chinese Embassy in Canada’s 77th anniversary national day reception on September 24, 2026, held in the capital Ottawa at the iconic Fairmont Château Laurier.
Prince Edward Island (PEI) is one of Canada’s easternmost provinces, situated on the Atlantic coast. This small island is 980 km from Ottawa. Yet the Chinese overseas community there, whose settlement began as early as 1850 amid racist discrimination by the then Canadian government, was well represented at the celebration. The Chinese Society of Prince Edward Island posted on their Facebook account:
“The Chinese Society of Prince Edward Island (CSPEI) was honoured to attend the National Day reception hosted by the Embassy of China in Canada. It was a valuable opportunity to reconnect with old friends, meet new partners, and share how our volunteers bring people together in PEI. We are grateful for the warm conversations, encouragement, and continued support. We’re bringing that energy back to the Island as we prepare for CSPEI’s Mid-Autumn Festival celebration this Saturday [September 26].”
The CSPEI representative at the Ottawa event, Mengyun Candice Chen, posted on her social media: “When you live far from home [China], it means a lot to know there is a place you can turn to for support.” Furthermore, on the eve of the October 1 national day, the CSPEI was instrumental, along with the mayor of PEI’s capital, Charlottetown, in proudly raising the five star red Chinese flag at City Hall.
On October 4, during Golden Week (October 1–7), the CSPEI visited Stratford Elementary School in the province’s capital to highlight Chinese culture, with the Chinese national flag clearly on display.
From the other coast, on the Pacific Ocean, Ali Feiz, from Burnaby (near Vancouver), 3,552 km from Ottawa, was not only present in the nation’s capital at the event, but, as usual on such occasions, made a very important contribution. Ali Feiz has visited and reported on Xinjiang seven times and is one of Canada’s main voices against disinformation about this autonomous region of the People’s Republic. He also posted a photograph with Canadian Senator Victor Oh, the first male Chinese Canadian senator, appointed in 2013, who has consistently advocated for the rights of Chinese Canadians and constructive bilateral engagement. Ali Feiz published this on social media:
In a period marked by renewed dialogue between Canada and China, the Honourable Victor Oh, a prominent figure in the Chinese Canadian community, has emerged as a leading voice for pragmatic engagement. As the first male Chinese Canadian senator, appointed in 2013, he has consistently advocated for the rights of Chinese Canadians and for constructive bilateral engagement. His recent firsthand visit to Xinjiang and his address at the 77th anniversary celebration of the People’s Republic of China in Ottawa illustrates a consistent approach that prioritizes direct observation and people-centered development over distant speculation. In September 2026, the Honourable Victor Oh visited China and traveled to Xinjiang. During his time in Xinjiang, he visited a range of locations. In his address, the Honourable Victor Oh told the story of asking three Uyghur children in a Urumqi school what they wanted to be when they grew up. Without hesitation, they answered, “I want to be a doctor.” This moment, he said, crystallized for him the true measure of development. It is not about abstract statistics but about giving the next generation confidence and hope, ensuring that every hardworking ordinary person can see a tangible future.
On the speech by Honourable Rob Oliphant, Parliamentary Secretary to the Canadian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Ali Feiz pointed out in his X account the following – (it is particularly useful to note Oliphant’s comment on the One China Policy, which is always under pressure):
In his remarks, Honourable Rob Oliphant acknowledged the remarkable achievements of the Chinese people over the past 77 years while also addressing the need for honest dialogue between Canada and China. He stated that Canada will honour and stand up for the One China policy. He emphasised that a mature relationship is built on mutual respect, direct communication, and a shared commitment to addressing global challenges such as climate change, public health, and economic stability. The speech was notable for its balance. Honourable Rob Oliphant highlighted the importance of people-to-people ties, the contributions of Chinese Canadians to the fabric of Canadian society and the value of educational, cultural, and economic exchanges. Honourable Rob Oliphant’s address comes at a pivotal moment in Canada-China relations. Earlier this year, PM Mark Carney’s visit to China brought new momentum to bilateral ties, with both governments describing efforts to build what has been called a new strategic partnership. As Canada and China navigate a pivotal moment in their relationship, the speech served as a reminder that diplomacy is not merely about managing differences but about building bridges. His words will likely be remembered as a significant contribution to that ongoing effort.
In addition to Rob Oliphant, in attendance were Kody Blois, Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Deputy Minister of International Trade, Glenn Purves; Deputy Minister of Canadian Heritage, Francis Bilodeau; and more than a dozen Members of Parliament and Senators, Members of the diplomatic corps, and representatives of Chinese enterprises.
HE Wang Di, the PRC’s Ambassador to Canada, and his wife Liu Yuyu were the hosts. Ambassador Wang addressed the gathering, noting that October 1 this year marks the 77th anniversary of the founding of the PRC, and this year also marks the 105th anniversary of the founding of the Communist Party of China (CPC), and the start of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan (2026—2030). Under CPC leadership, the Chinese people are advancing with confidence toward the goals of building China into a great modern socialist country in all respects and realising the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.
On September 30, the embassy published a special supplement in Ottawa-based The Hill Times celebrating the 77th national day. Ambassador Wang Di contributed a bylined article

articles.title_orig: Marco Rubio brushes off questions about Kimberly Guilfoyle pressing donor to pay credit card
articles.title_zh: Marco Rubio brushes off questions about Kimberly Guilfoyle pressing donor to pay credit card
articles.content_orig:
Eric Deters says US ambassador to Greece asked him to pay off American Express credit card bill in return for access
A Trump donor accused Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece and Trump family ally, of engaging in a “quid pro quo” by asking him to pay off her $100,000 debt in exchange for access to administration officials.
Eric Deters, a former congressional candidate and lawyer, told MS Now on Thursday that Guilfoyle had “ambushed” him last year with an offer to provide access to government officials if he paid her American Express credit card bill, before her US Senate confirmation hearing as ambassador to Greece.
“It absolutely was a quid pro quo,” Deters told the network in response to a Wall Street Journal report that she had pushed him for the money.
“Kimberly Guilfoyle is a grifter,” he added.
The Guardian has asked Guilfoyle’s lawyer for comment.
Jesse Binnall, a lawyer for Guilfoyle, told the Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages, but that she was “owed a balance” for travel and speaking at events before her nomination. Deters told the Journal that he did not owe Guilfoyle any balance.
The report is the latest allegation about Guilfoyle’s conduct as a US official. Deters shared messages he and Guilfoyle exchanged in which the US ambassador to Greece promised him “ride or die” access to Trump administration officials if he wired American Express $100,000.
Asked about the report during a press conference in Athens on Wednesday, Marco Rubio , the US secretary of state, said he would not address the allegations. He reaffirmed his support for the US embassy in Greece adding, “ Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.” Asked again about the reports on Thursday, Rubio refused to comment.
The top Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees have asked Rubio to open an investigation into Guilfoyle’s conduct as an ambassador.
A spokesperson for the Democratic staff of the Senate foreign relations committee confirmed to the Guardian that they were requesting further information and continuing to investigate.
JD Vance similarly expressed hesitation, similar to Rubio, on Thursday when asked to respond to a US ambassador offering access to government officials in exchange for money to pay off debts.
“With that hypothetical, Jen, obviously I don’t love that,” the vice-president replied. “But I don’t know exactly who you’re talking about. I don’t know the full details. What I find with these stories is you never want to comment in a purely abstract way because a lot of times the details really matter,” he added.
Concerns about Guilfoyle’s conduct were first raised in September when the Wall Street Journal reported she had used her position to invite Greek lobbyists to sit in on official diplomatic meetings and promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company.
Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee, sent a letter to Rubio on Tuesday , asking him to look into the allegations against Guilfoyle.
“Such actions do not serve US credibility overseas and risk undermining US diplomacy,” Shaheen wrote. “In advance of your upcoming travel to Greece , I request an immediate review of Ambassador Guilfoyle’s actions and a clarification of what steps have and will be taken to avoid undue influence and even the appearance of a conflict of interest.”
Separately, Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, sent a letter to Rubio in September, requesting more information about Guilfoyle’s conduct, her relationship with the Greek construction and energy company and her relationship with the lobbyist.
“If these reports are accurate, Ambassador Guilfoyle is unfit to represent the United States abroad and should be removed from her position,” Meeks wrote.
Guilfoyle, 57, was once a member of the Trump family’s inner circle, having been engaged to Donald Trump Jr, the US president’s eldest son, for roughly three years. The couple ended their engagement in 2024, and shortly after taking office, Donald Trump nominated Guilfoyle to be ambassador to Greece.
But now further allegations accuse Guilfoyle of promising a Trump donor, Eric Deters, access to the Trump administration in exchange for a $100,000 payment to American Express.
Deters shared messages exchanged between himself and Guilfoyle with the Wall Street Journal in which she reportedly pleaded: “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.”
Deters said Guilfoyle had promised himshe would “be your Trump ride or die, forever and ever” if he made the American Express balance. Deters said he never made the payment.
In other messages, Guilfoyle reportedly raised concerns about her communications with Deters becoming public and reprimanded him for not being discreet. “Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things. It’s really dangerous and not helpful to you or me while you could simply just call me on Signal,” she is said to have written in one message.
“What a nightmare, you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing,” Guilfoyle reportedly wrote in another message.
A lawyer for Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of messages Deters shared with the Wall Street Journal.
It is unclear whether Shaheen or Meeks will ask Rubio for further information about the latest report. The Guardian has asked Meeks and Shaheen for comment.

articles.title_orig: Houston Is Next: A Day of Real-World Healthcare Innovation
articles.title_zh: Houston Is Next: A Day of Real-World Healthcare Innovation
articles.content_orig:
We’re just days away from the Healthcare Innovation Summit in Houston , and I’m looking forward to a great day of listening to an impressive lineup of speakers, connecting with healthcare leaders and having the kinds of conversations that tend to happen when you get a room full of people who are all working through similar challenges.
On Thursday, Oct. 15, I’ll be at the InterContinental Houston with healthcare leaders from across the region for a day of conversations about AI, digital health, cybersecurity, virtual care and, perhaps most importantly, what it actually takes to turn innovation into meaningful change.
If you’ve been thinking about joining us but haven’t registered yet, there’s still time. And after looking at the program we’ve put together, I think there are some very good reasons to make the trip.
Our opening keynote with Pavitra Krishnamani, M.D., M.S., director for AI and digital health education at MD Anderson Cancer Center, takes on something we don’t always talk about enough when we’re discussing healthcare innovation: the human side of transformation.
Technology may be changing healthcare at an incredible pace, but lasting change still comes down to people — how leaders build trust, bring clinicians along and create an environment where innovation can actually take hold.
From there, we’ll tackle a question that every healthcare organization hopes it won’t have to face: What happens when the lights go out?
Richard Staynings, healthcare cybersecurity luminary, and Dr. Attila Hertelendy, assistant professor of information systems and business analytics at Florida International University, will look at disaster medicine and what happens when a hospital or critical vendor is hit by ransomware or a DDoS attack — or when a technology investment simply doesn’t work the way everyone expected.
I like that we’re having this conversation alongside all of our discussions about AI and digital transformation. Innovation is important. But resilience matters, too.
There’s no getting around it. AI is changing healthcare, and it will be a big part of our conversation in Houston. But I think the more interesting question now is what comes after the pilot?
Our session on “Beyond the AI Pilot: Preparing Health Systems for the Era of Agentic Intelligence” will look at the next phase of AI — systems that can orchestrate workflows, automate more complex tasks and play a greater role in clinical and operational decision-making. Adam Cherrington, founder and patient champion at Aligned Health Advisory, will moderate a conversation with Chad Wilson, CEO at Wild Duck Labs AI Research Lab and a former healthcare technology and cybersecurity leader at Stanford Health, Children’s National and MedStar; Elise Ghebremichael, founder and healthcare change strategist at Leader in Change Consulting; Jordan Dale, M.D., VP, CMIO and chief health AI officer at Houston Methodist; and Bryan Vartabedian, M.D., physician leader and former chief medical officer at Texas Children’s Hospital. Together, they’ll bring perspectives from clinical leadership, healthcare transformation, cybersecurity and AI to a conversation about what it will take to move beyond experimentation and responsibly put agentic AI to work.
That raises some pretty important questions about value, governance and human oversight. And those questions become even more interesting when you put them in the context of what health systems are actually doing today.
We’ll also get a firsthand look at how Houston Methodist is approaching clinical transformation, AI and digital innovation. Ginny Torno, senior director of Innovation and IT Clinical Systems, Jordan Dale, M.D., VP, CMIO and chief health AI officer, and Courtenay Bruce, J.D., M.A., chief experience officer and professor of care experience, will share their perspectives on what it takes to bring innovation into practice — from technology and clinical systems to the patient and care experience. It’s a chance to hear from leaders who are actually doing the work, and to explore what it takes to move an idea from the innovation stage into the day-to-day reality of a health system.
That’s another question we’ll explore with Robbie Bullough of KLAS Research, who will share findings from the latest KLAS HIT Trends Report.
AI adoption, cybersecurity, data strategy, interoperability, cloud investments and digital transformation are all competing for attention and budget. The question for healthcare leaders is where to put those resources, and which investments are actually making a difference.
AI may be one of the biggest themes in Houston, but it certainly won’t be the only one.
We’ll also take a look at the hospital of the future, and what happens when healthcare organizations begin thinking beyond the walls of the traditional hospital. Adam Cherrington will moderate a conversation with Mital Brahmbhatt, system director of Care Coordination and Population Health at Memorial Hermann Health System, and Ginny Torno of Houston Methodist about virtual hospitalists, virtual nursing, care coordination and population health — and what it really takes to redesign care around the needs of patients, clinicians and communities.
And we’ll close the formal program with “Protecting Patient Safety in an Environment of AI and Rising Risk.” Richard Staynings, Chad Wilson, Fernando De La Peña Llaca, CEO of AEXA, and David Finn, principal owner of Cyber Health Integrity, will look at the increasingly important role cybersecurity plays as health systems expand their digital and AI footprints. The conversation will touch on cyber resilience, patient safety, regulatory expectations and the challenge of supporting innovation while managing an increasingly complicated threat landscape.
One of the things I’ve always liked about these Summits is that the learning doesn’t stop when someone walks off the stage. There is built-in networking throughout the day, including breakfast, breaks, lunch and an afternoon networking happy hour. And the people in the room are a big part of what makes the day worthwhile.
The Houston Summit brings together CIOs, CISOs, CMIOs, clinical and IT leaders, physicians, healthcare executives and other decision-makers who are dealing with many of these same questions every day. Our Summit surveys tell us that 92% of attendees come to the event with at least one organizational challenge they’re trying to solve. That makes for a pretty interesting room, and hopefully a lot of useful conversations.
I’ll be wearing a few different hats that day, but mostly, I’ll be doing what I always try to do at these events: listening. I’m looking forward to hearing from this terrific lineup of speakers, learning from the experiences they’re willing to share and connecting with the healthcare leaders who will be in the room.
So if you’re coming to Houston, please come find me. Pull me aside during a break. Come say hello at lunch. Stop me after a session. Tell me what you’re working on, what’s going well, what’s keeping you up at night or what you think we should be talking about more.
Those conversations are one of the best parts of my job, and some of the best ideas for Healthcare Innovation have come from people I’ve met at these events.
If you’re still on the fence, there’s still time to register. We’ll be at the InterContinental Houston on Thursday, Oct. 15, beginning with registration, breakfast and networking at 8 a.m. The day wraps up with a networking happy hour at 3:30 p.m.
I hope you’ll join us. Come for the ideas. Stay for the conversations. And please, come find me and say hello.
Register for the Healthcare Innovation Houston Summit
Melinda Taschetta-Millane is Market Content Director of Healthcare Editorial, and Head of Content for Healthcare Innovation.

articles.title_orig: Amazon’s new Alexa Tablets drop the Fire branding but are more Android than ever
articles.title_zh: Amazon’s new Alexa Tablets drop the Fire branding but are more Android than ever
articles.content_orig:
For the last 15 years, you’ve been able to buy a Fire tablet from Amazon. Which Fire tablet? It doesn’t matter—like Kindles, they have been pretty much the same year to year. The company’s new tablet lineup is a big change, though. Amazon has dropped the Fire branding in favor of Alexa, and the new Alexa Tablets are now Google-certified Android devices.
Throughout the history of Fire Tablets, Amazon downplayed its use of Android. They ran Android apps from the company’s Appstore platform, but there was no Google integration with “Fire OS.” However, Amazon shut down its app store last year . The new Alexa Tablets run full-fledged Google-y versions of Android with the Play Store and all the apps you’d expect. This contrasts sharply with Amazon’s Fire Sticks, which have abandoned Android for the custom Linux-based Vega OS.
The Alexa Tablet lineup consists of three devices, all redesigned with unibody aluminum housings. The Alexa Tablet 8 starts at $230, and the Tablet 11 jumps to $330. They run on the budget MediaTek 8189 processor, but that’s still an upgrade from the last-gen Fire tablets . Both devices have 16:10 display ratios that are better for watching video, but the flagship tablet is a little different.
Starting at $500, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro has a taller 3:2 ratio that is better for running multiple apps side by side. It also offers a matte display upgrade for $50, and Amazon sells a keyboard ($150) and stylus ($90) for this device as well. This device runs on a more powerful MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor with 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage. The display clocks in at an impressive 2800×1840 with a 120 Hz refresh rate and 500 nits of peak brightness.
With access to Google apps and the Play Store, you can use Gemini or any other AI that works on Android, but Alexa Plus will be at the core of the experience. You’ll be able to converse with Amazon’s AI bot with the “Alexa” wake word, ask questions, and get product recommendations. Naturally, it will suggest you buy things on Amazon when possible. The AI can also use your screen context to answer questions.
These devices are more expensive than Amazon’s last Fire Tablets, but they’re still competitive with other tablet options in 2026. Apple’s iPad Mini now starts at $600, and the iPad Air is $750. But then there’s the base model iPad at $450, which gets you into the Apple software ecosystem. Amazon’s new tablets are getting a massive software upgrade with the Play Store, but despite Google’s repeated promises, there just aren’t very many Android apps optimized for tablets.
Amazon’s new tablet lineup is available for preorder now and will ship on October 14. By simply being heavily promoted on Amazon, they will probably be among the most popular Android slates on the market.

articles.title_orig: Scottie Pearman heads to Reno eyeing a World Long Drive title after hitting 486-yard drive
articles.title_zh: Scottie Pearman heads to Reno eyeing a World Long Drive title after hitting 486-yard drive
articles.content_orig:
Imagine hitting a golf ball 486 yards. For Scottie Pearman, smashing the ball far is what he's known for.
"A lot of the time it's about right place, right time and right conditions," Pearman said.
During the last year's World Long Drive Championships, Pearman's 468-yard drive helped elevate him to be the No. 1 player in the world. He accomplished that at 4,678 feet of elevation in La Salle, Colo. Now, he'll try to replicate that performance at Reno's  high attitude. The World Long Drive Championships presented by Caesars will make its first stop in Reno when Wildcreek Golf Course hosts the event for the next three years.
"Reno itself is a great hosting site," Pearman said. "When you think of long drive, you think of numbers that are unattainable by most average golfers. We're talking over 400 yards easily. I'm hoping the wind stays a factor because the way it was blowing I feel bad for everyone that has to hit against me."
The idea of a competition featuring golfers hitting the ball as far as they can began in the 1970s. It's gone through several iterations and name changes, but in 2024 the league became known as the World Long Drive Tour. The tour has four divisions, including the Elite Open, Rise, Senior and Women's with more than 100 competitors across those groups. WLD is made up of many former athletes from across several sports, including the NFL, MLB and NHL.
"A normal driver is probably nine to 10 degrees," Pearman said. "My driver, I keep it set three-to-five degrees. They're basically fishing rods attached to a putter. It is hard to hit. It's high-risk, high-reward. But at the end of the day, fortune favors the bold. You've got to go big or go home."
Pearman has never won the World Long Drive championship. But he knows the importance of being able to take home the coveted belt.
"It's basically our Super Bowl," Pearman said. "Of course everyone wants to win a tournament as the year goes on. But at the end of the day, no one really members who won what other than when you hold that belt over your head."
The 2026 World Long Drive Championship runs from Oct. 15-17. A last-chance qualifier event will be held Oct. 14 before Saturday's championship final. You can purchase tickets here . Golf Channel will produce a national broadcast Dec. 1.

What I Cover
Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the…
Global fuel stocks are tighter than they have probably ever been. China just imposed a ban on all fuel exports for the month. Russia has had a diesel export ban in place for months. The United States threatened Europe with a diesel export ban unless European countries released some fuel from storage.
The current crisis is increasingly about fuels, and everyone is prioritizing their own needs.
The topic of resource nationalism is a hot one in energy. Governments of resource-rich countries are being more active in seeking to clinch the best deal with private companies willing to develop these natural resources. But when it comes to energy, it is no longer about the best deal. When it comes to energy, it is about covering local demand for fuels, and because diesel plays such a crucial part in every single economy in the world, diesel is a top priority.
Analysts were warning as early as April that the crisis prompted by the war between the United States and Israel, and Iran, would hurt fuel supply more than crude oil supply. Six months later, the impact is painfully obvious: diesel crack spreads hit an all-time high of over $100 per barrel in September, before easing below that scary threshold; there are not enough refineries to make up for the lost refined product supply from the Middle East; and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky just said his forces will double down on attacks on Russian refineries.
These developments have pushed diesel prices to record highs, notably in the United States, which prompted talk about a potential diesel fuel ban in order to keep the domestic market supplied, the way that Russia and China are banning exports to keep their own markets well supplied. Only there is a difference: when it comes to the United States, it produces more diesel fuel than it consumes, so it is not exactly short. Related: Iraq Builds 2027 Budget on $58 Oil—and a Very Large Deficit
The problem for the U.S. is the price of the fuel, which trades globally.
The U.S. eventually dropped the idea of a ban, with President Donald Trump even saying it was never really going to happen, after he pressured the EU to release 100 million barrels of crude, diesel, and gasoline from storage. Diesel crack spreads declined. Prices ticked lower, though not much lower, with the U.S. national average at $6.3151 per gallon as of Tuesday. European countries are in a much worse position, however, because most of them are highly dependent on imported fuel. In the case of Europe—specifically the European Union—diesel nationalism may turn ugly.
There are plenty of refineries in the EU, but they are a lot fewer than they were 15 years ago. Capacity is not enough to supply all local markets, hence the growing dependence on both crude oil and fuel imports. Now, supply elsewhere is limited in both crude and refined products, regardless of all those optimistic reports about Hormuz reopening and oil flowing freely out of it. Even if it is, this oil is not flowing to Europe.
The diesel release, to take place over the first 20 days of the four-month period for the 100-million-barrel total release, will provide some relief, but it seems the market has already priced it in. It might have also priced in the fact it would be hard to repeat that release at a later date, which is bound to keep prices elevated. Countries that cover their demand with local refining capacity, such as Bulgaria, may be asked to boost exports. Indeed, Bulgaria recently lifted a ban on diesel exports imposed last year, because the country’s only refinery had output to spare. Should demand from other EU members rise, however, things might change.
The Chinese fuel ban will not do heavy fuel importers any favors, either, not to mention Russia’s diesel export ban extension, which will likely be repeated for another month as Ukrainian attacks on refineries continue. Middle Eastern supply is not coming back anytime soon, it seems. Almost all reports about tanker movement in the Strait of Hormuz focus on crude oil, and some LPG cargoes. Refineries in the top refining region, then, must still be under repair after Iranian missile and drone strikes. This leaves the United States as the only major source of refined fuels—a source that is fighting to keep domestic prices under control by any means necessary.
There may be arguable aspects about the war in the Middle East, but one thing has been proven beyond the shadow of a doubt by the fighting and the energy crisis it spurred. Energy security has reclaimed its position as a number-one concern for all countries, even those European ones that have spearheaded the decarbonization drive started after 2015. They still claim decarbonization is a top priority—but it is no longer the number-one priority. The number-one priority is securing enough fuel for the local market and local drivers.
By Irina Slav for Oilprice.com

articles.title_orig: Listening before speaking: conference participants meet local communities in Chiang Mai
articles.title_zh: Listening before speaking: conference participants meet local communities in Chiang Mai
articles.content_orig:
Listening before speaking and walking before leading set the tone for the Joint Conference of the World Council of Churches (WCC) Commissions and Reference Groups on Life, Justice, and Peace, taking place in Chiang Mai, Thailand this week.
Conference participants arrive at the Chiang Mai Breath Council, working with civil society, government, academia, and the private sector to decrease the air pollution that affects the region.
Participants started with encounters with seven civil society and faith-based organisations in and around Chiang Mai. These "sacred journeys of listening, learning, and accompaniment" tied the conference's theological and ethical reflection to local realities.
At the Chiang Mai Breath Council, participants learned how civil society, government, academia, and the private sector work together on the seasonal haze and air pollution that affect the region. The council's vision is sustainable clean air in Chiang Mai – which means addressing outdoor burning, traffic, industry, and cross-border pollution, and calling for a Clean Air Act. Its motto: "…Because we are in the same breath…"
Participants of the conference visited Chiang Mai Breath Council, working to decrease air pollution that affects the region.
Two groups visited Akha and other highland migrant communities that have moved to the city for work, education, and livelihoods. At Kamphaeng Ngam Church, home to an Akha congregation of about 51 families, participants heard stories of displacement and resilience. "Migration is not only movement of people. It carries memory, identity, and hope," the group reflected. At the second church they saw how a congregation offers fellowship and practical support with jobs, family care, and children's education.
At the Migrant Assistance Program Foundation, participants met a grassroots organisation working with migrant workers and their families, mostly from Myanmar. It promotes labour rights and offers information in migrants' own languages, with particular attention to the empowerment of migrant women.
Members of the local encounter group on Health & Well-being (HIV/AIDs) being greeted as they arrive at Happy Home, an HIV programme of the Church of Christ in Thailand run with the Baan Sabaay Foundation.
A visit to the Hua Rin Temple Drug Rehabilitation Center showed a community-based approach to recovery run by a Buddhist temple. It combines spiritual formation, counselling, and vocational activities with help for people returning to their communities.
At Happy Home, an HIV programme of the Church of Christ in Thailand run with the Baan Sabaay Foundation, participants saw a programme that grew from a shelter and crisis centre into outreach for the wider community. People who once received care have become trainers and leaders, and the focus is on overall wellbeing, not just medication.
The seventh group visited Mahachulalongkornrajavidyalaya University, a leading Buddhist university, to learn about its interfaith dialogue with Christian institutions and other communities on peacebuilding, human dignity, and sustainability.
Rev Marvia Lawes, the Abbot Phra Maha Inson Kunavuddho and Thai Muslim leader Ratifar Simarak during the interfaith dialogue visit at the leading Buddhist university near Chiang Mai, with participation of WCC delegates to the Joint Biennial Commisions and Reference Groups Meeting.
The Akha group summed up the lesson of the day: the church is called not only to speak for displaced people, but to walk with them.
The joint conference, being held from 4 to 10 October in Chiang Mai, brings together the WCC's commissions and reference groups on international affairs, climate justice, health, gender justice, racial justice, and ecumenical diakonia. Participants are reading the signs of the times and renewing a century of ecumenical social thought for today's challenges, aiming for shared commitments for the churches' witness in service of life, justice, and peace.

articles.title_orig: Apple Is Set To Show Off New Smart Home Devices At An October 13 Event
articles.title_zh: Apple Is Set To Show Off New Smart Home Devices At An October 13 Event
articles.content_orig:
The event, which it teased with the tagline "Welcome home," is set for 9AM ET.
Apple has announced its second event of the fall , and it sure seems like this one will be focused on smart home products. The event, which it's teased with the phrase, "Welcome home," is set for October 13 at 9AM ET. "We look forward to welcoming you to an Apple Experience," the company said in an invite. The event will take place in Tribeca, New York.
It had been expected for a while that the company would hold an event on that date . Along with refreshed versions of the Apple TV and HomePod mini, it's said that Apple will unveil its long-expected HomePad.
Welcome home. October 13. pic.twitter.com/ChelGSDOTI
— Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) October 8, 2026
It's been rumored for years that Apple has been working on a smart display to rival the likes of Amazon's Echo Show and Google's Next Hub. Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman reported that Apple delayed the device until Siri AI was ready.
The HomePad (as it's expected to be called) is said to have a seven-inch display, a fresh operating system dubbed homeOS and a dashboard that looks similar to the StandBy mode on iPhones. Rumors suggest it'll use face and voice recognition to personalize content based on the person who's operating it at the time. Along with the ability to control smart home products, it's believed that the HomePad will support FaceTime calls, video and music streaming, intercom communication with other devices and many other features.
As for the new Apple TV and HomePod mini, it's likely that those are getting spec upgrades so they can support Siri AI. However, recent macOS beta code suggests the revamped speaker may also gain a display with an Apple Watch-style interface.
October is shaping up to be a big month for Apple. Not only does the company have this latest event on deck, it's set to release the iPhone Duo , its first foldable phone, in a couple of weeks.

articles.title_orig: Feed the Children Marks World Food Day with "It All Begins with Food," Centering Children's Own Words
articles.title_zh: Feed the Children Marks World Food Day with "It All Begins with Food," Centering Children's Own Words
articles.content_orig:
OKLAHOMA CITY, Oct. 8, 2026
OKLAHOMA CITY , Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- On World Food Day, Oct. 16, Feed the Children, a global movement working to end child hunger, is sharing "It All Begins with Food"—a World Food Day awareness effort built on the words of children themselves. Daniela in El Salvador, Halima in Tanzania, Andrew in the Philippines and Bodi in the United States each describe, in their own words, who they hope to become. Their voices are central to Feed the Children's World Food Day observance, appearing across feedthechildren.org , social content and more. The reality behind these stories is urgent: according to UNICEF, one in four children under age 5 worldwide is living in severe child food poverty—181 million children who don't have reliable access to the nutritious food they need to grow, learn and thrive.
Food is the starting point for everything a child can become. When children eat consistently and well, they show up to school ready to learn, they grow into their potential and they begin to imagine and pursue futures that are entirely their own. That's what World Food Day, observed each year on Oct. 16, calls the world to recognize: food isn't just sustenance—it's the foundation of possibility.
"No child should go to bed hungry. No child. Anywhere," said Emily Callahan, president and CEO of Feed the Children. "When children have enough to eat, they show up to school, they stay healthy and they start building the futures they deserve. Ending child hunger is possible—but only if we do it together."
Children Share What Food Makes Possible
Daniela is 9 years old and wants to be a police officer in El Salvador—someone who protects her country and looks out for her family. Half a world away in Tanzania, 12-year-old Halima wants to become a journalist, determined to tell the stories of her village to the world. In the Philippines, 10-year-old Andrew channels a love of math and problem-solving into a dream of becoming an engineer. And in the United States, 9-year-old Bodi is already imagining a future shaped by his love of soccer.
Each child's story reflects countless others across the communities Feed the Children works alongside. Their words speak for themselves. "Food is important to be a good athlete," says Bodi. Andrew is just as direct: "I like eating at school because I get to eat good food with my classmates." In Tanzania, when Halima's family's sweet potato harvest fell short, Feed the Children worked alongside her community to strengthen nutrition while advancing Livelihoods & Resilience programming. The experience helped shape the future she imagines for herself. "I want to study hard, tell the stories of our village, and show how we can achieve great things together," she says.
The scale of the challenge is clear. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, an estimated 645 million people faced hunger in 2025. In the U.S., up to 40% of the food supply goes to waste each year, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration—a stark reminder of how much inequity exists within our food system and how much more is possible when communities, partners and donors work together. The data is striking, but the conclusion isn't hopelessness. It's urgency.
Scale of Reach, Depth of Impact
In fiscal year 2025, Feed the Children distributed nearly 78 million meals to nearly 15 million people spanning almost every U.S. state and eight countries: El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Kenya, Malawi, Tanzania, Uganda and the Philippines.
This October, the organization is celebrating the opening of two new Feed the Children Food & Essentials Hub locations: School of Dreams Academy Charter School in Los Lunas, New Mexico and Mater Academy of Nevada East Campus in Las Vegas. The program works directly with school districts to provide students with food, essential household items, personal care products, books and school supplies throughout the school year.
Program-wide in fiscal year 2026, Feed the Children Food & Essentials Hubs reached more than 154,900 students and 58,600 households across 834 schools in 11 states—providing more than 686,000 meals and more than $6.7 million in food, essentials, books and school supplies. The results speak to what consistent access makes possible: 87% of participating school districts reported improvements in student confidence and attendance, and nearly two-thirds of caregivers said the program helped reduce the need to cut or skip meals for their children.
This World Food Day, Feed the Children invites supporters to explore and read the stories of children whose own words are at the heart of "It All Begins with Food" because when children have the food and support they need most today, they can begin to imagine who they will become tomorrow. Together, we can help create a world where no child goes to bed hungry.
Feed the Children is a global movement working to end childhood hunger in the U.S. and around the world. Together with communities, the organization provides food, essentials and opportunities to children and families who need them most so every child can survive and thrive. Learn more at feedthechildren.org .
Create a world where no child goes to bed hungry.

articles.title_orig: Maker’s Mark Launches New World Wood Collection
articles.title_zh: Maker’s Mark Launches New World Wood Collection
articles.content_orig:
Maker’s Mark Launches New World Wood Collection
Maker’s Mark announced the World Wood Collection, a new Global Travel Retail-exclusive series celebrating the influence of oak from around the world.
The inaugural release, Expedition 01 , marks the first Maker’s Mark whisky to feature three oak finishes across three continents: Japanese Mizunara, French and American white oak staves.
The World Wood Collection represents the evolution of Maker’s Mark’s wood finishing philosophy, first introduced with Maker’s Mark 46, which demonstrated how oak staves could unlock new dimensions of flavor in bourbon while remaining true to the brand’s handmade heritage. Maker’s Mark has long treated oak as a key ingredient—not simply a container for its whisky, and has invested in advancing both the art of wood finishing and the stewardship of American white oak at Star Hill Farm.
“At Maker’s Mark, we celebrate bourbon as an agricultural product and the universe of flavor that can be unlocked through nature—water, wheat, oak and time,” Rob Samuels, managing director and eighth-generation whisky maker, said in a news release. “That belief has long guided our commitment to sustainable forestry and to protecting the future of American white oak. Through intentional wood finishing, The World Wood Collection explores exceptional oak from around the world to create a whisky that expands the boundaries of flavor while staying true to our craft.”
Expedition 01 brings together Japanese Mizunara, French and American white oak, with each whisky individually finished before being expertly blended into a single expression. The result is a complex, balanced whisky in which every oak contributes its own distinctive character.
“Expedition 01 represents the kind of premium, story-driven whisky experience that resonates with today’s global travelers,” Vanessa Widmann, managing director for Global Travel Retail at Suntory Global Spirits, said. “With its exclusive availability in Global Travel Retail, distinctive oak-forward story and premium presentation, it offers travelers a rare opportunity to discover a truly unique expression from Maker’s Mark — one that celebrates craftsmanship, exploration and the influence of exceptional oak.”
Available exclusively through Global Travel Retail ahead of Holiday 2026, Expedition 01 is bottled at 1L and 47.5% ABV and presented in premium packaging inspired by the distinctive grain of each oak species, reinforcing the collection’s focus on craftsmanship and discovery.
The limited-edition expression will be available beginning today in New York (JFK), London (LHR), Istanbul (SAW), Perth (PER), and Bengaluru (BLR) through Avolta retail outlets for the suggested retail price of $84.99.
For more information, visit www.makersmark.com.
Read more: Maker’s Mark to Release 2026 Cellar Aged Bourbon
In 1953, founders Margie and Bill Samuels, Sr. broke from tradition — burning the family’s 170-year-old recipe to create a bold, balanced bourbon made with soft red winter wheat for signature sweetness and creaminess. Every bottle is still hand-dipped in red wax, every barrel rotated by hand and every decision guided by the brand’s higher purpose. Maker’s Mark is proud to be both B Corp and Regenified Certified – milestones driven by the sustainability leadership at Star Hill Farm, home of the Maker’s Mark Distillery. For more information, visit www.makersmark.com .

articles.title_orig: Attorneys general cite China ties in call to end judicial training partnership
articles.title_zh: Attorneys general cite China ties in call to end judicial training partnership
articles.content_orig:
DES MOINES, Iowa  — Iowa's Attorney General is leading a group of 23 attorneys general asking the National Judicial College (NJC) to end it's relationship with an environmental organization they say has ties to China.
The NJC offers courses in courtroom skills to judges across the country. In January, the school offers a course titled "Climate Change and Water: Droughts" focusing on legal questions about water management in a changing climate. The coalition says that course was sponsored by the Environmental Law Institute (ELI).
"Judges should rule based on an impartial interpretation of the law,” said Attorney General Bird. “But if they are trained by an organization that has been influenced by another government, and a hostile one at that, that impartiality is at risk. That’s not right for Iowans who believe they are getting a fair shake when they appear in front of a judge. The NJC needs to end their relationship with an organization with ties to China.”
Earlier this month, ELI issued a statement about allegations in a report about their work. "...we have repeatedly explained our judicial education work and the principles that govern it: CJP provides voluntary, evidence-based judicial education about climate science, impacts, and solutions, and how they arise in the law. CJP does not tell judges how to rule in any case or on any issue. Nor are its programs designed to achieve a particular outcome," the statement says.
The attorneys general want the college to suspend the partnership, preserve records and review whether its educational materials were improperly influenced.
The letter does not identify a judge or court decision shown to have been influenced by China.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias threatens northern Gulf Coast with heavy rain, flooding. See maps, forecast path.
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias threatens northern Gulf Coast with heavy rain, flooding. See maps, forecast path.
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Isaias is intensifying Thursday and expected to make landfall along the U.S. Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday, threatening parts of Mississippi, Alabama and the western part of the Florida Panhandle. It became the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season after strengthening from a tropical storm late Wednesday night.
A hurricane warning is in effect for the northern Gulf Coast, from the Mississippi-Alabama state line, across southern Alabama, to Panama City, Florida.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for more than two dozen counties in his state, and Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties. Government buildings will close in nine Alabama counties on Friday, Ivey announced.
The U.S. Coast Guard also said it was preparing for Friday's landfall and urged seafarers near the Gulf to stay informed and remain vigilant leading up to the hurricane's approach.
"Extremely high seas, heavy rains, and damaging winds that accompany tropical storms and hurricanes present serious dangers to the public," the agency said in a statement Thursday.
Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," had maximum sustained winds of 85 mph at 2 p.m. ET, and its core was located about 355 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River, according to the National Hurricane Center. Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 15 miles from the storm's center, and tropical-storm-force winds extended outward up to 90 miles.
"Additional strengthening is expected through early Friday, and Isaias should remain a dangerous hurricane as it approaches the northern Gulf Coast on Friday night," the center said, emphasizing that "preparations to protect life and property from storm surge and damaging winds along the warning area of the Gulf Coast should be rushed to completion."
Mandatory evacuations have been ordered in parts of Florida's Okaloosa and Walton counties, which took effect Thursday at 12 p.m. ET. Voluntary evacuations were in place for coastal spots in southeastern Alabama, with officials in the city of Gulf Shores urging non-residents to leave the area to "help reduce congestion, support emergency operations, and ensure the safety of those who may be most vulnerable during the storm."
Dauphin Island Mayor Jeff Collier told CBS News on Thursday that his biggest concern for the coastal Alabama community was whether its residents and visitors would heed official warnings.
"Because what inevitably happens is people hear the warnings, but they don't actually take any action until it's much too late," Collier said. "And oftentimes if it's really bad, first responders can't get out to people until things calm down a bit."
Along with the hurricane warning, a tropical storm warning was issued from the southeast corner of Louisiana to Biloxi, Mississippi, plus in and around Apalachicola, Florida. A storm surge warning was issued from the mouth of the Mississippi River in southeastern Louisiana, across the coasts of Mississippi and Alabama, into the Florida Panhandle. A storm surge watch was also in effect for parts of Florida's Big Bend region, along the Gulf Coast.
The hurricane center forecasts 3 to 7 inches of rain and as much as 15 inches in some places along the coast from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. Much of the Southeast, and as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas, could see heavy rainfall.
Forecasters said rain could cause flooding, including in urban areas and around rivers, "some of which could be significant." Tornadoes may also materialize Friday night into Saturday in coastal parts of Alabama, Georgia and the Florida Panhandle, they added.
Isaias' progression into a hurricane on Wednesday marked the latest date in 121 years for the Atlantic season's first hurricane to develop, just missing a record set on Oct. 8, 1905, according to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data.
The season, which has been unusually quiet in the Atlantic this year, runs from June 1 through Nov. 30.
An Atlantic hurricane season typically produces, on average, 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes, according to the hurricane center, which used climate data collected between 1991 and 2020 to calculate those figures. A season's first named storm normally forms in mid- to late-June, while the first hurricane tends to form in early- to mid-August, and the first major hurricane often comes in late August or early September.
Forecasters predicted there would be less Atlantic storm activity than usual this year, but so far it has been even quieter than anticipated. Meteorologists say that's largely due to the onset of a strong El Niño over the summer, which typically correlates with cooler water temperatures and greater fluctuations in wind patterns over the Atlantic, conditions that dampen the growth of tropical systems. The Pacific, meanwhile, has seen an unusually active series of hurricanes.
Nikki  Nolan contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Army probe results in sweeping recommendations after Washington air disaster
articles.title_zh: Army probe results in sweeping recommendations after Washington air disaster
articles.content_orig:
A US Army report on a deadly midair collision between a Black Hawk helicopter and an American Airlines regional jet landing at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport is now public, after months of pressure from the families of the passengers killed when the aircraft collided.
The 50-page document dated on May 14, 2026, was first reported by The Washington Post and details a series of systemic failures on the night of January 29, 2025, that ultimately led to the deaths of 67 people on the two aircraft.
The report, which was provided to victims’ families by the Army, summarizes the internal military investigation that coincided with the National Transportation Safety Board’s public probe completed earlier this year.
Army investigator Lt. General Michael McCurry found the helicopter crew was qualified and the Black Hawk didn’t have a mechanical failure, but “broken radio communications, instrumentation inaccuracies, intense urban lighting while operating under night vision goggles, and gusty winds with turbulence” made it hard to see and stay away from the American Airlines regional jet.
“Simultaneously, the layers of structural, procedural and technical risk mitigation failed to prevent a collision,” the report added.
The report also details recommendations the Army made to prevent a similar accident from happening again, but it does not assign individual responsibility or detail any disciplinary actions.
“Recommendations for change are important, but they are not a substitute for accountability,” said Tim Lilley, whose son Sam was the first officer flying American Airlines Flight 5342. “The Army owes the families and the American public a full accounting of how these risks were allowed to persist, who was responsible for the decisions that allowed them to persist and what will be done to make sure this never happens again.”
One recommendation included calling for wider use of anti-collision systems, called ADS-B on Army aircraft. The Black Hawk was not transmitting its location on the night of the collision, investigators found.
The Army’s report called for transmitting data, called ADS-B Out, when flying near Washington, DC, and receiving data, called ADS-B In, when flying in busy urban environments.
The families are calling for the systems to be implemented in all aircraft.
Two competing bills have stalled in Congress – one passed by the House and the other by the Senate – that would require the systems. The families want the measures to be combined, and the reconciled bill approved by both bodies.
“We have waited long enough,” Families of Flight 5342 said in a statement. “We waited for the NTSB. We waited for the Army. Both investigations are complete, and both make clear that collision avoidance technology must be part of the solution. There is nothing left for Congress to wait for.”

articles.title_orig: A year into Trump’s peace plan, Netanyahu stands in the way of rebuilding
articles.title_zh: A year into Trump’s peace plan, Netanyahu stands in the way of rebuilding
articles.content_orig:
Three years after Hamas militants launched their assault on southern Israel, killing 1,200 people, taking 251 others hostage and triggering Israel's war in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians, CBS News met two teenagers on both sides of the Gaza border to find out how they are coping.
Ron Shargian, 15, said growing up in southern Israel has meant learning to live with fear. He was 12 when he watched Hamas militants on paragliders soar over a wall meant to protect his community.
"It feels like some kind of nightmare," he told CBS News three years later, calling the experience on that fateful day surreal, "and something I wouldn't believe if anyone told me it's going to happen."
The attackers killed 17 of his neighbors in Netiv HaAsara, the Israeli community that was closest to the Gaza border.
As the assault unfolded, he and his family locked themselves inside their home's bomb shelter.
"Every time the gunshots get close to you, you think that that's the end, that they're coming to your house now," he recalled.
His family escaped after 11 hours, when security forces came to the rescue, but like thousands of other Israelis displaced by the war, they couldn't go back home, at least not right away.
After Oct. 7, Shargian's family lived in a hotel for evacuees, and then in Tel Aviv, and then in another hotel, and then a year and a half in the coastal town of Gan Yavne. Finally, a little over a year ago, his family returned to their home.
"It was really hard to come back," he said. "But I also anticipated it very much. I really missed my home, my friends, the community — it's something that you don't have anywhere else."
Across the border in Gaza, safe places have been hard for Palestinian children to find since Israel launched its full-scale military assault in retaliation for the Hamas attack.
"Lots of things has been destroyed for me," Kazem Doghmash told CBS News. He was 11 when the war started.
Israel pummeled Gaza for years with daily airstrikes in a grueling war that, despite a cease-fire in place since last October ending major combat, continues to claim lives three years later . Palestinian officials in Gaza say more than 1,400 people have been killed in Gaza since the cease-fire officially came into effect.
"They say a lot of times that the war will finish, but the war has been not finished, the war has been more difficult," said Doghmash, who is now 14.
"Before the war, I am just being a kid," he said, remembering it as "a good life."
In Israel, Shargian said he struggles with how to think about people on the other side of the Gaza border after everything that happened.
"I don't know if there are good people there," he said. "Up until October 7th, I thought that we could make peace. But from that day, something inside me broke."
He is trying to move forward and lead a normal teenage life — learning the guitar, hanging out with friends at the beach, and he told CBS News the wider conflict now engulfing the Middle East can, at times, even feel distant.
"I don't think we feel the war so much, like, it's in other countries," he said.
When the sound of a rocket or an air raid siren jolts him back to reality, he said like most Israelis, he takes it in his stride.
"Because we're so used to this reality," he said. "So, we just don't make a big deal out of it."
But even though it has happened throughout his life, he said he still feels it inside, every time he and his family or friends hear an alarm and have to rush for shelter.
"Your muscles get tight and you have an adrenaline rush," he said. "It's something we just got used to."
Moving forward has been hard for Doghmash, too. He still can't think about returning to normal teenage pursuits.
"My life has been destroyed," he said. "My school has been destroyed, a lot of things have been destroyed for me."
"We are focusing [on] how we're going to live," he said.
But he hasn't given up on his dreams. He told CBS News he hopes to become a doctor, and he has resumed studying at the British International School in Gaza —   in its new location, as the original building was destroyed by Israeli airstrikes —   where his favorite subject is English.
As he led CBS News through the rubble of what used to be his family's home, he longed for anything resembling a return to his life before the war.
"We need to live in a good life, not to just, thinking how we're gonna get food and the water," he said. "We're gonna need to go to school, to go, to be happy and smile."
The United Nations Children's Fund says more than 21,000 Palestinian children have been reported killed in Gaza since Oct. 7, 2023, as a result of Israel's counteroffensive.
Dozens of Israeli children have died, too, including 37 killed in the initial Hamas attacks.
Despite everything they've been through, both boys are still finding moments in life to just be kids.
CBS News' Becky Perlow and Anas Zeyad Fteiha contributed to this report.
Tucker  Reals contributed to this report.
