articles.title_orig: Webull Stock Falls 20% Over China Ties: Who Really Controls the App?
articles.title_zh: Webull Stock Falls 20% Over China Ties: Who Really Controls the App?
articles.content_orig:
Digital investment platform Webull , which counts 28 million global users , is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government, representing a national security threat to U.S. finance, according to a bipartisan congressional panel's findings shared exclusively with CNBC.
The bipartisan House Select Committee on China in its new report being released Wednesday found "a profound gap" between Webull's public marketing as "an American company" and actual control of the St. Petersburg, Florida-based firm.
"Webull's ownership architecture, technical workforce, technology infrastructure, cross-border data routing, corporate financing, and compliance frameworks are tied in structural ways to the People's Republic of China," the committee found.
The panel asserted that national security concerns around the company have "escalated" since October 2025, when Webull began carrying customer cash directly, according to a regulatory filing the panel cited. The committee alleges that creates a "structural exposure of billions of dollars in American capital."
The committee said the company's corporate structure means the firm's "software development, data pipelines, and core engineering operations" are dependent on infrastructure subject directly to Beijing's laws. And those laws in China can compel firms to cooperate with the government in myriad ways, including data transfers.
Webull took issue with the report, saying via a spokesperson, "It is deeply disappointing that the Select Committee published a report containing significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions without ever seeking clarification from Webull." "Webull's U.S. business is conducted from its global headquarters in St. Petersburg, Florida and its office in New York City, while U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S. and access to sensitive customer data is controlled by the U.S.," the spokesperson said via email. "We remain prepared to address any questions directly and with the same transparency we bring to the SEC, FINRA, and regulators worldwide."
Webull's stock plummeted 18% in morning trading.
Rep. John Moolenaar , R-Mich., told CNBC in a statement that Webull's "China-based operations put American investors and their data at risk."
"Using technology providers in mainland China and an opaque China-linked ownership structure, Webull exposes its data to our foremost adversary," said Moolenaar, who chairs the House committee that issued the report. "Investors should heed this information when choosing who they do business with."
Webull, which trades on the Nasdaq stock exchange, says it operates a "global network of licensed brokerages," offering investment services in 18 markets around the globe. The online brokerage says it provides retail and institutional investors with 24/7 access to global financial markets. Users of the platform can trade global stocks, exchange-traded funds, options, futures, fractional shares and digital assets on the service.
Former Alibaba and Xiaomi manager Wang Anquan founded Webull in 2016 . Its competitors include Robinhood , Charles Schwab and E-Trade .
The congressional committee, which had requested information from the company in 2024, said Webull represents a national security risk because "critical backend systems, personnel and data flows may remain exposed to the Chinese Communist Party's mandatory intelligence laws and coercive demands."
The committee said in its report that Webull Financial's "intricate corporate and technology framework" is tethered directly to China.
Webull Corp. is a Cayman Islands-incorporated holding company, and the report found it holds $24.6 billion in customer assets. And although the company has a U.S. holding company known as Webull Holdings (US) Inc., the report says the company's technology structure also includes Webull Technologies Pte. Ltd, which is a Singapore-based entity. And the report says Webull uses a mainland China-based subsidiary that supports technology development and platform operations. The company traces its origins to Hunan Fumi Information Technology Co., Ltd., a Chinese company that originally launched the business.
The release of the report comes on the heels of a largely friendly summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in September, and it comes ahead of further meetings between the two leaders later this year. It reflects concerns on Capitol Hill that the Chinese government could be planting seeds inside the U.S. financial system that could later be used to disrupt the American economy in the event of further conflict.
The committee also alleges Webull misrepresented the number of its China-based employees. In the report, the committee said the company initially told the committee it "does not have any offices or employees based in the PRC," and that "all Firm employees are located in the United States." But the committee says the firm remains operationally concentrated in China, with its mainland subsidiary, Hunan Weibu, growing to 863 employees, or 62% of the company's global workforce.

articles.title_orig: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro expected to face more charges this week
articles.title_zh: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro expected to face more charges this week
articles.content_orig:
Federal prosecutors are expected to bring additional charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, the BBC's US media partner CBS has reported.
The new charges accuse them of playing a role in the torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan prisons, according to CBS.
US forces seized Maduro and Flores from their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, in a dramatic, night-time raid on 3 January, and brought them to New York to face charges for alleged weapon and drug offences, which they deny.
The BBC has contacted Maduro's lawyer for comment as well as the US Attorney's office in Manhattan ​which brought the charges.
Additional people may be charged for their role in torturing more than a dozen Americans who were wrongfully detained by the Venezuelan government under Maduro, CBS reports.
Maduro's attorney, Barry Pollack, told CBS that he was not provided notice about any additional charges.
Flores, who is facing drug trafficking and weapons charges, is scheduled to appear in federal court for a bond hearing on Thursday in New York.
The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027.
The US has accused Maduro of narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine-importation conspiracy, and possession of and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.
He and 14 others were first indicted in 2020, during President Trump's first term.
Prosecutors have alleged that Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices engaged in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnered with cartels designated as terrorist groups.
They said the accused "abused their positions of public trust and corrupted once-legitimate institutions to import tons of cocaine into the United States".
Maduro has previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.
He and his wife's lawyers have asked the court to dismiss the charges because he is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal. The judge has not ruled on their requests.

Guilfoyle, 57, now the U.S. ambassador to Greece, begged for a cash infusion from Eric Deters, a 63-year-old former congressional candidate from Kentucky, he tells the Wall Street Journal , which also reviewed alleged Signal texts between the two.
Deters released a dossier of photos with Guilfoyle during the time in which he was paying her.
âIt wonât show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,â the Trump-appointed Guilfoyle texted Deters, according to the Journal. âPlease.â
In another message shared with the Journal, she allegedly wrote: âHoney please I need you to get this done for me today. You could just send it here.â
This is the message Guilfoyle sent to Deters asking for the money saying "It won't show up anywhere of you wire money to American Express..."
The Journal reports that the latter text, complete with a prayer hands emoji and a PDF with bill payment instructions from American Express, was sent on July 3, 2025, less than a week before her July 9 confirmation hearing.
The texts came as Deters was seeking Guilfoyleâs help in âgetting the attention of the new Trump administration on some personal tax and legal issues,â according to WSJ.
Among the pictures of Deters and Guilfoyle are images from the Kentucky Derby.
Deters ultimately did not make the payment. He says he told Guilfoyle, then still freshly split with Donald Trump Jr., that doing so would end his marriage. However, the Journal reports that in one message, Deters wrote that he has paid Guilfoyle $300,000 over the years and had ânot received one favor.â

Guilfoyle responded that Deters needed to stop creating a paper trail.
Deters and Guilfoyle posed for photographs together repeatedly.

The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Daily Beast.
Deters appeared in a series of photographs with Guilfoyle when they met.
Guilfoyleâs lawyer, Jesse Binnall, told WSJ that he disputes the messagesâ authenticity, but declined to provide specifics to the paper. He said Guilfoyle âwas owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events.â Deters denies he owed Guilfoyle anything.

The bipartisan Senate Foreign Relations Committee fully vetted her, and the U.S. Senate confirmed her. The Ambassador remains committed to representing the American people with dedication and integrity.â
However, in texts reviewed by WSJ, she appeared aware of the seriousness of her dealings with Deters.
âItâs unbelievable when we have a private arrangement with you that you would now CC a producer talking about money,â she allegedly texted him, upset that Deters told a producer on her podcast about their deal. âDo not say we have any arrangement.â

articles.title_orig: Nobel physics winner's pride at pioneering AI role
articles.title_zh: Nobel physics winner's pride at pioneering AI role
articles.content_orig:
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory, the world’s largest telescope.
Will Cushman, wcushman@wisc.edu, (563) 543-2318
Today, Francis Halzen , a University of Wisconsin–Madison professor of physics, was named the recipient of the Nobel Prize in physics at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden.
The prize was conferred for Halzen’s contributions to our understanding of the astrophysical particles known as neutrinos, produced by the universe’s most energetic events.
Watch the livestream of the press conference with Professor Halzen and leaders from UW–Madison.
“This is a celebration of a very unusual project,” says Halzen. “It is difficult to imagine that we could have pulled this off anywhere but at UW–Madison with its unique research infrastructure. The success of this project involved some luck, and I was fortunate to be at UW, where unconventional ideas can thrive and where I had the support of a remarkable community, from talented engineers at the Physical Sciences Laboratory to long-time colleagues on the faculty and supportive administrators. It is hard to imagine this project happening anywhere else.”
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory , the world’s largest — and perhaps strangest — telescope. The U.S. National Science Foundation-funded observatory is operated by an international collaboration of scientists led by the Wisconsin IceCube Particle Astrophysics Center based at UW–Madison.
Embedded in a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice, IceCube uses thousands of light sensors to survey the universe for neutrinos, nearly massless particles that rarely interact with other matter. Neutrinos provide information about the workings of black holes, galaxies and other objects in the cosmos.
“IceCube is like no other telescope in the world,” says UW–Madison interim Chancellor Eric M. Wilcots. “And there is no other scientist quite like Francis Halzen, whose idea to create a neutrino detector under almost a mile of ice has led to a remarkable multinational and multi-institutional scientific collaboration and a fundamental shift in how we think about the universe.”
Unlike the neutral neutrino, cosmic rays are charged particles whose paths cannot be traced directly back to their sources. But the powerful cosmic accelerators that produce them, like supermassive black holes, will also produce neutrinos. These so-called “ghost particles” travel nearly undisturbed from their accelerators, giving scientists an almost direct pointer to their source.
Along with observations by other telescopes, the neutrino first detected by IceCube provided the first-ever evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic rays, whose origins have been notoriously difficult to pinpoint since their discovery over 100 years ago by 1936 physics Nobel laureate Victor Hess.
In 2013, IceCube announced the first detection of high-energy neutrinos from outside the solar system. The finding opened a new era of “multi-messenger astrophysics” in which not only light but particles like neutrinos and gravitational waves can provide us with information about distant cosmological events, like supermassive black holes located at the heart of galaxies. The discovery won the 2013 Physics World Breakthrough of the Year Award.
Four years later, in September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from a supermassive black hole at the center of a distant galaxy in the direction of the constellation Orion. More recently, IceCube provided the first evidence of high-energy neutrino emission from an active galaxy 47 million light-years away, in 2022, and from the Milky Way, in 2023. These detections demonstrated that all three of these sources produce cosmic rays. Most recently, IceCube was successfully upgraded, marking the observatory’s first significant expansion since its completion 15 years ago.
With this award, Halzen becomes the sixth physicist connected to UW–Madison to earn the Nobel Prize. It’s the 23rd Nobel Prize tied to UW–Madison overall , in a legacy that spans medicine, chemistry, economics, engineering and physics. The last active UW–Madison faculty member to win a Nobel Prize was Howard Temin in 1975 , honored for his discovery of reverse transcriptase — a breakthrough that reshaped molecular biology and deepened understanding of diseases like Hepatitis B and HIV.
Tags: faculty awards , IceCube , Nobel Prize , physics , research
Francis Halzen, winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics, joins a community of Badgers who’ve changed the world.
UW–Madison has been named the top volunteer-producing university since 2017.
“Best Value Schools” ranking also jumps 23 spots, placing UW–Madison 24th in the nation.
The project ensures that UW–Madison’s efforts at IceCube remain at the forefront of neutrino astronomy for years to come.

articles.title_orig: World leader in livestock fertility research closes out 58-year career
articles.title_zh: World leader in livestock fertility research closes out 58-year career
articles.content_orig:
After 58 years, Fuller Bazer, Ph.D., a University Distinguished Professor in the Texas A&M College of Agriculture and Life Sciences Department of Animal Science , will close out his scientific career in October.
During his groundbreaking tenure, Bazer also held joint appointments in the College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences Departments of Veterinary Integrative Biosciences and Veterinary Physiology and Pharmacology ,
“Dr. Bazer has built an enduring legacy as one of the foremost reproductive scientists in the world,” said Clay Mathis, Ph.D., head of the Department of Animal Science, “Dr. Bazer may be retiring, but his innovative work that transformed our understanding of pregnancy establishment in livestock will continue to have an impact on the industry for many years to come.”
Bazer is a Regents Fellow, Distinguished Professor, Presidential Impact Fellow, and the O.D. Butler Chair in Physiology of Reproduction, as well as a top researcher in the world in the “Animal Science and Veterinary” category, as named by Research.com .
At 88, he is ranked, according to Google Scholar, as the most highly cited researcher in the field of reproductive biology. He is credited with discovering uteroferrin, a phosphatase, produced in response to progesterone that transfers iron to the developing embryo and stimulates red blood cell development. He also identified estradiol as the pregnancy recognition signal in swine and interferon tau as the signal in ruminants — findings that have reshaped animal management practices to improve pregnancy outcomes.
Those findings were published across 58 years, from 1968 to 2025, averaging 16.9 papers a year, with 46 of the 982 publications appearing in the last two years.
Bazer earned his bachelor’s in biology from Centenary College of Louisiana, his master’s in animal science from Louisiana State University and his doctorate in animal science from North Carolina State University. He was a member of the Department of Animal Science, University of Florida from October 1968 to 1992 before joining the Texas A&M Department of Animal Science on May 1, 1992.
In addition to maintaining highly productive research and teaching programs, Bazer served as director of the Center for Animal Biotechnology and Genomics, 1992–2001; director of the Institute of Biosciences and Technology, Texas A&M University and Texas A&M Health Sciences Center, Texas Medical Center, Houston, 1994-2001; the inaugural vice president for research and interim dean of the Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, January 1999 to December 2000, Texas A&M University System Health Science Center.
He also served as the associate vice chancellor and associate director of the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station, and executive associate dean of the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, January  2001 to December  2004; associate vice president for research, January 2005–December 2008; interim department head, Department of Veterinary Pathobiology, May-February 2010; and the World Class University Professor, Biomodulation Major, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea, March 1, 2010 to Aug. 31, 2013.
Bazer has had an outstanding career and significant impact on livestock fertility and reproduction, signified by his recognition as the recipient of the 2003 Wolf Prize in Agriculture for his interferon tau discovery as well as his discovery of other pregnancy-associated proteins. Additionally, he received the Alexander von Humboldt Award in Research in 2000. These are two of the highest awards in the field of agricultural sciences.
Bazer is also past recipient of the highest awards from each of his scientific societies: the Carl Hartman Award from the Society for the Study of Reproduction in 2004, the Morrison Award from the American Society of Animal Science in 2014, and the Marshall Medal from the Society for Reproduction and Fertility in 2025. He is also a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science and a recipient of the L.E. Casida Award for Graduate Education and the Animal Physiology and Endocrinology Award, both from the American Society of Animal Science. He earned awards for research, graduate education and service from the Society for the Study of Reproduction.

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Investigates Wells Fargo for Race-Based Lending
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Investigates Wells Fargo for Race-Based Lending
articles.content_orig:
Wells Fargo stock slipped as federal housing officials announced a probe into its mortgage programs aimed at boosting black and minority homeownership — with Housing Secretary Scott Turner blasting the bank’s race-based approach as “immoral” and “un-American.”
The investigation from the Department of Housing and Urban Development, which put Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf on notice in a Wednesday letter — marked the latest Trump administration effort to crack down on DEI programs and similar efforts.
“Even if Wells Fargo did not violate the law, its practice of dividing Americans based on race is immoral, unethical and un-American,” Turner said in a statement.
“Wells Fargo and all of its employees that engaged in race-based decision-making should be ashamed of themselves.”
News of the probe, first reported by the Wall Street Journal , sent the bank’s shares sliding 1.5% to $80.26.
The examination comes four years after Wells Fargo unveiled a $210 million push aimed at narrowing racial gaps in homeownership, including a Special Purpose Credit Program tied to mortgage refinancing.
Wells said in 2022 that the effort would begin by locating black borrowers in its servicing portfolio who might qualify for refinancing assistance.
It set aside $150 million for reduced rates and other refinancing costs, along with $60 million in grants intended to support homeowners of color.
The Biden-era policy came in the wake of a Bloomberg report finding Wells turned down half of all refinancing applications by black families in 2020.
Back in 2017, the bank committed to providing $60 billion in mortgages intended to help create at least 250,000 African-American homeowners by 2027.
But recent years have seen the feds’ stance on race-conscious lending shift dramatically.
HUD said in 2021 that Special Purpose Credit Programs complying with federal lending requirements generally did not violate the Fair Housing Act. A year later, it joined seven other agencies in encouraging creditors to explore them.
That position changed earlier this year.
A Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rule effective July 21 prohibits for-profit Special Purpose Credit Programs from using race, color, national origin or sex as an eligibility criterion.
HUD and six other agencies withdrew the earlier federal guidance the following month.
The policy reversal could complicate scrutiny of initiatives created under the previous framework, particularly if Wells contends that its actions were based on the government’s earlier guidance.
It was not immediately clear whether the HUD probe has advanced to a formal Fair Housing Act complaint.
The agency is looking at comparable efforts by other banks, potentially broadening the issue beyond Wells Fargo and forcing lenders to reassess programs that explicitly incorporate race into mortgage eligibility or pricing.
“The Fair Housing Act forbids racial discrimination in housing. It does not say: discriminate, so long as the discrimination is called a ‘special purpose credit program’ and justified as advancing ‘racial equity in homeownership,’” Assistant Secretary for Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity Craig Trainor said in a statement.
“No matter an institution’s size, wealth, or power, if there is reasonable cause to believe it has violated Americans’ civil rights, the Trump Administration will hold it to account.”
The Post has sought comment from HUD. A Wells Fargo spokesperson declined to comment.

articles.title_orig: USS Lincoln nearly home after more than 300 days at sea
articles.title_zh: USS Lincoln nearly home after more than 300 days at sea
articles.content_orig:
ABOARD THE USS LINCOLN IN THE PACIFIC OCEAN — After spending more than 300 days at sea, service members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln will finally return home this week.
The beleaguered aircraft carrier with about 7,500 personnel is scheduled to dock Thursday in San Diego, amid sharp criticism over its prolonged deployment in the Middle East.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth acknowledged to crewmembers on Wednesday that he was the “only thing standing between you and home” and that he had been the one “who signed that orders book twice” to extend the ship’s deployment.
On Wednesday, the evening before they were set to dock, the mood seemed far more jovial aboard the ship; sailors were chatting and laughing, some were running a 5K around a deck now free of aircraft. A band played in the setting sun.
Navy reports eight suicide attempts on USS Lincoln
The Lincoln left San Diego in November and was initially expected to return before the summer months. Its deployment was extended after the Iran war began in February. The ship was at sea without a port of call for 286 days until early September, when it docked in Thailand for a handful of days. By that point, family members of those on board had raised concerns about dwindling food supplies and low morale.
At least eight service members attempted suicide during the many months at sea, according to a letter sent last month to Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., by a top Navy official. The letter, obtained by NBC News , prompted concerns about the impact to mental health that such a lengthy deployment can have on service members. No deaths on the ship have been attributed to suicide.
Some family members of those on the ship said the extended time at sea was “wreaking havoc” on sailors’ mental health, and one described it as a “scene out of the ‘American Horror Story’” television show.
“Where he had been very positive, he started getting very dark,” one woman told NBC News about her son’s time at sea. Another parent said that she and her daughter, who is serving aboard the ship, grew increasingly frustrated as the Trump administration continued to push back the ship’s arrival date.
According to U.S. officials, a sailor assigned to the air wing on the Lincoln went overboard in early August and was quickly rescued and treated. That sailor was transferred off the ship for further medical care, the official told NBC News .
Navy officials initially said leadership had not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship.
According to the letter, suicide attempts occurred among crewmembers and sailors from the carrier air wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons.
Courtney Kube is a correspondent covering national security and the military for the NBC News Investigative Unit.
Alicia Victoria Lozano is a California-based reporter for NBC News focusing on climate change, wildfires and the changing politics of drug laws.
I am NBC News’ producer & off-air reporter covering stories about and related to the Defense Department around the world.

The four astronauts of NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 mission will return home from the International Space Station as early as Thursday, Oct. 8 , and you'll be able to follow the landing live here. NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway will return to Earth on the Crew Dragon Freedom alongside European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and Andrew Fedyaev of Roscosmos. Splashdown is set for 11:34 a.m. EDT (1534 GMT) , with live coverage ebginning at 10:20 a.m. EDT (1420 GMT) .
Landing Webcast! | Meet Crew-12 astronauts | SpaceX | Dragon | Falcon 9
The four astronauts of NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 mission to the International Space Station will return to Earth on Thursday, Oct. 8, at 11:34 a.m. EDT (1534 GMT) after a smooth undocking today.
The Crew-12 astronauts , commanded by NASA's Jessica Meir, undocked from the ISS today at 8:05 a.m. EDT (1205 GMT) to begin their two-day trip home. They launched to the ISS on Feb. 13 .
Tune in on Thursday for live landing coverage of the Crew-12 astronauts. In addition to Meir, the SpaceX Dragon will return to Earth with NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway, European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and Russian cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev.
After conducting standard leak checks and equalizing the pressure between their Dragon spacecraft and the International Space Station, SpaceX Crew-12 members Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway of NASA, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev entered their orbital home for the next eight months at 5:30 p.m. EST (2030 GMT).
Welcoming them aboard were their new Expedition 74 crewmates Chris Williams of NASA and Roscosmos cosmonauts Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergey Mikaev.
"We say welcome to Crew-12 today and we are happy they all arrived safe and sound," said Kud-Sverchkov, Expedition 74 commander, during a brief arrival ceremony. "We have been waiting for this moment for a very long time. So we are very happy and proud to work as a team here."
SpaceX's Crew Dragon "Freedom" has docked to the International Space Station! The capsule made first contact with the international docking adaptor on the space-facing side of the Harmony node at 3:15 p.m. EST (2015 GMT).
"Soft capture complete," radioed Jessica Meir, Crew-12 commander as the two spacecraft were flying south of South Africa.
SpaceX's Crew Dragon "Freedom" has passed its final pause on approach, called "Waypoint 2," at 20 meters from the International Space Station. Go for docking!
Crew Dragon "Freedom" has proceeded through Waypoint 1 at about 220 meters away from the International Space Station and is on its way to Waypoint 2 at 20 meters. Once at the second point, the Dragon will briefly pause its approach and then proceed directly to a docking with the zenith or space-facing side of the Harmony node.
Docking is expected at about 3:11 p.m. EST (2011 GMT).
Crew-12 aboard SpaceX's Crew Dragon "Freedom" have completed a midcourse burn that began at 2:00 p.m. EST (1900 GMT), refining their approach to the International Space Station.
The astronauts also passed a standard pressure check of their SpaceX suits after discovering a partially open zipper on one of pilot Jack Hathaway's gloves. This is the first mission where all four crew members are wearing upgraded suits with improved joint mobility and a streamlined zipper design to aid in their donning and doffing.
Freedom is scheduled to dock to the space-facing port of the station's Harmony node at about 3:11 p.m. EST (2011 GMT).
Crew-12 aboard the SpaceX Dragon "Freedom" initiated their approach to the International Space Station at 1:33 p.m. EST (1833 GMT).
Before the thruster burn, they got their first look at their destination and configured their audio to connect directly with NASA astronaut Chris Williams on the station.
"Station, Dragon on the Big Loop, how do you hear?" radioed Jessica Meir, Crew-12 commander.
"It is great to hear yur voice! I hear you loud and clear and see your from the Cupola," replied Williams.
"We've got you loud and clear, too, Chris," said Meir. "And we were incredibly excited to see the ISS through our docking port window before we even got started getting suited. Can't wait to see you buddy."
"You too. Really looking forward to seeing you guys here," he responded.
Good morning, Space Fans! Welcome to docking day for NASA's Crew-12 astronauts, and it will be a match made in the stars as the SpaceX Dragon capsule carrying the four astronauts arrives at the International Space Station later today just in time for Valentine's Day.
The Crew-12 Dragon capsule Freedom will dock at the ISS at about 3:15 p.m. EST (2015 GMT) to end a 34-hour trip that began with a predawn launch from Florida's Space Coast early Friday.
Space.com's Spaceflight Editor Mike Wall has a preview for your docking webcast needs here:
SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have a Valentine's Day date with the space station today. Watch the docking live
You'll be able to watch the docking live on Space.com, courtesy of NASA, via the video feed at the top of this page and here .
Our live coverage will begin at abtou 1:15 p.m. EST (1815 GMT), when NASA's live webcast begins.
Here's a schedule to follow for today (all times in EST, GMT-5):
After a successful and smooth launch, the Crew-12 astronauts are now in transit and will soon change out of their SpaceX launch and entry suits to settle to their eight-month mission to the International Space Station.
Read our full launch story by Josh Dinner from Cape Canaveral:
SpaceX launches Crew-12 astronauts to short-staffed International Space Station. 'We have left the Earth, but the Earth has not left us.'
The next major event will be their arrival and docking at the International Space Station. Docking is scheduled for Saturday, Feb. 14, at about 3:15 p.m. EST (2015 GMT). NASA's live coverage for that will begin at 1:15 p.m. EST (1815 GMT), and you will be able to see it live on this page.
It will be a Valentine's Day arrival for the new ISS crew.
NASA will hold a post launch press conference at 6:45 a.m. EST (1145 GMT). You can watch that live here:
With that, we'll be pausing our updates until the next major event and docking. Thanks so much for joining us on the Crew-12 launch!
The Crew-12 astronauts have unveiled their zero-gravity indicator and it is truly a one-of-a-kind bobble.
Crew-12 commander Jessica Meir announced that crew chose a handmade crocheted model of Earth with four connected satellites, each representing one of the crew. The Gaia Earth model has a small moon connected to it representing Meir and bananas represetning mission specialist Sophie Adenot, for example. It was made by Meir's childhood best friend, as well as Crew-12 pilot Jack Hathaway's daughter.
The Crew-12 astronauts are now flying free on their way to the International Space Station, a journey that will take about 34 hours.
As they did just before launch, the four astronauts shared a message of inspiration and hope after reaching orbit.
"We're reminded that we're all connected," one of the four astronauts said. "Take care of one another and keep reaching higher. That's how human beings soar and how we make each other proud."
The nose cone covering the Dragon capsule's docking port has opened for flight.

President Donald Trump says he is seeking more answers about the death of a Russian worker from plague at a Siberian lab , a case that has ignited public health concerns worldwide.
During an Oval Office event Wednesday, the president was asked by Fox News if the death was the result of “a bioweapon.”
“Well, we don't think so,” Trump said. “We’re gonna find out soon enough, but we don’t think so, and if you listen to them, it's under control.”
“We've heard this before, a couple of years ago during your first term,” Fox reporter Peter Doocy then asked. “Are you getting the same vibe right now from Russia that you got from China at the start of Covid?”
“Well China didn’t say much, and Russia's not saying much either, but they do say they have it very much under control,” Trump said. He added that he plans to call Russian President Vladimir Putin later in the day Wednesday, noting it is Putin’s birthday.
Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old worker at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute in Siberia , died Friday from pneumonia of an unknown cause. Authorities subsequently quarantined about 200 people.
Most have since been released, and Russian officials said no plague cases had been detected among Shipilova’s contacts. Officials also said she had been vaccinated and was “immune to ​the dangerous infections with which she worked,” adding there was no risk of an epidemic.
Global health officials have closely monitored the case and called for greater transparency, citing concerns about parallels to the early days of the Covid pandemic, which began with a small number of fatal respiratory illnesses.
World Health Organization chief Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Wednesday that a “full risk assessment” has not yet been possible.
He added that “timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”
U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz said the agency is prepared to screen travelers, though she described the risk to Americans as very low.
The U.S. State Department also warned Moscow this week that its failure to disclose details about Shipilova’s death violated international health obligations, The Wall Street Journal reported.
“Plague infections occur regularly with a few hundred cases a year globally,” Paul Hunter, a professor of medicine at the University of East Anglia, previously told The Independent .
“There are different forms of the disease, bubonic and septicaemic are spread by flea bites from close contact with infected animals,” Hunter said. “Pneumonic plague is spread person to person through respiratory droplets.”

articles.title_orig: World Girls Hockey Weekend comes to Carbondale
articles.title_zh: World Girls Hockey Weekend comes to Carbondale
articles.content_orig:
psullivan@postindependent.com
For the first time, World Girls Hockey Weekend is coming to the Roaring Fork Valley, giving girls and women a chance to hit the ice in Carbondale with no registration, fees or equipment required.
Colorado Extreme, a nonprofit dedicated to expanding hockey access in the Roaring Fork Valley, will host the free event at 5 p.m. Oct. 17 at the Steadman Philippon Outdoor Arena in Carbondale.
The event invites women of all ages in the Roaring Fork Valley, whether a seasoned skater or completely new to the sport, to come together and celebrate women’s hockey.
Colorado Extreme will provide free equipment to those who need it. Participants can bring a stick and play with friends, practice their skills or simply learn how to skate.
In addition to the free skate, Colorado Extreme will host a watch party with pizza for professional women’s hockey games.
No registration is required for the event.
World Girls Hockey Weekend is a global event that began in 2011. This year marks the first time the event has come to the Roaring Fork Valley as Colorado Extreme continues its mission to expand hockey opportunities for girls in the region.
“The biggest thing is just we’re trying to grow the girls’ game,” said Maddy Moses, a high-performance coach at Colorado Extreme.
Moses grew up playing hockey on the East Coast, where she said girls-only hockey programs were much more common.
“I grew up on the East Coast, so girls’ hockey is extremely prominent, and there’s so many opportunities,” Moses said. “That’s just not the case out west, and I feel like Colorado is getting on board with that finally, and giving girls opportunities to learn to play and to skate and to do it together, rather than just being a handful of girls on a boys’ team.”
Colorado Extreme has made accessibility a central part of its efforts to introduce more girls to the sport.
“It’s a really great place for young athletes that haven’t maybe experienced the sport to come to specifically Colorado Extreme and just try it,” Moses said. “I mean, it’s pretty unheard of that you go somewhere and you get completely free equipment and you get to get on the ice and you get to try it on multiple occasions.”
That same approach will carry into World Girls Hockey Weekend.
“No registration, no fees, nothing. Just show up. If you have gear, bring it. If you don’t have gear, we can get you some gear and get you out on the ice,” Moses said.

articles.content_orig:
SINGAPORE , Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TOKEN2049 , the world's largest crypto conference, today announced its expansion into the United States with the launch of TOKEN2049 New York. The inaugural US edition will take place on 16-17 June 2027, with 15,000 attendees expected from around the world.
The announcement was made at TOKEN2049 Singapore ahead of Eric Trump and Zach Witkoff's highly anticipated main stage session.
The launch establishes New York as TOKEN2049's third flagship and a permanent fixture on its annual event circuit alongside Singapore and Dubai , extending its presence across Asia, the Middle East and North America. It brings the world's largest crypto conference to the heart of global capital markets and creates a major new US meeting point for the international digital asset industry.
Alex Fiskum, Co-Founder of TOKEN2049 said: " Bringing TOKEN2049 to the US has been a long time coming. Our attendees and partners have been asking us to make it happen, and we've been waiting for the right moment and the right setting. Everything has now come together in New York. We're incredibly excited to bring the full TOKEN2049 experience our community knows and loves to the US. New York will be a permanent part of our annual calendar alongside Dubai and Singapore. We have an exciting year ahead."
Beyond the two-day conference, TOKEN2049 Week will take over New York with a citywide programme of events and experiences.
Tickets for TOKEN2049 New York are now on sale for US$599.
Alex Fiskum, Co-Founder of TOKEN2049, is available for interview.

articles.title_orig: The Richest Man in the World Needs More Money
articles.title_zh: The Richest Man in the World Needs More Money
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here.
Apparently, Elon Musk's SpaceX, valued at $2.2 trillion and led by a CEO worth $1 trillion, needs even more money.
The Financial Times reported late Tuesday that the rocket company is seeking $40 billion to buy more chips from its longtime partner and AI confidant, Nvidia.
"We've decided to build exclusively on Nvidia because we think the Vera Rubin architecture is the best architecture," Musk said in August.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Musk have a history of praising each other. On the BG2 Pod in October 2024, Huang called Musk the "ultimate GPU."
"He has a great sense of urgency and a real desire to build it. When will comes together with skill, unbelievable things can happen," he added.
One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.
SpaceX is seeking $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt, or corporate bonds rated BBB- or Baa3 and above, the safer tier of company debt. With the company rated Baa1 by Moody's and BBB by S&P Global Ratings, Apollo has plenty of options as it leads the financing and helps sell the debt to everyone from pension funds and life insurers to regulated financial institutions.
Wall Street didn't love the prospect of the company more than doubling its debt load, which stands at about $30 billion, according to companiesmarketcap.com . Shares of SpaceX (SPCX) are down 2.4% today. Its total debt-to-equity ratio is 0.31x, below the sector average. Boeing sits at the extreme, with a 10.0x D/E ratio, while Rocket Lab (RKLB) is around 0.61x.
Nvidia, on the other hand, got plenty of affection from Wall Street. News that Musk planned to buy exclusively from the AI-chip company sent its stock to another all-time high of almost $240 before it turned lower near the close. Nvidia is trading at $236 today.
But not everyone is as bullish on Elon's debt, the FT reports. Investors previously approached by the company received only a "short two-page deal memo" with "pictures of outer space" and "an arrow pointing out that the company was going to build data centers 'somewhere in the universe.'"
Given that the same company approved Musk's compensation package on the condition that he build a Mars colony with a permanent population of at least 1 million, and no deadline, this checks out.

articles.title_orig: Georgia vs. Alabama weather tracker: SEC officials expect game to be played on time despite messy forecast
articles.title_zh: Georgia vs. Alabama weather tracker: SEC officials expect game to be played on time despite messy forecast
articles.content_orig:
It seems like the entire world will be descending upon Tuscaloosa this weekend, including Tropical Storm Isaias. The storm -- which is expected to bring heavy rains and possible flooding -- could impact this weekend's marquee showdown between No. 2 Georgia and No. 6 Alabama .
Despite speculation that the storm could move the game to a different day or location, the Crimson Tide and Bulldogs plan on playing in Bryant-Denny Stadium this Saturday, CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz reports. It's possible the kickoff time could shift, but the current plan is to play as scheduled.
Earlier this week, an SEC spokesperson told CBS Sports that the conference is "keeping an eye on forecasts and staying in communication with schools with games that could be impacted by weather."
The storm is expected to bring locally heavy rain, potential flooding and high winds throughout the Southeast this weekend, although the exact path and timing is unknown. With that in mind, Alabama released a statement on Tuesday saying that there are currently "no plans to alter the contest."
As things stand at the moment, the forecast is calling for a good deal of rain and wind in Tuscaloosa on Saturday, but the conditions could be playable.
During their SEC teleconference, Alabama coach Kalen DeBoer and Georgia coach Kirby Smart both addressed the possibility of Tropical Storm Isaias affecting the game.
Smart said it's hard to simulate tropical storm conditions in practice. Neither Georgia nor Alabama can import a special effects department from Hollywood to create a monsoon on the practice field, but players can learn from how teams have managed messy conditions in the past.
"It's uncertainty. [It's] beyond my control," Smart said, per 247Sports . "We as coaches game plan for multiple situations - weather conditions - when they're there. We had that same prep last week with the threat of those things. Doesn't change a lot about practice. You have to practice good on good. You've got to practice for the long term of the season, not just for one week.
"You can't really practice conditions. You can't simulate them, so you're much better off to educate, learn from the past of other people who have played in them, and prepare your team to play and not make it about that."
DeBoer shared Smart's sentiment, saying there's little that can be done other than preparing as usual. The Crimson Tide will implement wet-ball drills for the second week in a row after prepping for rainy conditions ahead of last weekend's win over Mississippi State .
"Depends on the level of weather you get, it would affect what happens," DeBoer said, according to 247Sports . "It's just -- that's not my area of expertise. I'm just getting our football team ready. It hasn't affected us much, other than we're doing wet ball drills and get wet ball involved in some of our team reps, just like we did last week at times, preparing for the rain a week ago. I'm not really involved in too much."

articles.title_orig: China’s Export Controls on Japan: Salami-Slicing or Strategic Signalling?
articles.title_zh: China’s Export Controls on Japan: Salami-Slicing or Strategic Signalling?
articles.content_orig:
Peace and Security in Northeast Asia
Image: Keitma / Shutterstock
In today’s international political economy, interstate rivalry and diplomatic friction are increasingly intertwined with economic interdependence. Trade restrictions and export controls can provide governments with powerful instruments of strategic influence, particularly when supply chains depend heavily on a limited number of countries. China’s tightening of export controls affecting Japan illustrates this broader transformation. One possible interpretation is that Beijing is employing a form of’ ‘salami-slicing‘: gradually expanding restrictions rather than immediately imposing a comprehensive embargo, thereby maintaining pressure while preserving room for further escalation. However, other explanations, including political retaliation and strategic signalling, must also be considered.
The reasons behind China’s export controls on Japan are closely connected to the deterioration of bilateral relations, particularly over Taiwan and Japan’s evolving security policy. In November 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made remarks concerning a possible Taiwan contingency, which Beijing strongly criticized. China subsequently linked its tightening of trade and export controls to what it described as Japan’s interference in the Taiwan issue. On January 6, 2026, China announced tighter controls on dual-use exports to Japan, explicitly citing remarks by Japanese leadership concerning possible armed intervention in the Taiwan Strait as part of the rationale.
This suggests that the measures can also be understood as political signalling or retaliation. Rather than simply seeking to impose economic damage, Beijing may be attempting to demonstrate that actions it regards as crossing sensitive security thresholds can generate tangible economic consequences. The export controls could therefore serve two purposes simultaneously: responding to Japanese policies while signalling that deeper Japanese involvement in a Taiwan contingency could carry additional economic costs.
Another possible interpretation is the logic sometimes associated with the Chinese expression “kill the chicken to scare the monkey”: imposing costs on a particular target in order to send a broader warning. By targeting selected Japanese companies and organizations rather than immediately restricting Japanese trade as a whole, China can demonstrate its ability to impose economic pressure while avoiding the disruption associated with a comprehensive embargo. This interpretation is particularly relevant because several of the entities targeted by recent measures are connected to Japan’s defence and security sectors.
China has progressively expanded such measures. On February 24, 2026, Beijing placed 20 Japanese entities on an export-control list and another 20 on a watch list. The entities included companies and organizations involved in areas such as aerospace, defence, maritime systems and advanced technology. On June 29, China added another 20 Japanese entities to its export-control list and 20 more to its watch list. Beijing presented these measures as necessary to protect national security and prevent activities that could contribute to enhancing Japan’s military capabilities.
The pattern nevertheless contains characteristics associated with salami-slicing. Rather than adopting a single comprehensive embargo, China has introduced and expanded restrictions in stages. This approach allows Beijing to calibrate the degree of pressure according to developments in the bilateral relationship while retaining additional options for future escalation. At the same time, gradual escalation does not by itself demonstrate that salami-slicing is the underlying strategy. The pattern may simply reflect Beijing’s responses to successive developments in Japan–China relations.
This distinction is important because economic restrictions can have effects beyond the products or companies directly targeted. Japan remains closely connected to China through manufacturing and supply chains involving rare earths, critical minerals, machinery, electronics, and other industrial inputs. China’s restrictions on rare earths have already created uncertainty for Japanese industries. Reuters reported in June 2026 that exports of several heavy rare earths to Japan remained severely constrained amid the diplomatic dispute. Such restrictions demonstrate how economic measures can affect industries that are highly dependent on Chinese supplies.
The strategic significance therefore lies not only in the immediate economic impact of individual restrictions but also in the uncertainty they generate. Companies may become more cautious about relying on Chinese suppliers if they believe future licensing decisions could be influenced by diplomatic developments. Even where an export is not formally prohibited, the possibility of tighter screening, delayed approvals or additional restrictions can encourage firms to diversify their supply chains. Economic pressure can thus emerge not only through formal restrictions but also through changing expectations about future access to critical inputs.
For Japan, the challenge is consequently broader than responding to individual Chinese measures. Tokyo must determine whether each restriction represents a temporary diplomatic response, an attempt to influence Japanese security policy, or part of a longer-term strategy to exploit economic dependence. These explanations are not necessarily mutually exclusive. Political retaliation can occur alongside strategic signalling, while incremental implementation can simultaneously produce characteristics associated with salami-slicing.
China’s export controls on Japan should therefore not be reduced to a single strategic concept. ‘Salami-slicing’ provides one useful framework for understanding the gradual expansion of economic pressure, but retaliation over Taiwan-related statements, strategic signalling, and China’s broader national-security approach to export controls offer alternative and potentially complementary explanations. The measures may represent not one fixed strategy but the interaction of several objectives.
For Japan, the central issue is how to manage the intersection of diplomacy, national security, and economic interdependence. Strengthening supply-chain resilience, diversifying critical sources of supply, improving early-warning capabilities, and maintaining channels of dialogue with China will become increasingly important. As economic interdependence becomes more deeply integrated into strategic competition, understanding both the visible restrictions and the political signals behind them will be essential to Japan’s economic security.

articles.title_orig: Trump considers ‘terminating’ campaign advisers after Balkans trip
articles.title_zh: Trump considers ‘terminating’ campaign advisers after Balkans trip
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday distanced himself from two of his top political advisers — less than 30 days before the midterm elections — writing that if their outside work presents a conflict, “I will terminate them, immediately!”
Trump’s warning came after The New York Times published a report detailing how James Blair, one of the president’s former deputy chiefs of staff who now leads his outside political operation, and Chris LaCivita, Trump’s 2024 co-campaign manager, traveled to the Balkans last week for paid work on behalf of a pro-Russian government.
Trump was unaware that the two men had traveled to the Balkans – or that the pro-Russian government was among their clientele – until he was briefed on the impending New York Times piece, sources familiar with the situation told CNN. The president then made a series of phone calls Tuesday night asking his allies what their take on the story was, the sources said.
One source said Trump appeared annoyed, and another veteran Republican who is in touch with the president told CNN that Trump was “pissed” by the report – particularly at the revelation that the two advisers had been abroad in the home stretch of the midterm campaign, profiting off their association with him.
“Tone deaf,” the veteran Republican said of the advisers’ conduct.
But another source said Trump was simply seeking a range of opinions on what had been reported.
Trump – who has been actively campaigning for Republicans ahead of November’s midterms – ultimately decided he wanted to respond to the story, two of the sources told CNN. So on Wednesday, one of the sources said, he dictated a Truth Social post to aide Natalie Harp while in the Oval Office, commenting to those in the room that both Blair and LaCivita are outside consultants and are allowed to have other clients. One source said that at that moment, he did not seem irked.
“Chris LaCivita and James Blair are outside consultants. They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them,” Trump posted.
“I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” Trump wrote.
The president continued distancing himself from the two advisers and downplayed any conflict of interest later Wednesday. “They don’t have a conflict because they’re independent people,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
“I assume they have a lot of clients,” he went on. “So I don’t know their contract. If I thought they had a conflict … I would terminate.”
He also noted that neither currently works in the White House.
“Well they’re allowed to do that,” Trump told CNN. “They have a lot of clients and it’s okay. I’m a client over there, they have a consulting firm I guess, separately, as all people in Washington do. That’s pretty common.”
According to the Times, Blair and LaCivita traveled to Republika Srpska, a territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina, ahead of elections there on Sunday. The trip came as polls show Republicans are facing severe electoral challenges in the United States.
Blair and LaCivita “were paid hundreds of thousands of dollars each through a Washington-based law firm that was retained by Republika Srpska’s government to provide counsel on voting issues,” the Times reported.
They said the work was for the government and not the nationalist party that controls it, though they are essentially one and the same.
Blair currently leads Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., and has been tasked with heading up the president’s midterm elections strategy. LaCivita is a senior adviser at MAGA Inc.
The group has been spending tens of millions of dollars trying to bolster Republican candidates ahead of the midterms, including some in reliably red territory who now appear vulnerable.
This story has been updated with additional developments.
CNN’s Kevin Liptak contributed to this report.

The end could be nigh for the iconic OP-1 according to a Highsnobiety interview.
Teenage Engineering founder and CEO Jesper Kouthoofd told Highsnobiety that it plans to stop making synths. And yes, that includes the iconic OP-1, which put the company on the map. TE isn’t just a music gear maker; it’s also a sought-after design firm. It’s collaborated with Ikea , Nothing , and Playdate , among others . But almost everything the company makes itself — the OP-1 , the OP-XY , EP-133 , TP-7 , et cetera — is music or audio-focused. Which makes the supposed decision to abandon the market all the more confusing.
Here’s the relevant quote from Highsnobiety :
Kouthoofd tells me that, as part of a reorganization last fall, he announced to his team he is planning to stop making synthesizers altogether. The OP-1 is no exception. Launched in 2011, it put Teenage Engineering on the map and has been central to its success ever since.
“Everyone was like, ‘What are you talking about?’ But I’ve come to the conclusion that, for us, the products aren’t the business,” Kouthoofd says. “We can be so much more than that.”
Teenage Engineering did not immediately return a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: Hispanic Heritage Month: Israel Balderas helps students find their passion in a world ‘out of control’
articles.title_zh: Hispanic Heritage Month: Israel Balderas helps students find their passion in a world ‘out of control’
articles.content_orig:
A self-described “Texan American with a Mexican heart,” Assistant Professor of Journalism Israel Balderas says at the center of his sense of belonging at Elon are his students.
Israel Balderas is no stranger to the public eye. The First Amendment attorney and former television journalist regularly speaks with media outlets about current events, an extension of the work he does as an assistant professor of journalism at Elon University.
“As an academic, my relationship is going out in the name of Elon, even though I speak for myself,” said Balderas. “I’m always saying, ‘Here at Elon, we don’t make small plans. We’re always thinking bigger, and because we are a national school, what would help us to continue to be a national school?’ To me, my responsibility as an academic is to get my name out there.”
For Balderas, that work is closely connected to the sense of belonging he has found at Elon and the university’s teacher-scholar-mentor model. At the center of it all are his students.
“When my students leave, and the class is over, I say, ‘Love you. Mean it.’ And we throw the word love around a lot,” Balderas said. “But, to me, as a teacher, I think love from a teacher to a student is this idea, and it’s my ‘why.’ My ‘why’ is that I’m passionate about teaching students how to find their passion in a world that is out of control.”
Balderas began his journalism career as a freelance reporter and producer for several outlets in Washington, D.C. His coverage of the 2000 presidential election helped spur an interest in legal studies, as did a friendly competition with his sister over who could earn the higher score on the LSAT.
Growing up in a single-parent Hispanic household, Balderas said education was “non-negotiable.” He went on to earn his Juris Doctor from the Catholic University of America while working as a producer at FOX News Channel.
In the years that followed, Balderas worked for television stations across Florida, North Carolina and Texas. His work earned multiple industry accolades, including an Emmy for Best Continuing Coverage and recognition from the Radio Television Digital News Association of the Carolinas as best TV news anchor.
My ‘why’ is that I’m passionate about teaching students how to find their passion in a world that is out of control.
-Israel Balderas, assistant professor of journalism
Alongside his journalism career, Balderas took on legal work for the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law, We The Action and the Society of Professional Journalists. His pro bono work included representing migrant children at the U.S.-Mexico border and helping nonprofits navigate financial aid during the COVID-19 pandemic.
In 2017, Balderas left television news to spend more time with his family and transitioned to higher education, first teaching at a university in West Palm Beach, Florida, before joining Elon’s faculty in 2021.
“I love the mission of Elon University,” Balderas said. “The mission of Elon is that it ‘embraces its founder’s vision of an academic community that transforms mind, body, and spirit and encourages freedom of thought and liberty of conscience.’ And I said during my interview, that’s what a First Amendment professor teaches. That’s it.”
Journalism major Lily Molina ’27 took Balderas’ Media Law & Ethics course and says having a Latino professor in the journalism department made her feel welcomed as an aspiring Latina journalist.
“ I am really passionate about covering stories centered around my community, and Balderas has supported me in doing that. It’s comforting to have someone who I can speak Spanish to and not feel judged,” she said. “This is just one of the reasons why having diversity within departments is so important.”
A self-described “Texan American with a Mexican heart,” Balderas views Hispanic Heritage Month through the lens of the cultures that have shaped the United States.
“It’s about celebrating many cultures who have been able to adapt their cultures to this idea of ‘American citizen,’” he said. “What I love about Hispanic Heritage Month is that we get to show off the beauty of our diversity in a society that is diverse.”
Balderas describes that blending of cultures as a “stew,” one he sees reflected regularly on Elon’s campus. He points to El Centro, a space within the Center for Race, Ethnicity and Diversity Education that celebrates Latine and Hispanic cultures while sharing them with the broader Elon community.
“Every time I go to El Centro, there are kids from all over, and they’re all happy, and they’re ready to tell us about their abuelita (grandmother), they’re ready to tell us about their family,” Balderas said. “They’re ready to tell us about the history of their country. And in sharing all that, we get to build community together.”
As part of Hispanic Heritage Month, Elon University is sharing stories that celebrate the contributions, identities and experiences of students, faculty and staff. This month recognizes the rich histories and cultures of Hispanic and Latine communities, while also honoring the ways these traditions connect with and inspire people of all backgrounds. This month provides a special opportunity to honor Hispanic and Latine heritage, but it also serves as an invitation for all members of the university to engage, learn and celebrate together.

articles.title_orig: World of Warcraft: Forever- The Future of Skyborne Visual Updates
articles.title_zh: World of Warcraft: Forever- The Future of Skyborne Visual Updates
articles.content_orig:
The World of Warcraft development team began our journey into World of Warcraft: Forever with ambitions that grew and evolved over time. Our aim has always been to uphold the original WoW era aesthetic, while giving players more choice in how they experience Azeroth.
Over the course of development, we have been aligning on the right range of fidelity and what feels like it belongs in the WoW: Forever world and what does not. The team has learned much in the process, and that will continue to strengthen more with future content.
Along the way, there were some ideas the team wanted to explore that ultimately didn’t quite meet the consistency and cohesion we are aiming for. To align with our goals better, we are taking aim at updating some of those visuals for the future. Here is one example of how we are revisiting the High Definition (HD) Skyborne Druid forms.
We removed a bit of the softness, added more detailed fur textures, and adjusted the color saturation. The Skyborne are from an exotic environment, and their Druid forms reflect that, but we don't want that to be dissonant with the visual language of other creatures in the world.
In choosing to offer an SD or HD toggle for player characters, we focused on the pre-existing races from original World of Warcraft since many people have an attachment to those models. However, we have heard feedback that the HD Skyborne can be jarring by contrast when placed in the same world as the SD models and world, and we agree.
So, for those of us that prefer the look of SD models and want more choice, Skyborne player characters (and yes SD Druid forms) are in development and arriving early 2027. We look forward to sharing more information closer to that date. For now, here is an early work in progress image.
This is just the start of our journey, and the whole team is thrilled with the reception for World of Warcraft: Forever . As we continue refining this vision together, we look forward to what lies ahead—for the Horde! For the Alliance! Forever!

articles.title_orig: China’s AI startups can match the U.S.’s models. They can’t yet match the U.S.’s money
articles.title_zh: China’s AI startups can match the U.S.’s models. They can’t yet match the U.S.’s money
articles.content_orig:
Alvin Yap is the chief executive officer for Asia at EquitiesFirst
By many measures, China is fast catching up with the U.S. in AI development. Moonshot’s Kimi K3—the world’s largest open-weight model—has approached the performance of America’s frontier systems. Analysts estimate the best Chinese models are now just four months behind the most sophisticated releases from OpenAI and Anthropic, compared to seven months at the start of the year.
Chinese models have gone from 1.2% of token traffic (a common way to calculate AI usage) in 2024 to more than half of the total by the summer of 2026.
But the biggest threat to that next wave is not technology. It’s money. Between 2023 and 2026, venture funding into U.S. AI companies topped $380 billion; China’s start-ups received barely a tenth of that figure, according to Boston Consulting Group.
In the past, Chinese entrepreneurs looked to state guidance funds and venture capital backing, but policy-driven funds are known to prioritize later-stage startups while early-stage venture capital is only just recovering from a three-year fundraising drought .
There are three reasons why broader funding channels should be a priority for entrepreneurs in the AI economy.
First, inflation is taking hold inside the AI economy. CXMT, for example, has been raising memory prices for months and held firm even when Huawei, one of its largest customers, demanded relief .
The war for AI talent is just as fierce: postings for AI-related roles surged roughly twelvefold year-on-year in early 2026. Algorithm engineers specializing in large language models command some of the highest pay packages of any technical role in China.
Founders must also outcompete deep-pocketed former employers and U.S. rivals. More than half of studies presented at the world’s top AI conference had lead authors based in China. China’s AI talent is known to be in demand worldwide.
Second, external funding is scarce. Venture investment in China totaled just $20 billion in the first quarter of 2026, against $267 billion in the U.S. China has raised impressive sums this year—assets under management for newly registered VC funds hit 154 billion yuan ($22.8 billion) in the first five monthes, already exceeding last year’s total—but that is still far below what US venture capital regularly deploys.
Meanwhile, China’s state banks, although directed to prioritize technology lending, are absorbing rising non-performing loans elsewhere on their books, which could lead to weaker overall credit supply.
Third, profitability will take a while to achieve. Chinese enterprise software firms primarily sell into the domestic market , which limits their revenue base. U.S. rivals have a head start: a global customer base, stronger brand recognition, and R&D budgets deep enough to fund everything from enterprise-grade cybersecurity to polished customer experience design.
To be sure, the next generation of AI ventures may not need vast amounts of capital to build applications on top of existing models or fill the gaps in the tech value chain.  Enterprise customers can also provide essential development funding.
Entrepreneurs must nevertheless cope without the kind of financial support that is available for the AI sector in the U.S. Closing the performance gap increasingly depends on bulking up in-house computing capacity—yet China’s AI infrastructure spending remains a fraction of what is being spent in the U.S.
This is where access to Hong Kong’s finance industry will play a growing role. Its capital markets remain one of the few channels still capable of moving global capital toward Chinese enterprise at scale. More than 430 applicants are in the IPO pipeline in the second half of 2026.
The IPO pipeline, however, tells its own story. Many Chinese technology startups are choosing to list earlier than the previous generation of companies did because they lack an alternative.
Compare that with the U.S., where the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic have grown to an enormous scale by raising private capital. OpenAI closed a round of more than $100 billion earlier this year, while Anthropic raised $65 billion in May. China’s leading model developers, Zhipu AI and MiniMax, beat OpenAI and Anthropic to the public markets—but their Hong Kong IPOs in January raised just $558 million and $620 million respectively, despite heavy over-subscription.
Private credit is another route. Asia-Pacific private credit assets are projected to grow from $59 billion in 2024 to $92 billion by 2027, with China accounting for a fifth of the region’s activity . However, these loan providers tend to prioritize bigger or established companies.
It is already clear that the AI sector, unlike the software sector, will not be dominated by U.S. firms alone. China’s startups have learned the lessons of the previous decade, commanding global respect and winning a growing customer base. The country’s open-weight strategy has given its leading AI companies a cost advantage – even Silicon Valley leaders acknowledge it.
For China’s latest generation of AI entrepreneurs, venture capital and bank loans—the two main sources of start-up funding – may not be enough in the coming years. Keeping pace in the AI race will require using every asset and every channel available. It may mean a public listing earlier than they would have preferred, exploring the growing private credit ecosystem, revenue sharing with customers or leveraging the equity they hold as collateral.
The entrepreneurs involved in the next wave of China’s AI development will need to be creative with funding to maintain their competitive edge at a time when overseas rivals are spending 10 times as much.

articles.title_orig: A potential hurricane is moving toward the Gulf Coast. Could it affect Alabama-Georgia football?
articles.title_zh: A potential hurricane is moving toward the Gulf Coast. Could it affect Alabama-Georgia football?
articles.content_orig:
Alabama said on Wednesday evening that its game against Georgia was set to proceed as scheduled.
A weather system in the Gulf of Mexico has become Tropical Storm Isaias , and will likely be upgraded to a hurricane in the coming days. The track of the storm is currently aimed east of Texas and potentially toward the Gulf Coast of Mississippi and Alabama with potential landfall later in the week.
That means the No. 6 Crimson Tide's home game in Tuscaloosa against the No. 2 Bulldogs on Saturday could be plagued by lots and lots of rain.
"Alabama athletics continues to closely monitor the weather forecast ahead of Saturday's football game, with the safety and well-being of the student-athletes, coaches, staff and fans as our highest priority," the school said in a statement on Wednesday night . "We remain in close communication with the National Weather Service, the Southeastern Conference office and the University of Georgia as we observe conditions.
"At this time, kickoff remains scheduled for 6:30 p.m. CT Saturday. We continue to encourage fans to rely on official Alabama athletics and SEC channels for the latest information regarding Saturday's game."
Alabama's statement was similar to one the school put out on Tuesday night. Al.com published a story on Tuesday interviewing meteorologist James Spann, the most widely respected weather voice in the state.
"We've got potential for a hurricane making landfall in Mobile Bay," Spann told the site. "The Alabama-Georgia game, a presidential visit, 'College GameDay.' You got the big [Zach Bryan] concert at Auburn. This is the National Shrimp Festival at Gulf Shores this weekend, which is huge. I mean you could not … it's gonna be a nightmare."
Yes, Spann is referring to President Donald Trump. The president is expected to be in attendance for the game. It's the second SEC game he's attended in three weeks. He was at Texas' win over Tennessee in Week 4. ESPN's pregame show was also in Knoxville for that game.
When asked by reporters on Wednesday about his plans for the game, Trump said that a potential hurricane could impact his attendance before saying he was unaware that there was a potential hurricane.
"I love Alabama, I gotta go to a game, it would be awfully hard — look, I mean if there's an emergency, if there's a hurricane, I don't want to do anything to take the focus of all of the great people who work on those things, you know they have some tremendously great people, I don't want to take the focus," Trump said. "So we'll have to see, I hadn't heard about a hurricane. A hurricane is going in the vicinity of Alabama? That's not good. Certainly, I'm going to let the hurricane determine — I want people to be safe, that's all."
Saturday's game is the only matchup of top-10 teams and one of just two matchups between teams in the AP Top 25 in Week 6.

articles.title_orig: Cornell students hold sit-in over alleged 2024 fraternity assault
articles.title_zh: Cornell students hold sit-in over alleged 2024 fraternity assault
articles.content_orig:
ITHACA, N.Y. — Cornell University students began a seven-hour sit-in Wednesday in solidarity with Jane Doe, the woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted by members of the Chi Phi fraternity nearly two years ago.
“Seven hours for the seven hours she endured. Seven hours of solidarity. Seven hours demanding change,” a coalition of Cornell student groups said in a post on Instagram ahead of the demonstration.
Roughly 80 students had gathered inside a campus dining hall named for Pulitzer Prize-winning author Toni Morrison by around 3 p.m. Outside the building, students displayed posters bearing slogans such as “Justice for Jane Doe” and “Stop Protecting Rapists.”
The organizers said the sit-in is part of “Zero Day,” an “economic blackout calling on students to disrupt business as usual by not attending class or spending on campus.”
The protest illustrates the tense mood on the Ivy League campus following Jane Doe’s allegations that she was sexually assaulted and plied with drugs Oct. 19-20, 2024. She filed a civil lawsuit against the university and seven fraternity members last month, leading to renewed national attention on sexual misconduct and collegiate Greek life.
Three of the accused men have publicly denied the allegations through attorneys.
The sit-in comes two days after Cornell faculty members introduced a resolution calling for a no-confidence vote in the university administration over its handling of the alleged assault at the Chi Phi fraternity house. The resolution was submitted to the University Faculty Committee on Monday night, according to a copy obtained by NBC News.
Cornell has drawn intense scrutiny over how it responded to Jane Doe’s allegations in November 2024, and Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has been criticized for declining to charge the accused. The university and the district attorney have each defended their original 2024 probes.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul effectively replaced Van Houten as lead investigator last week, appointing state Attorney General Letitia James to oversee the case. Cornell and Van Houten have publicly welcomed James’ involvement. “I trust that she will examine the facts and apply the law,” Van Houten said in a statement on Friday.
Wednesday’s sit-in was announced on Instagram by a group of campus organizations, including Black Students United, Cornell NAACP, Mecha de Cornell, Planned Parenthood Generation Action at Cornell, Students for a Democratic Cornell and a student-run chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union.
“The sit-in will be a space for students to share their support for survivors of sexual violence in myriad ways, including the share of resources and teach-ins,” the student groups said on Instagram.
Daniel Arkin is a senior reporter at NBC News.
Adam Reiss is a reporter and producer for NBC and MSNBC.
